exemplars.why_excellent: The single best package in the repo (207.9 KB, 799 index chunks, 454 distinct Salesforce API identifiers). Three things make it uncopyable: (1) references/error-codes.md is a decoder ring of ~60 StatusCode values organised by failure category, each with an investigation path rather than a definition; (2) it has explicit 'What errors cannot tell you' and 'Errors that look scary but are often benign' sections — it teaches the platform's SILENCES, which no doc page does; (3) it is the only package that exceeds the retrieval-footprint ceiling and it defends itself against that by splitting into 12 topic-scoped reference files plus an anti-pattern that forbids preloading them. It also cites a real managed-package field name (`TracRTC__Realtime_Clean_Error_Message__c`) as evidence of error-fidelity loss — a detail that can only come from having read a real org's logs.
exemplars.quoted_example: `cannot merge with entity that is not accessible: []`: merge failed because a related record ... is outside the user's visibility. **Empty brackets are deliberate**: Salesforce refuses to name the blocking record to prevent information disclosure. The log cannot tell you which object is the issue.

exemplars.why_excellent: The canonical shape for the whole library: 9-section SKILL.md (Before Starting / Core Concepts / Common Patterns / Decision Guidance / Recommended Workflow / Review Checklist / Salesforce-Specific Gotchas / Output Artifacts / Related Skills), and every single one of its 5 gotchas is a *negative* platform fact a model would confidently get wrong — classification has zero runtime enforcement, ComplianceGroup is read-only over Tooling API, standard-field classification needs a stub file, Data Detect never sets SecurityClassification, and API < v46.0 silently drops the attributes. The Decision Guidance table's third column is 'Reason', not a restatement of the recommendation. Related Skills entries explain the *relationship*, not just the name.
exemplars.quoted_example: **Detection hint:** Any sentence pairing "classification" with "restrict", "prevent access", "block", or "protect from unauthorized" is likely describing a false capability.

exemplars.why_excellent: Best-in-repo anti-patterns file for a declarative domain. Each entry renders the WRONG flow as an ASCII element diagram with an inline `← BAD` annotation, then the RIGHT one as a second diagram — so the failure is visible in the same notation the practitioner works in. It models the LLM's actual cognitive error ('the LLM does not internalize the implicit lock chain'), and every detection hint is mechanically checkable against flow XML. It also corrects a numeric fact a model reliably invents: Salesforce already retries lock failures, so a hand-rolled retry loop is strictly harmful.
exemplars.quoted_example: Trust Salesforce's automatic retries (10 attempts with exponential backoff). When they're not enough, the contention is severe and requires architectural decoupling, not more retries.

exemplars.why_excellent: Ten gotchas, every one of them a production post-mortem compressed into What happens / When it occurs / How to avoid. It repeatedly corrects arithmetic a model would do confidently and wrongly: Bulk API V2's 10,000-record batch does not change the 200-row trigger transaction; the API-call budget is blown by job-status polling, not by batches; 'load completes' is not 'org usable' because sharing recalculation is an invisible async tail. Gotcha 8 is the rarest kind of depth — it enumerates what a mitigation does NOT cover (Defer Sharing Calculations misses account/opportunity/case-team, territory, and manual shares).
exemplars.quoted_example: The load fails with `CPU_TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` at the same rate as a 5,000-batch attempt because the platform internally chunks the upload to **200-row server transactions** for trigger evaluation regardless of the upload batch size.

exemplars.why_excellent: Proof that depth is not length. At 4 KB the anti-patterns file is smaller than the corpus median, yet all five entries are hard cardinality/activation constraints of Salesforce Loyalty Management that no amount of general reasoning recovers: one qualifying currency per tier group, one loyalty program per Experience Cloud site, two separate partner DPE definitions, qualifying vs non-qualifying currency split. This is the model to imitate under the zero-sum retrieval constraint — maximum unrecoverable-fact density per token, zero connective prose.
exemplars.quoted_example: Partner loyalty requires two DPE definitions: "Create Partner Ledgers" AND "Update Partner Balance". Both must be activated. Omitting one results in partner transactions being recorded without balance updates.

exemplars.why_excellent: Best example of naming the *exact licence* that silently gates a feature. It identifies `CareProviderSearchableField` (a denormalized index object almost nobody knows exists), states that it is not auto-populated, names the Data Processing Engine job that populates it, names the `Data Pipelines Base User` permission set license that the job needs, names `HealthCloudICM` for record access, and names the required record types (HealthcareProvider / HealthcarePractitioner). The Decision Guidance row for the failure mode is blunt about frequency rather than hedged.
exemplars.quoted_example: Without this license, the Data Processing Engine (DPE) job that populates CareProviderSearchableField will fail silently or throw a license error, making provider search return zero results.

exemplars.why_excellent: Highest concentration of verbatim platform error strings and exact numeric ceilings in the flow domain. It quotes the literal deploy failure text, gives the exact character cap and the safe composition size, explains the non-obvious execution-model fact that Formula resources are lazily re-evaluated on every reference (with the multiplication worked out: 6 references x 200 iterations = 1,200 evaluations), and flags `=` on a picklist as a *locale* bug that appears only after a translation pack is enabled — with 'No deploy error, no runtime warning' stated explicitly.
exemplars.quoted_example: Deploy fails with `The formula expression is invalid: Compiled formula is too big to execute (5,001 characters)`. No partial-deploy fallback — the entire flow rejects.

exemplars.why_excellent: The best template for a NON-CODE domain, and the answer to '196 examples.md have no code fences'. Its examples use Scenario / Limit Risks Identified / Recommended Approach and are dense with hard governor arithmetic instead of code: 763 of 800 custom objects, 12 MB async heap divided by scope 200, the 50M-record/24h Batch Apex ceiling as a *shared* rolling budget, the 5-concurrent-job queue. It also names the authoritative way to check rather than guess (the Limits API endpoint), which is the architect-domain analogue of shipping runnable code.
exemplars.quoted_example: A 12MB async heap limit at scope 200 means roughly 60KB of in-memory object data per account before overflow. Complex graphs require reducing scope to 50 or 100.

exemplars.why_excellent: Textbook 'cross-platform syntax bleed' coverage — it knows the model's failure is contamination from the more-represented platform (GitHub Actions) and names the exact tokens to grep for. Every anti-pattern's detection hint is a literal string search a CI linter could run. Anti-pattern 4 captures the highest-value silent default in Salesforce DevOps (sandbox deploys default to NoTestRun) and Anti-pattern 5 catches an ordering bug — cleanup on the happy path instead of `after_script:` — that only shows up when the deploy fails.
exemplars.quoted_example:
after_script:
  - rm -f /tmp/server.key  # always runs, even on failure

exemplars.why_excellent: Its examples.md is the gold standard for the file: three full incident narratives (retry storm from a JSON ack, session-ID callback for data not in the payload, 4,200 messages expired after a 36-hour TLS outage) each with Context / Problem / Solution / Why it works and *runnable receiver code in the language the receiver is actually written in* (Java servlet, Python Flask, Apex batch). Its well-architected.md is equally strong: five named pillars each with a concrete tradeoff, plus an adaptability note giving the feature a stated end-of-life horizon.
exemplars.quoted_example: Salesforce treated every response as a delivery failure because the response body did not match the expected SOAP acknowledgment structure. The result was a 24-hour retry storm for every triggered message.

exemplars.why_excellent: Strongest anti-patterns in a domain where the model's priors are actively misleading. It draws a hard boundary around what the Testing API does and does not do (routing/reasoning yes; DML, callouts, Flow/Apex no), gives a differentiated CI gate policy because LLM-judge scores have variance so a 100% hard gate produces false failures, and corrects tooling drift by pointing at the `sf agent test` command family instead of hand-rolled Connect API poll loops — including the trap that `sf agent test run` is async by default unlike `sf apex run test`.

Instruction adherence:    Soft gate — run as informational, track trend over time
                            Only enforce a hard gate after establishing a stable

exemplars.why_excellent: Best demonstration of correcting a framework-dialect mismatch inside the same language. It shows the standard LWC idiom (`dispatchEvent` with `bubbles: true`) as the WRONG answer with an inline comment saying why, gives the pubsub replacement, and carries the managed-package namespace fork inline. Its detection hints are compound and precise — not 'look for dispatchEvent' but 'look for dispatchEvent in a component that also declares @api omniJsonData' — which makes them low-false-positive.

quality_markers.marker: examples.md ships a runnable artifact — a code fence containing Apex/JS/YAML/XML/SOQL, or (for non-code domains) an explicit worked numeric budget. The failing shape is '## Key Considerations' + '## Worked Examples (see `references/examples.md`)' + '## Top LLM Anti-Patterns (full list in ...)', which restates the reference bullets verbatim and adds zero information while consuming retrieval chunks. The two shapes are perfectly disjoint in the corpus (0 overlap).

quality_markers.marker: Quotes at least one VERBATIM platform error/message string (the text the user will paste into a search box). This is the rarest and highest-leverage marker in the corpus: it is the thing a competitor cannot generate and a user can grep for. Example: `Compiled formula is too big to execute (5,001 characters)`.
quality_markers.how_to_detect: cd "$REPO" && grep -rlEi '`[^`]*(exceeded|is invalid|not permitted|no rows for assignment|too many|cannot be null|Refused to|is not supported|Attempt to de-reference|expired)[^`]*`' --include='*.md' skills | cut -d/ -f1-3 | sort -u | wc -l

quality_markers.marker: Salesforce API-identifier density: at least 0.8 DISTINCT API-shaped identifiers per KB of markdown (CamelCase object/field names, `__c`/`__e`/`__mdt` suffixes, ALL_CAPS status codes). Catches packages that describe features only by UI label. Verified failure mode: skills/security/permission-set-groups-and-muting is 17 KB and never once writes `PermissionSetGroup`, `MutingPermissionSet`, or `PermissionSetGroupComponent` in any .md — so a consuming agent cannot build a query or a metadata file from it.
quality_markers.how_to_detect:
cd "$REPO" && python3 -c "
import re,glob,os
P=re.compile(r'\b(?:[A-Z][a-z0-9]+){2,}(?:__(?:c|e|mdt|x|b))?\b|\b\w+__(?:c|e|mdt|x|b)\b|\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+_[A-Z0-9_]{3,}\b')
for d in sorted(glob.glob('skills/*/*/')):
  t=''.join(open(os.path.join(r,f),encoding='utf-8',errors='ignore').read() for r,_,fs in os.walk(d) for f in fs if f.endswith('.md'))
  k=max(len(t)/1024,.001); n=len(set(P.findall(t)))
  if n/k < 0.8: print(round(n/k,2), n, round(k,1), d)"

anti_pattern_taxonomy: FALSE-CAPABILITY TRANSFER — the model imports enforcement semantics from a same-named concept in another domain and attributes them to an inert Salesforce feature. The fix always names the real control. Canonical: 'Set SecurityClassification = Restricted to prevent unauthorized access' (classification is metadata-only; FLS is the control). Sibling: 'use ComplianceGroup = PCI to mask cardholder data'. Detection shape: a sentence pairing the feature name with restrict / prevent / block / protect / mask.

CROSS-PLATFORM DIALECT BLEED — the model emits the syntax of whichever platform dominates its training data, inside a file that belongs to another. Canonical: `uses: actions/checkout@v4` inside `.gitlab-ci.yml`; `dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(...))` inside an OmniScript custom LWC; `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` reasoning imported from PostgreSQL. Detection shape: grep for the foreign platform's reserved tokens in the native file.

READABLE-THEREFORE-WRITABLE — the model assumes any field an API exposes for read is also writable, or that any object it can hold is a live handle. Canonical: Tooling API PATCH on FieldDefinition.ComplianceGroup (reads fine, write silently no-ops); mutating `this.omniJsonData` to push state back into an OmniScript (one-way input). Detection shape: an update/PATCH/assignment targeting an identifier that only ever appears in SELECT or @api-input position elsewhere.

SILENT-DEFAULT OMISSION — the model omits a flag or version whose unstated default is the dangerous one, so the artifact runs green and does nothing. Canonical: `sf project deploy start` without `--test-level` (sandbox default is NoTestRun); deploying classification metadata at sourceApiVersion 45.0 (attributes dropped, deploy succeeds). Detection shape: a generated command missing a flag whose default differs from the user's evident intent.

PROCEDURAL LOOP TRANSFER — 'for each X, update X' translated literally into a set-based, governor-limited platform. Canonical: Update Records inside a Flow Loop; DML inside an Apex for-loop. Best entries show that the cost is not just the limit but self-induced lock contention on the parent the trigger already holds. Detection shape: a DML/Update element whose ancestor is a loop construct.

REDUNDANT RETRY ON TOP OF PLATFORM RETRY — a generic distributed-systems 'transient failure → retry with backoff' pattern layered over machinery that already retries, usually making it worse. Canonical: a Flow fault path with a Wait element re-attempting the Update (Salesforce already retries lock failures 10 times with backoff, and a Wait ends the transaction so each 'retry' re-acquires locks from scratch). Inverse form: assuming a retry exists when it does not (Bulk API V2 does not retry row-skew lock failures). Detection shape: a Wait/sleep followed by a re-attempt of the same failed operation.

PARTIAL FEATURE SOLD AS COMPLETE — the model treats a tool that covers one axis as covering all of them, and ends the checklist there. Canonical: 'run Einstein Data Detect and your fields are classified' (it only recommends ComplianceGroup, never SecurityClassification); 'the Testing API confirms the action created the case' (it validates routing and reasoning, never executes DML or callouts); 'the eval suite passes, ship it'. Detection shape: a workflow whose final gate is the partial tool with no subsequent layer.

MISSING MANDATORY ACTIVATION STEP — the model describes configuration and assumes the platform self-starts the job that makes it work. Canonical: Loyalty tier processing without activating the Data Processing Engine definitions; provider search without the DPE job that populates CareProviderSearchableField; partner loyalty with only one of the two required DPE definitions activated. Detection shape: setup instructions that never mention activating, scheduling, or first-running a job.

CARDINALITY-CONSTRAINT BLINDNESS — the model assumes an N:N relationship where the platform enforces 1:1 or requires exactly 2. Canonical: one currency serving both tier assessment and redemption (Loyalty requires a qualifying/non-qualifying split); multiple qualifying currencies on one tier group (exactly one allowed); multiple loyalty programs on one Experience Cloud site (exactly one allowed). Detection shape: any design sentence of the form 'associate all your Xs with the Y'.

IGNORING DOCUMENTED PLATFORM SILENCES — the model manufactures specificity where the platform deliberately withholds it, rather than naming the limit. Canonical: inventing a stack trace with plausible class names and line numbers; naming the blocking record for `INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS ... : []` when the brackets are empty by design; narrating what a managed package is doing inside `ENTERING_MANAGED_PKG`. The correct pattern is always a 'what this cannot tell you' statement PLUS a concrete out-of-band next step (impersonate user X, query CronTrigger, open the field metadata). Detection shape: cited class/line/record identifiers that do not appear when the user greps the source evidence.

ATTRIBUTION FROM THE MOST PROMINENT SIGNAL — the model answers from whatever is visually loudest rather than from the causally relevant field. Canonical: blaming the `USER_INFO` header user in an async log (async runs as the ENQUEUING user; cross-reference AsyncApexJob.CreatedById); concluding root cause from the first 200 lines of a multi-MB log; reporting a field as changed from a `VARIABLE_ASSIGNMENT` with no paired successful DML. Detection shape: the conclusion cites exactly one early//prominent artifact and no corroborating second signal.

WRONG TOOL FOR THE SYMPTOM CLASS — the model pattern-matches the symptom's noun to a tool without diagnosing which of two failure classes it is. Canonical: prescribing `FOR UPDATE` for parallel-transaction contention when the real issue is bulk shape (FOR UPDATE is correct only for read-modify-write lost-update races, and otherwise extends the lock-hold and makes it worse); recommending more `System.debug` as the fix for a cascade; hand-rolling a curl+jq poll loop where `sf agent test run --wait` exists. Detection shape: the remedy is proposed before any question that would distinguish the two classes is asked.

UNIFORM GATE POLICY OVER NON-UNIFORM SIGNALS — 'fail fast' applied identically to deterministic and stochastic checks. Canonical: hard-gating LLM-judge instruction-adherence scores at 100% alongside deterministic topic/action routing tests, which produces false pipeline failures on a valid agent. Correct pattern is a per-signal gate table with a stated rationale. Detection shape: generated CI config applying one `if result != 100% then fail` across heterogeneous test types.

TEARDOWN ON THE HAPPY PATH — cleanup, revert, or re-enable placed where it is skipped precisely when it matters. Canonical: `rm -f /tmp/server.key` at the end of `script:` instead of `after_script:` (never reached if the deploy fails, so the private key persists on the runner); re-enabling field history tracking or Defer Sharing Calculations only in the success branch of a load runbook. Detection shape: a destructive-state-restoring command with no always-runs construct around it.

PLAUSIBLE ARITHMETIC OVER THE WRONG UNIT — the model does correct math on a number that does not mean what it thinks. Canonical: setting Bulk API V2 batch size to 10,000 to reduce trigger CPU pressure (the platform still chunks to 200-row server transactions; the 10,000 is an upload-payload cap); summing `DML_BEGIN.Rows` to report 'records touched' (bulk ops log overlapping counts and platform-internal DML is not attributable to user code); sizing an API budget from batch count while job-status polling burns the real quota. Detection shape: a single derived headline number with no cited limit event backing it.

META — OVER-LOADING THE CONTEXT — the agent reads every reference file 'for full context' before classifying the question, wasting attention and drifting off-topic. Only one package needs this entry today, but it is the shape that scales: any package that grows past ~140 index chunks must ship a symptom-to-file routing step and an anti-pattern forbidding preload.
quality_bar.scoring_rubric:
SFSKILLS DEPTH RUBRIC v1 — apply per package; 100 points; ship bar is 70 with zero hard-gate failures.

Measured against the corpus of 1,027 packages as of 2026-08-01. All thresholds are real percentiles, not guesses.

=== HARD GATES (any failure = do not ship, regardless of score) ===
G1. Retrieval budget. Total .md bytes <= 50 KB AND index chunks <= 140 (corpus p99; median is 74 chunks / ~25 KB). Exceeding it starves neighbours through the 30-chunk lexical window. The sole exception pattern: split into symptom-scoped reference files AND ship an anti-pattern forbidding preload (see apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis).
G2. No pointer-stub SKILL.md. If the body contains "Worked Examples (see `references/" or "## Key Considerations" without "## Core Concepts", it is previewing its own reference files and adding nothing. 47 packages currently fail this.
G3. llm-anti-patterns.md has >= 5 entries in full quad form (What the LLM generates / Why it happens / Correct pattern / Detection hint). A numbered list of labels is an automatic fail.
G4. Recommended Workflow is not the shared filler body (149 packages share one byte-identical version starting "Gather context — confirm the org edition").
G5. Every factual claim is either grounded in a cited official source or explicitly flagged as field observation. No invented API names, no invented limits.
G6. Official Sources Used contains >= 1 URL specific to this skill, not only the corpus-generic three (Well-Architected overview / Metadata API intro / Object Reference concepts).

=== SCORED (100 pts) ===

A. UNRECOVERABLE FACTS — 35 pts. The core of the moat: things a competent generic LLM cannot derive.
  A1 (12) Named API/metadata/object/field identifiers a model would not produce unprompted — CareProviderSearchableField, ClinicalServiceRequest, MutingPermissionSet, omniOutputMap, WorkflowOutboundMessage. Target density >= 0.8 distinct API-shaped identifiers per KB (corpus median 0.46, p75 0.75). 12 pts at >= 1.0/KB, 8 at >= 0.8, 4 at >= 0.5, 0 below.
  A2 (8) At least one VERBATIM platform error/message string, reproduced exactly, in backticks. Only 11.0% of the corpus has this — it is the single largest available lift. Full marks require the string be greppable by a user who pasted it from an org.
  A3 (8) Named licence / permission set / permission-set-licence gating, with the consequence of its absence. Only 8.4% of the corpus has this. Award only if the failure mode is stated, not just the licence name.
  A4 (7) Exact numeric limits with the unit and the scope they apply to (per org / per transaction / per 24h rolling). "Bulk API V2 processes up to 150 million records per rolling 24-hour period per org" scores; "large volumes" scores zero.

B. FAILURE-MODE FIDELITY — 25 pts. What actually goes wrong in production.
  B1 (10) At least one documented SILENCE: an operation that fails, no-ops, or truncates with no error surfaced, plus the out-of-band way to detect it. Best form gets its own section ("What the log cannot tell you").
  B2 (8) Gotchas use the What happens / When it occurs / How to avoid triple (or the 4-part variant adding Why it matters), and each one reads as a compressed post-mortem with a specific trigger condition — not a restated best practice. Half marks if the structure is present but the content is generic.
  B3 (7) At least one "what a mitigation does NOT cover" statement. This is the rarest and most trusted content in the library (see Defer Sharing Calculations missing team/territory/manual shares).

C. ANTI-PATTERNS — 20 pts. The library's most differentiated asset. Score the file, not the count.
  C1 (7) Each entry models the LLM's ACTUAL cognitive error in "Why it happens" — names the competing prior (training-data prevalence, another platform's dialect, a general-CS pattern). "The LLM forgets to do X" scores zero; "GitHub Actions is more prevalent in training data than GitLab CI" scores full.
  C2 (7) Every entry has a MECHANICAL detection hint — a grep, an XML/AST predicate, or a compound structural condition. Prefer compound and low-false-positive ("dispatchEvent in a component that also declares @api omniJsonData") over a bare token search.
  C3 (6) The "Correct pattern" is a concrete artifact — code, XML, a flow diagram, or a decision table — not a sentence of advice. Entries must map to distinct shapes from the taxonomy; three entries that are the same shape restated score as one.

D. ACTIONABILITY — 12 pts.
  D1 (6) examples.md ships runnable artifacts under Context / Problem / Solution / Why it works, in the language the reader will actually write (a Java servlet for a SOAP receiver, Python for a webhook handler, Apex for in-platform). Non-code domains substitute worked numeric budgets under Scenario / Limit Risks Identified / Recommended Approach and score identically — but generic prose scores zero either way.
  D2 (6) Recommended Workflow steps each name a concrete surface (Setup path, `sf` command, metadata element) AND a verification signal ("Confirm the badge appears in the app nav").

E. ROUTING & FIT — 8 pts.
  E1 (3) description states what the skill does NOT cover, and the exclusions name the real sibling features it is confusable with (not a generic disclaimer).
  E2 (3) Related Skills entries state the RELATIONSHIP, not just the name ("Fields classified ComplianceGroup=GDPR feed into the erasure processes covered there").
  E3 (2) Decision Guidance table's third column gives the REASON, and the reason is a platform fact rather than a restatement of the recommendation.

=== THE DISTINCTIVENESS TEST (apply before writing a single line) ===
For every sentence, ask: could a strong generic LLM produce this from the public docs plus reasoning? If yes, delete it. Retrieval is zero-sum — 130,151 chunks compete for a 30-chunk window, so generic prose does not merely fail to help, it actively displaces a neighbouring skill's chunks and can make that skill unreachable.

Corollary, and the most important lesson from the corpus: DEPTH IS NOT LENGTH. integration/loyalty-management-setup has a 4 KB anti-patterns file — below the corpus median — and is a top exemplar, because all five entries are hard platform cardinality and activation constraints that cannot be recovered by reasoning. Meanwhile several 40-60 KB packages score in the bottom decile on A1 because they describe everything by UI label and never name a single API identifier. Prefer 15 KB of unrecoverable facts over 45 KB of well-organised restatement. When a package is already at the bar, the correct move on new research is to REPLACE its weakest paragraph, not append.

practices.practice: For same-record field updates on a record-triggered flow, always use a before-save flow; never an after-save flow with an Update Records element pointed at $Record.
practices.why_it_matters: An after-save same-record update issues a second DML, which re-enters the entire save order (validation rules, other flows, triggers, roll-ups, sharing recalculation) for that record. Salesforce measured bulk same-record updates as 10–20x faster in before-save.
practices.specifics: Architects decision guide: 'Bulk same-record updates performed anywhere between 10-20x faster when implemented using before-save triggers than when implemented using Workflow Rules or Process Builder.' Mechanism: 'The record's field values are already loaded into memory... the update is performed by changing the values of the record in memory, and relying on the original underlying DML operation to save the changes' — avoiding 'not only an expensive DML operation, but also the entire associated ensuing recursive save.' In a before-save flow you write to $Record directly; adding an Update Records element for $Record is redundant and unsupported.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked for 'a flow that stamps a field when Status changes', an LLM almost always produces an after-save record-triggered flow with an Update Records element targeting the triggering record, because 'record-triggered flow' plus 'Update Records' is the highest-frequency pattern in its training data. It then compounds the error by adding a Decision element to prevent the recursion its own design created.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — admin/flow-for-admins (1.400), admin/workflow-field-update-patterns (1.300), flow/flow-performance-optimization, flow/flow-record-save-order-interaction, flow/record-triggered-flow-patterns. See coverage_verification[0].

practices.practice: Do not plan Apex actions, subflows, cross-object DML, or fault paths into a before-save flow — the element palette is Assignment, Decision, Get Records, and Loop only.
practices.why_it_matters: A design that assumes 'before-save for speed, and call the Apex action there' is unbuildable and gets discovered only at build time, forcing a redesign of the whole automation.
practices.specifics: Supported elements in a before-save record-triggered flow: Assignment, Decision, Get Records, Loop. Architects guide: 'You cannot extend a before-save flow trigger with Apex invocable actions or subflows.' The flow 'can't perform actions other than updating the triggering record's field values, and the flow can't update values in records that are related to the triggering record.' Because there is no DML element, there is nothing that can throw — fault connectors are therefore not available. Fields populated only at save time (Id on insert, formula fields, roll-up summaries, LastModifiedDate) are not readable.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM told 'use before-save for performance' will happily emit a before-save flow containing an Action element calling invocable Apex, or advise 'add a fault connector to the Assignment element'. It treats the four flow trigger types as having a uniform element palette.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/fault-handling references/llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 3 ('Advising fault handling for before-save record-triggered flows'), apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis references/flows.md. See coverage_verification[1].

practices.practice: When more than one record-triggered flow exists on an object, set an explicit Trigger Order value in 1–1000 on every one of them; leaving any flow unnumbered puts it in a middle band ordered by activation date, not last.
practices.why_it_matters: The run sequence is not 'numbered ascending then unnumbered'. Unnumbered flows run BETWEEN the 1–1000 band and the 1001–2000 band, so a flow you deliberately numbered 1500 to 'run last' actually runs after the unnumbered ones — and 'activation date' order silently reshuffles the moment someone deactivates and reactivates a flow in production.
practices.specifics: Order for flows with the same trigger (before- or after-save) on the same object: (1) trigger order 1–1000 in ascending order; ties broken alphabetically by flow API name; (2) flows with no trigger order value, in order of their activation dates; (3) trigger order 1001–2000 in ascending order. Valid range is 1–2000. Flows created in Winter '22 and earlier default to no trigger order value. Flow Trigger Explorer (Setup > Object Manager > object > Flow Triggers) displays versions and trigger order values and lets you reorder.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM says either 'the order is non-deterministic, set Trigger Order' (stopping there) or 'flows run in ascending trigger order 1 to 2000'. It does not know about the three-band rule, so it will suggest 1000 and 2000 as 'first and last' — which is exactly backwards for the second one. It also never mentions that reactivating a flow re-dates it and reshuffles the unnumbered band.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — flow/record-triggered-flow-patterns and apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis state 'Unless Trigger Order is set, the order is undefined', and devops/go-live-cutover-planning has a gotcha on activation order. No file in skills/flow, skills/admin or skills/architect contains the strings '1,001', '1001 to 2000', or the activation-date band rule (grep returned zero hits). See coverage_verification[2] and [3].

practices.practice: Treat the 2,000-executed-element interview limit as removed only for flows whose flow API version is 57.0 or later; audit the actual <apiVersion> in the flow metadata rather than assuming.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the single most commonly repeated stale Flow fact. A flow inherited from a pre-Spring '23 org and never re-saved still carries API 56.0 or lower and still throws the element error, while an identically-shaped new flow does not — so the same design 'works in sandbox, fails in production' purely on version drift.
practices.specifics: Spring '23 removed the 2,000-executed-element runtime limit, 'limited to flows and processes that are configured to run on API version 57.0 or later'. API 56.0 and earlier still enforce it. The runtime error surfaces as 'Number of Iterations Exceeded' (Salesforce KB 000382258) / 'Number of executed elements has exceeded the maximum number of 2000'. Removal does not remove the real ceiling: 10,000 ms synchronous Apex CPU time still applies, and every flow element consumes CPU. Note that any Save in Flow Builder bumps the flow's API version, so the version is not stable across edits.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM states the 2,000-element limit as a live, unconditional Flow governor limit — it is in essentially every Flow-limits blog post in the training corpus. It never conditions the answer on the flow's API version, and it never mentions that CPU time became the binding constraint afterwards.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — and worse, existing content is STALE. skills/flow/flow-loop-element-patterns/references/gotchas.md Gotcha 3 and skills/architect/solution-design-patterns/references/gotchas.md Gotcha 5 both assert the limit as currently enforced with no API-version condition. grep for 'API version 57' and 'ITERATION_LIMIT' across skills/flow, skills/admin, skills/architect returned zero hits. See coverage_verification[4] and [5].

practices.practice: Stop designing around Flow Orchestration licensing cost — as of Spring '26 it is a standard feature with no per-run charge; re-evaluate multi-step human workflows that were previously routed to Approval Processes or custom Apex to avoid the SKU.
practices.why_it_matters: Architecture decisions made in 2022–2025 deliberately avoided Orchestration because of the $1/run consumption SKU. Those decisions are now cost-optimising against a price that no longer exists, and teams are still hand-rolling multi-stage approvals in screen flows plus custom objects.
practices.specifics: Flow Orchestration became a standard Flow type — no separate license, no add-on purchase, no usage-based limitation — available the week of 16 February 2026 (Spring '26). Prior model: consumption SKU at $1 per orchestration run, sold in yearly increments, with 600 annual runs included in Professional/Enterprise/Unlimited editions regardless of org size. Orchestration metadata is processType 'Orchestrator'; interactive steps reference an active screen flow and generate an orchestration work item surfaced in the Flow Orchestration Work Guide; background steps reference an autolaunched flow; only one stage can be In Progress at a time and all interactive steps are processed asynchronously.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Every model with a pre-2026 cutoff will say Flow Orchestration 'requires a separate Flow Orchestration license / consumption credits' and will steer the user to Approval Processes to avoid the cost. This is now actively harmful advice, and it is stated with high confidence because the $1/run figure was widely published.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the pricing change. architect/org-edition-and-feature-licensing has an example titled 'Flow Orchestration "Missing" in Enterprise Org — Enablement Issue, Not Licensing' and flow/flow-orchestration-patterns covers persistence and Approval-Process tradeoffs, but neither mentions per-run consumption pricing or the Spring '26 change; grep for 'orchestration run' across skills/flow, skills/admin, skills/architect hits only architect/event-driven-architecture (unrelated). See coverage_verification[6] and [7].

practices.practice: In a record-triggered flow, the Custom Error element must be terminal — never place an Assignment, DML, or any other element after it on the same path.
practices.why_it_matters: This is a silent failure: if the path continues past the Custom Error element, the flow keeps executing, the transaction COMMITS, the record change is not rolled back, and the user never sees the error. The validation you built simply does not fire, with no log entry saying so.
practices.specifics: When a Custom Error element is reached and the path ends there, the associated record change is rolled back and the message is shown as a pop-up or as an inline field error. 'However, if you add other elements (e.g., "Assignment" or DML elements) after the "Custom Error", the flow continues the execution and commits the transaction, and the error message is not shown and the record is not rolled back.' The Custom Error element exists only in record-triggered flows (Winter '24); the screen-flow equivalent is the Roll Back Records element.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM builds 'validate, then throw a custom error, then log the attempt to a custom object' — putting a Create Records logging element after the Custom Error because that is the standard defensive-programming shape. That single element silently disables the validation. Models treat Custom Error like an Apex addError(), which does not have this ordering constraint.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — 'Custom Error' appears only in skills/admin/flow-for-admins/SKILL.md across skills/flow, skills/admin and skills/architect; flow/flow-rollback-patterns and flow/fault-handling cover rollback scope but not the downstream-element commit behaviour. See coverage_verification[8] and [9].

practices.practice: Flow DML is all-or-none by default; only the Create Records element offers partial success (Winter '25), and even with it enabled the element still takes its fault path.
practices.why_it_matters: Designs that assume 'the good records will save and the bad ones will be reported' are wrong for Update Records and Delete Records entirely, and are half-wrong for Create Records — the successful rows persist but the element is still marked failed, so a naive fault path that logs 'the create failed' will be misleading about what is actually in the database.
practices.specifics: 'By default, Salesforce Flow is designed to work only when the header allOrNone is true' — one bad row rolls back the whole collection. Winter '25 added a partial-success option on the Create Records element: 'Process successful records' vs 'Process no records'. Because Create Records supports upsert, this is also the route to partial-success updates. 'If some records fail, the element itself fails as well, even though the remaining records are processed successfully' — so a partial commit and the fault path both happen.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM maps Flow DML onto Apex's Database.insert(records, false) mental model and asserts flows give per-row SaveResults with itemized errors. It also claims Update Records supports partial success, which it does not. This is a case where Apex knowledge actively corrupts Flow answers.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — and existing content is WRONG. skills/flow/flow-bulkification/SKILL.md:136 states collection DML 'fails more predictably — if one record in the collection violates a validation rule, you get an `AllOrNone=false` partial success with itemized errors rather than a rollback.' grep for 'Process successful records' across skills/flow, skills/admin, skills/architect returns zero hits. See coverage_verification[10] and [11].

practices.practice: Never reference $Record__Prior, ISCHANGED, or PRIORVALUE on an asynchronous or scheduled path — put that comparison in the entry conditions or stamp the prior value onto a field on the immediate path.
practices.why_it_matters: Prior values exist only inside the triggering transaction. On an async or scheduled path the comparison is unavailable, and a Decision element with 'Is Changed = true' on a scheduled path does not error — it just never takes the branch you expect, so time-delayed automation silently does nothing.
practices.specifics: 'Only flow paths that run immediately can reference the prior values of the triggering record.' Scheduled paths cannot access $Record__Prior at all, and Salesforce has stated no plan to support it because scheduled paths may fire months or years later. Asynchronous paths don't support the ISCHANGED operator, including inside Decision elements. Additionally, a scheduled path is only offered when the flow's entry condition is 'Only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements' — and that option is itself incompatible with an Is Changed entry condition. Workaround: write the prior value to a field on the triggering record on the immediate path so the delayed path can read it. Note $Record__Prior is also all-null on a create-only trigger.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM writes 'add a scheduled path 24 hours after the update, then use a Decision comparing {!$Record.Stage} to {!$Record__Prior.Stage} to confirm the change still holds' — a design that is unbuildable but reads perfectly. It also routinely suggests ISCHANGED() inside a flow Decision, importing validation-rule syntax that the flow formula engine does not implement.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — flow/flow-formula-and-expression-patterns gotcha 19 and llm-anti-pattern 8 cover 'Flow formula language does NOT include PRIORVALUE or ISCHANGED' generally, and process-builder/workflow-rule migration skills cover rebuilding ISCHANGED criteria. Nothing covers the async/scheduled-path-specific unavailability of $Record__Prior or the entry-condition interlock. See coverage_verification[12].

practices.practice: Use an asynchronous path (not the immediate path) for callouts, for updates to setup objects such as User, and for anything whose failure must not roll back the user's save — and size it against ASYNC Apex limits, not synchronous ones.
practices.why_it_matters: An HTTP callout on the immediate path of a record-triggered flow is illegal in the same transaction as uncommitted DML, and setup/non-setup object mixes throw MIXED_DML_OPERATION. The async path is the low-code equivalent of Queueable Apex and moves the work past commit.
practices.specifics: 'The work on the Run Asynchronously path does not begin until all work on the Run Immediate paths gets completed and those transactions are committed.' 'Both asynchronous and scheduled paths are subject to the same asynchronous per-transaction Apex limits' — i.e. 200 SOQL queries, 12 MB heap, 60 s CPU rather than the synchronous 100/6 MB/10 s. Canonical use: 'in a flow triggered when an opportunity is created or updated, use an asynchronous path to update a value on a user record' to avoid the mixed-DML error. Execution is best-effort — 'in certain load conditions, the path's execution may be delayed'.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM puts an HTTP Callout action directly on the immediate after-save path and adds a fault connector, believing the fault connector handles the uncommitted-work exception. It also usually cites the synchronous limits (100 SOQL / 10 s CPU) when sizing async-path work, understating available headroom by 2x on SOQL and 6x on CPU.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-transactional-boundaries references/gotchas.md contains MIXED_DML content, flow/flow-external-services ships a checker that flags callouts in record-triggered flows, flow/flow-cross-object-updates covers mixed DML. Async-path Apex-limit numbers not verified as present. See coverage_verification[13].

practices.practice: Size scheduled paths and schedule-triggered flows against the 250,000-interviews-per-24-hours ceiling and the 200-record batch, and use Summer '26's configurable maximum batch size rather than accepting the default.
practices.why_it_matters: Scheduled automation looks free until a mass data load queues a quarter of a million interviews. Exceeding the daily interview ceiling drops work silently rather than raising a per-record error the admin will see.
practices.specifics: Maximum schedule-triggered flow interviews per 24 hours: 250,000, or the number of user licenses in the org multiplied by 200, whichever is greater. Maximum for a single schedule-triggered flow: 250,000. A schedule-triggered flow's query retrieves records in batches of 200 by default; a scheduled path's Batch Size is settable 1–200 with a default and maximum of 200. Batching is per interval — 'if you specify a batch size of two and seven records are scheduled to be processed in the same time interval, Flow Builder groups them into four batches.' Summer '26 added a configurable maximum batch size for schedule-triggered flows, overriding the 200 default.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM recommends a scheduled flow for '50,000 records nightly' without mentioning any interview ceiling, and describes batch size as a performance knob rather than a governor-limit knob. It also conflates a scheduled path (inside a record-triggered flow) with a schedule-triggered flow, which have different context and different limits.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — admin/scheduled-path-patterns (1.822) covers batch size and offset anchors; flow/scheduled-flows llm-anti-patterns.md and flow/flow-bulkification llm-anti-patterns.md both push back on high-volume scheduled flows; '250,000' appears in flow/flow-batch-processing-alternatives, flow/scheduled-flows, flow/scheduled-flow-not-running-debug. Summer '26 configurable batch size not present. See coverage_verification[14] and [15].

practices.practice: Do not design around a cap on paused and waiting flow interviews — the 50,000 per-org limit was removed in Spring '24.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams still architect Pause-element flows to 'drain' below a cap that no longer exists, adding unnecessary Apex schedulers or artificial batching. Conversely, the real risk moved: nothing now throttles paused-interview accumulation, so the constraint is FlowInterview record volume and resume-batch throughput, not a hard exception.
practices.specifics: Spring '24 release note 'Have Unlimited Paused and Waiting Flows' removed the per-org limit for paused and waiting flow interviews. The previous behaviour was a 50,000 cap on pending schedules plus paused interviews, surfacing as 'Your org has too many waiting flow interviews, including processes that are waiting to execute groups of scheduled actions.' What did NOT change: the maximum flow interview size is 1,000,000 bytes — an interview above that cannot be persisted or paused.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM confidently quotes '50,000 paused and waiting flow interviews per org' as a current limit — it is in every Flow-limits listicle. It has no awareness of the Spring '24 removal, and it never mentions the 1 MB interview-size limit, which is the constraint that actually bites on flows carrying large record collections across a Pause.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL / STALE — flow/pause-elements-and-wait-events references/gotchas.md Gotcha 6 ('Concurrent Paused Interview Count Is Org-Wide, Not Per-Flow') and references/well-architected.md item 3 both present the cap as live. grep for '1,000,000' and '1 MB' across skills/flow returns zero hits (only architect/admin skills, unrelated). See coverage_verification[16].

practices.practice: State that a Subflow element runs the referenced flow's currently ACTIVE version at runtime — not the version that was active when the parent was activated — and use the debug option 'Run the latest version of each flow called by subflow elements' when testing.
practices.why_it_matters: The distinction determines whether shipping a subflow change is a live behaviour change for every existing parent (it is) or an inert one requiring parent re-activation (it is not). Getting this backwards produces a release plan that either under-tests or needlessly re-deploys every caller.
practices.specifics: 'If a child flow has multiple versions, the parent flow runs the child flow's active version. If a child flow has no active version, the parent flow runs the latest version.' Flow Builder's debug dialog exposes 'Run the latest version of each flow called by subflow elements'; unchecked, debug uses the active version. Hard limit: 50 versions per FlowDefinition (active + obsolete + draft); the 51st save fails.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs split roughly evenly between 'the parent pins the subflow version at activation' and the correct answer, and assert whichever they pick with equal confidence. The pinning story is intuitively appealing (it resembles how managed-package dependencies work) which is why it propagates.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED but INCORRECT — flow/flow-versioning-strategy references/gotchas.md #4 states 'A subflow call resolves to whatever active version of the subflow existed when the parent version was activated', which contradicts the official behaviour. The 50-version limit is correctly covered in flow/flow-versioning-strategy and flow/flow-deployment-and-packaging. See coverage_verification[17].

practices.practice: To deploy a flow to production already Active, turn on Setup > Process Automation Settings > 'Deploy processes and flows as active' and meet the flow test coverage threshold — the Metadata API <status>Active</status> alone is overridden in production.
practices.why_it_matters: A change set or Metadata API deploy that ships a flow marked Active silently lands as Inactive in production, so the automation the release depended on does not run and nothing in the deploy result says so.
practices.specifics: The Metadata API Flow 'status' field exists ('Active', 'Draft', 'Obsolete', 'InvalidDraft', 'UnderReview'), but production deployment settings override it by default. The setting is production-only — 'This setting isn't available in developer, sandbox, or other non-production orgs because you can always deploy a new active version.' Before deploying a process or autolaunched flow as active you must meet a 75% flow test coverage requirement, satisfied by Apex tests that invoke the flows. Note that sf project deploy start --test-level does NOT run Flow Builder Flow Tests — those are a separate, non-deployable framework ('Packaging and change sets aren't supported for flow tests').
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM says 'set <status>Active</status> in the flow metadata and deploy' and stops there. It does not know the production override exists, does not mention the org-level setting, and conflates Flow Tests with Apex test coverage — so its CI advice produces a green deploy and a dead automation.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-deployment-and-packaging (1.529) explicitly documents that --test-level does not run Flow Tests, and devops skills cover the 75% threshold. See coverage_verification[18].

practices.practice: Treat Flow Builder Flow Tests as a partial safety net: they cover only record-triggered (and Data Cloud-triggered) flows, only immediate paths, and are capped at 200 per flow — everything else needs an Apex test that performs the DML.
practices.why_it_matters: A team that reports 'the flow is tested' on the strength of Flow Tests has no coverage of the delete trigger, the scheduled path, the async path, or any cross-object assertion — which is where flows actually break.
practices.specifics: Flow tests are available only for record-triggered and Data Cloud-triggered flows; they 'support only flow paths that run immediately'; they cannot test a delete-triggered flow; tests can only be created for the flow's own object, not parent or child objects; maximum 200 tests per flow; they do not count toward test-coverage requirements; formulas are not supported for setting test data (use fixed values); a date set to 'today' when the test was created stays frozen at that date and the test fails later; 'Packaging and change sets aren't supported for flow tests'; 'The owner of the triggering record in a flow test changes to the last person who edits the test.'
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM answers 'how do I test my flow' with 'use Flow Tests in Flow Builder' and presents it as complete coverage. It never mentions the 200-test cap, the frozen-date failure mode, the delete-trigger exclusion, or that the record owner mutates to whoever last edited the test — the last of which quietly invalidates any sharing- or owner-dependent assertion.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — flow/flow-testing (1.600) covers path matrices and the debug-is-not-regression argument, flow/flow-debugging gotcha 5 covers tests not auto-running in deployed orgs. grep for '200 tests' across skills/flow, skills/admin returns zero hits; the frozen-date and record-owner behaviours are absent. See coverage_verification[19] and [20].

practices.practice: Put every filter you can into the record-triggered flow's Start entry conditions rather than into a first Decision element, and prefer 'Only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements' over 'Any time a record is updated'.
practices.why_it_matters: Entry conditions are evaluated before an interview is created, so a filtered-out record costs nothing. A Decision element inside the flow still creates an interview, still counts CPU, and still shows in logs — and on a bulk load of 50,000 records that difference is the whole CPU budget.
practices.specifics: Well-Architected: 'Entry conditions can lead to significant performance improvements for your record-triggered automation if they are used to exclude changes that do not impact a specific use case.' Since Spring '22 entry conditions are evaluated up front, like validation rules. Condition Requirements also accepts 'Formula Evaluates to True', which admits ISCHANGED()/PRIORVALUE() at the Start element even though those functions are unavailable in flow formula resources elsewhere. Choosing 'Only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements' is also the precondition for adding a scheduled path.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM builds the entry condition as 'None — run on every update' and then a Decision named 'Check if Status changed' as the first element, because that mirrors how it would write an Apex trigger guard clause. It also does not know that ISCHANGED is legal in the Start formula but illegal in a Formula resource — it applies one rule to both places, usually the wrong one.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — flow/workflow-rule-to-flow-migration and flow/process-builder-to-flow-migration cover rebuilding ISCHANGED criteria in a Decision element (arguably the anti-pattern), flow/flow-testing covers testing Decision branches. The entry-condition-vs-Decision cost argument and the Start-formula ISCHANGED exception did not surface. See coverage_verification[21].

practices.practice: Hoist Get Records above the loop and Create/Update/Delete Records below it; a data element inside a Loop is the defining flow bulkification failure.
practices.why_it_matters: Flow runs one interview per record, but data elements inside a loop multiply within a single interview. 34 iterations with three Get Records each exhausts the query budget on one record.
practices.specifics: 100 SOQL queries and 150 DML statements per synchronous transaction; the 101st query throws 'System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries: 101' and the 151st DML throws 'Too many DML statements: 151'. Salesforce bulkifies the SAME element across interviews in one transaction — 10 records hitting one Get Records element is one query — but it cannot bulkify repeated executions of that element within a single interview's loop. Apex invocable actions are automatically bulkified across interviews; a Loop is not.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM produces the loop-with-Get-Records shape whenever the requirement is phrased per-record ('for each Opportunity Line Item, look up the Product'), because that is the natural reading of the sentence. It also over-generalises Flow's bulkification, telling users 'Flow bulkifies automatically, so loops are fine' — true across interviews, false within one.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-bulkification (SKILL.md, templates/flow-bulkification-template.md 'Loop Audit'), flow/flow-governor-limits-deep-dive step 2 ('Loop + DML/SOQL inside is the #1 limit-breach pattern'), flow/flow-loop-element-patterns, apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis error-codes.md carries the exact strings. See coverage_verification[22] and [23].

practices.practice: Add a fault connector to every element that performs DML, a callout, an Apex action, or a subflow call; without one the user sees 'An unhandled fault has occurred in this flow' and the entire transaction rolls back.
practices.why_it_matters: The unhandled-fault message names nothing actionable to the end user, and the rollback silently undoes the user's own save. Support tickets arrive as 'Salesforce is broken', with no record of which element failed except in an email nobody reads.
practices.specifics: Unhandled fault message: 'An unhandled fault has occurred in this flow. Please contact your system administrator for more information.' The fault email names the element that failed, that element's error message, and which elements executed during the failed interview. {!$Flow.FaultMessage} carries the error text into a fault-path Assignment. A Get Records element that returns nothing does NOT fault — it returns null, so a fault connector there is dead code and a Decision null-check is required instead.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM adds a fault connector to the Get Records element to 'handle the no-records case' — a very common and completely inert construction. It also omits fault connectors on Action and Subflow elements while adding them to DML, treating 'fault path' as a DML-only concept.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/fault-handling, flow/flow-runtime-error-diagnosis llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 5 ('Adding Fault Paths as a Substitute for Null Checks'), admin/flow-for-admins llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 2. See coverage_verification[24].

practices.practice: Route flow fault emails to a monitored address via Setup > Process Automation Settings > 'Send Process or Flow Error Email to' > 'Apex Exception Email Recipients' — the default sends them to the user who last modified the flow.
practices.why_it_matters: The default recipient is a moving target: it changes every time someone saves the flow, and it points at ex-employees' disabled inboxes for the flows nobody has touched in two years — exactly the flows most likely to break.
practices.specifics: Two options only: 'User Who Last Modified the Process or Flow' (default) and 'Apex Exception Email Recipients'. The latter reads from Setup > Email > Apex Exception Email, which accepts both Salesforce users (via Add Salesforce User) and arbitrary external addresses, so it can be pointed at a ticketing-system intake address. This is an org-wide switch — there is no per-flow recipient, which is why high-volume flows need in-flow fault paths that write to a log object rather than relying on email at all.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM says fault emails go to 'the flow owner' or 'the flow creator'. It is the LAST MODIFIER, which is a different and unstable person. Models also imply the recipient is configurable per flow, which it is not.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED and notably strong — flow/flow-error-monitoring references/gotchas.md Gotcha 1, flow/flow-error-notification-patterns (including an anti-pattern that pushes back on the org-default recipient as sufficient), flow/flow-runtime-error-diagnosis gotcha 1 correctly says 'last modifier, not the admin'. See coverage_verification[25].

practices.practice: Treat a Screen, Pause, or local action as a hard transaction boundary — pending DML commits there and governor limits reset — and never rely on a later screen to 'undo' earlier work.
practices.why_it_matters: Practitioners assume a screen flow is one atomic unit and design a Cancel button that reverses records created three screens ago. Those records are already committed. Conversely, teams fighting CPU limits miss that inserting a screen is a legitimate, supported way to reset the budget.
practices.specifics: 'When the flow executes a screen element, the flow transaction ends, which means it commits the pending record changes to the database and resets the flow limits.' Screen, Pause, and local action all end the transaction. On resume after a Pause, 'a new transaction begins' and 'everything after the pause element is executed as part of a batch transaction that includes other resumed interviews' — so a resumed interview shares limits with unrelated interviews resuming in the same batch. The screen-flow mechanism for reversing committed work within the current transaction is the Roll Back Records element (record-triggered flows use Custom Error instead).
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM describes a screen flow as a single transaction from Start to End, then designs a multi-screen wizard that creates a parent record on screen 1 and 'rolls everything back' if the user abandons on screen 4. It also does not know that a resumed interview is batched with other unrelated resumed interviews, so its limit math for post-Pause logic is per-interview when it should be per-batch.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-transactional-boundaries (1.250) SKILL.md documents screen save points, Pause writing the FlowInterview record and starting a new transaction, and ships a checker script; flow/pause-elements-and-wait-events covers serialization. See coverage_verification[26].

practices.practice: When migrating Process Builder, run Migrate to Flow only for the supported subset and plan a manual rebuild for scheduled actions with multiple criteria, cross-object (field-traversal) criteria, custom metadata references, custom-event/invocable process types, and anything recursive.
practices.why_it_matters: The tool produces an inactive flow that looks complete. The unsupported constructs are dropped or degraded rather than flagged as blockers, so the gap is discovered after activation in production.
practices.specifics: Migrate to Flow 'supports only record-triggered processes; custom event and custom invocable type processes aren't supported.' It does not support processes containing custom metadata types, nor criteria referencing a field from a related object (field traversals). Scheduled actions migrate only if you select a single criteria associated with the scheduled action — 'if multiple criteria are selected, no scheduled actions are migrated' — and 'if you deploy the flow to a new org, scheduled paths are not migrated to new scheduled actions.' Processes with recursion aren't fully supported. Processes with callouts, external actions, or pauses must be redesigned onto an asynchronous path. Output is always an INACTIVE flow for review. Context: Workflow Rules and Process Builder went end-of-support 31 December 2025 — existing automations still execute, but defects reported after that date are not fixed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM presents Migrate to Flow as a general-purpose converter: 'run the Migrate to Flow tool and it will convert your processes.' It also frequently states that Process Builder 'stops working' or 'is switched off' at end of support, which is false and drives panicked, badly-tested migrations.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/process-builder-to-flow-migration (1.450) documents the tool producing inactive flows, supported action types, a Decision Guidance table routing unsupported actions to manual rebuild, and a gotcha that generated flows have no fault paths; flow/workflow-rule-to-flow-migration covers ISCHANGED rebuilds. See coverage_verification[27].

practices.practice: Draw the Flow-vs-Apex line by automation density and transactional control, not by complexity: use record-triggered Flow as the orchestration layer and invocable Apex for the heavy step.
practices.why_it_matters: 'Use Flow because it's declarative' produces 400-element flows nobody can debug; 'use Apex because it's complex' produces logic invisible to Flow Trigger Explorer. The architecture guidance is a hybrid, and it has a named rationale.
practices.specifics: Architects guidance: 'Use Apex for Salesforce objects with high automation density, and for use cases that require high performance, sophisticated logic, or granular control over transactions.' Well-Architected: 'For a given Salesforce Object, use one mechanism as your entry point into automation. Try to avoid mixing Flow and Apex triggers as entry points for the same Object.' And: 'You don't need to put all of your record-triggered automation into a single "mega flow" per object.' The recommended shape is Flow as the routing/topology layer with high-complexity operations encapsulated in invocable Apex, precisely so the process topology stays visible in Flow Trigger Explorer. Things Flow structurally cannot do: Database.Savepoint, try/catch around an arbitrary block, per-row SaveResult handling on update, callouts on the immediate path.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM answers Flow-vs-Apex with a complexity heuristic ('simple = Flow, complex = Apex') and never mentions automation density, the one-entry-point-per-object rule, or Flow Trigger Explorer visibility as an architectural asset. It will also cheerfully recommend both an Apex trigger and a record-triggered flow on the same object in the same answer.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-governance llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 5 ('Ignoring the interaction between multiple automations on the same object'), admin/process-automation-selection llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 3, flow/flow-record-save-order-interaction well-architected.md ('One before-save flow per object maximum'), plus standards/decision-trees/automation-selection.md. See coverage_verification[28].

practices.practice: Never add a retry loop to a flow to work around 'unable to obtain exclusive access to this record' — the platform already retries, and a hand-rolled loop makes contention worse.
practices.why_it_matters: A retry loop inside the contended transaction holds locks longer and burns the CPU budget that the successful attempt needs, converting an intermittent failure into a reliable one.
practices.specifics: Salesforce automatically retries row-lock failures (10 attempts with exponential backoff). UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW surfaces as 'unable to obtain exclusive access to this record'. When platform retries are insufficient the correct response is architectural decoupling — async path, Pause, or a queue — not more retries. The classic flow-specific cause is many child-record flows updating a shared parent (Account, or an Opportunity's parent), where the implicit parent lock chain is invisible in the flow diagram.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM's standard answer to a lock error is a retry loop with a wait — a pattern imported wholesale from general distributed-systems advice. It does not know the platform already retries, so its 'fix' is strictly harmful.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED and cited by the task brief as a repo exemplar — flow/flow-record-locking-and-contention. Not re-searched; listed here as a known-covered practice for completeness rather than a gap claim.

practices.practice: Read a Get Records result by null-checking the record variable itself (automatic output handling), not by checking one of its fields.
practices.why_it_matters: With 'Choose fields and assign variables (advanced)', a no-match Get Records leaves every target variable null and the flow continues; the failure surfaces several elements later as a NULL_REFERENCE pointing at a formula, not at the Get Records that actually failed. Checking a field also gives a false negative when the record exists but the field is genuinely blank.
practices.specifics: 'When a Get Records element is set to "Choose fields and assign variables (advanced)" and no records match the filter conditions, the variables used to store field values are empty or null.' The Flow team's guidance is to use Automatic Output Handling and test whether the record object itself is null, referencing the Get Records element directly in the downstream Decision rather than a manually-assigned variable. Get Records does not throw when nothing matches, so a fault connector on it never fires.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM writes the null guard as 'Decision: {!Get_Account.Id} Is Null = True' — checking a field of a possibly-null record — and separately attaches a fault connector to Get Records to 'catch the not-found case'. Both are wrong for the same underlying reason: the model treats Get Records like a SOQL call that raises on empty, which it isn't.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-runtime-error-diagnosis llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 5, SKILL.md Pattern 1 ('Tracing NULL_REFERENCE to Its Source'), references/examples.md Example 1. See coverage_verification[29].

practices.practice: Cap versions per flow well below the platform maximum and delete obsolete versions on a cadence — the hard limit is 50 versions per FlowDefinition, counting active, obsolete and draft.
practices.why_it_matters: Hitting the cap blocks the next save, which happens during an incident when someone is trying to hotfix. The remedy at that moment is deleting versions under pressure, which is when a version still referenced by paused interviews gets removed.
practices.specifics: Maximum 50 versions per flow (active + obsolete + draft); the 51st save fails with a flow limit exceeded deploy error. A version cannot be deleted while paused or waiting interviews reference it. Every Save in Flow Builder — including a save that only repositions elements on the canvas — creates a version and can bump the flow's API version.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM does not mention a version cap at all when asked about flow release process, and when it does it usually cites 50 as 'active versions', not total versions. It also does not connect version deletion to paused interviews.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-versioning-strategy references/gotchas.md #6 ('Platform Hard Limit 50 Versions Per Flow') and SKILL.md cleanup cadence (cap at 10), flow/flow-deployment-and-packaging gotcha 19 and llm-anti-pattern 15. See coverage_verification[30].

practices.practice: For interactive Flow Orchestration steps, remember that the referenced screen flow must be ACTIVE and that all interactive steps process asynchronously, one stage at a time.
practices.why_it_matters: An orchestration referencing a draft screen flow deploys and activates cleanly, then stalls at the first work item with no obvious cause. The single-in-progress-stage rule also invalidates designs that assume two stages can overlap.
practices.specifics: 'An interactive step references an active screen flow and generates an orchestration work item.' The assignee completes it in the Flow Orchestration Work Guide on the specified record page and receives an email with a link. 'All interactive steps are processed asynchronously.' 'Stages are executed sequentially, and only one stage in an orchestration can be in progress at a time'; steps within a stage may run sequentially or concurrently. Background steps reference autolaunched flows. Reassigning a work item falls back to the default notification — the customised work-item email applies only to the initial assignee. Metadata: processType 'Orchestrator'.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM describes orchestration stages as parallelizable and does not mention the active-screen-flow requirement for interactive steps. It also tends to describe work items as records users find in a list view rather than through the Work Guide component that must be placed on the record page — omitting the component is a common reason 'the orchestration doesn't do anything'.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — flow/flow-orchestration-patterns (1.267) SKILL.md covers persistence, work items, interactive-vs-background steps, and the Orchestration-vs-Approval-Process tradeoff; architect/org-edition-and-feature-licensing ships a checker keyed on processType = Orchestrator. See coverage_verification[7].

practices.practice: When entry conditions and a Decision both exist, remember that a flow filtered out by entry conditions leaves no FLOW_START_INTERVIEW_BEGIN in the debug log — absence of log evidence is the confirmation the entry condition worked, not evidence the flow is broken.
practices.why_it_matters: Debugging 'my flow isn't running' hinges on distinguishing 'never entered' from 'entered and took the wrong branch'. The two look identical in the UI and are trivially distinguishable in the log.
practices.specifics: Interview lifecycle log events: FLOW_START_INTERVIEW_BEGIN / FLOW_START_INTERVIEW_END, FLOW_CREATE_INTERVIEW_BEGIN / _END, FLOW_ELEMENT_BEGIN / _END, FLOW_WAIT_EVENT_WAITING_DETAIL when pausing. No FLOW_CREATE_INTERVIEW pair for a given flow in a transaction means entry conditions excluded the record before an interview existed. Flow Trigger Explorer plus the WORKFLOW debug-log category is the pairing that answers 'which of the ten flows on this object actually ran'.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM debugging 'the flow didn't run' goes straight to entry-condition syntax review and never suggests reading the log for the interview-creation events, so it cannot tell the user which of the two failure modes they have. It also rarely names the specific FLOW_* event types.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis references/event-types.md carries the FLOW_* event table and references/flows.md covers multiple flows on one object; flow/flow-interview-debugging and flow/flow-debugging exist. See coverage_verification[21] (event-types.md chunk) and [2].
