practices.practice: Treat API version 67.0 (Summer '26) as a hard security-behaviour boundary: recompiling a class at v67.0 flips its SOQL/SOSL/DML from system mode to user mode and flips an omitted sharing keyword from `without sharing` to `with sharing`. Before bumping any class to 67.0, inventory every query and DML in it and add `WITH SYSTEM_MODE` / `AccessLevel.SYSTEM_MODE` / explicit `without sharing` where elevated access was intentional.
practices.why_it_matters: An API-version bump that looks like housekeeping silently removes records from results and starts throwing FLS exceptions in integration and batch code that legitimately needs elevated access. The change is invisible in a diff — the class body is unchanged, only the meta.xml apiVersion moved.
practices.specifics: API v67.0 = Summer '26. Opt-outs: `Database.query('SELECT…', AccessLevel.SYSTEM_MODE)`, `Database.insert(records, AccessLevel.SYSTEM_MODE)`, `[SELECT … WITH SYSTEM_MODE]`, `public without sharing class X`. Carve-outs: triggers still run implicitly `without sharing` (they cannot carry a keyword) but their database operations still default to user mode at v67.0; inner classes never adopt the container class's sharing mode; anonymous Apex and Connect in Apex always run `with sharing`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models trained before Summer '26 state the pre-v67 rule as timeless: 'Apex runs in system mode by default' and 'a class without a sharing keyword runs without sharing.' They also assert the inverse of the trigger rule — that because a trigger is `without sharing`, its DML bypasses sharing — which is now false. And they routinely 'modernize' a class by raising apiVersion to the newest number as a cosmetic cleanup, unaware they just changed its data-access semantics.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/apex/apex-security-patterns — gotchas.md has '## The Default Sharing Mode Changed In API 67.0' and SKILL.md has '### Triggers Are Always `without sharing` But DML Defaults To User Mode'. Also skills/apex/apex-with-without-sharing-decision. See coverage_verification[0].

practices.practice: When migrating `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` to `WITH USER_MODE`, catch `QueryException` and call `getInaccessibleFields()` to log the complete set of blocked fields, rather than surfacing the raw exception message.
practices.why_it_matters: `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` reports only the first inaccessible field, so a permission-fix cycle becomes fix-one-field / redeploy / repeat. `getInaccessibleFields()` returns them all in one pass, turning an N-iteration support loop into one.
practices.specifics: `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` throws `System.QueryException` with the message `Insufficient permissions: secure query included inaccessible field` and stops at the first violation; it also ignores polymorphic fields (Owner, Task.WhatId) and never inspects WHERE-clause fields. `WITH USER_MODE` inspects the whole query including WHERE, handles polymorphic relationships, and exposes `QueryException.getInaccessibleFields()` returning a `Map<String, Set<String>>` of object → field names. `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` no longer compiles in classes at API v67.0.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models emit `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` as the default 'secure SOQL' idiom because it dominates 2019–2022 training data, and they describe it as 'filtering out inaccessible fields' — it throws, it does not filter. When they do use `WITH USER_MODE` they catch `Exception e` and log `e.getMessage()`, discarding the one piece of information the newer clause exists to provide.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL. skills/apex/soql-security/references/gotchas.md covers 'WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED Throws on ANY Inaccessible Field'; skills/apex/dynamic-apex/references/gotchas.md covers 'WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED Throws, It Does Not Filter'; skills/apex/apex-with-without-sharing-decision covers 'WITH USER_MODE enforces FLS/CRUD, not just sharing'. But `grep -rl getInaccessibleFields skills/` = 0 and `grep -rl 'Insufficient permissions: secure query included inaccessible field' skills/` = 0. See coverage_verification[1].

practices.practice: Pass the third `enforceRootObjectCRUD` argument to `Security.stripInaccessible` when the records originate from an untrusted caller; the two-argument overload checks field-level security only and will happily strip every field then attempt DML on an object the user cannot create.
practices.why_it_matters: The two-argument form leaves an object-level CRUD hole: a user with no Create on the object passes FLS-stripping cleanly and the subsequent insert either succeeds via system-mode DML or fails with a confusing DML error rather than a clear access exception.
practices.specifics: Signatures: `stripInaccessible(AccessType, List<SObject>)`, `stripInaccessible(AccessType, List<SObject>, Boolean enforceRootObjectCRUD)`, and a Developer Preview `stripInaccessible(AccessType, List<SObject>, Boolean, Id permissionSetId)`. Docs: 'Indicates whether an object-level access check is performed. If this parameter is set to true and the access check fails, the method throws an exception.' AccessType values: CREATABLE, READABLE, UPDATABLE, UPSERTABLE. Recover what was dropped with `SObjectAccessDecision.getRemovedFields()`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models always generate the two-argument overload — it is the one in every blog post — and describe stripInaccessible as 'enforcing CRUD and FLS'. They also never call `getRemovedFields()`, so the generated code silently discards user input and the caller gets a 200 OK with fields quietly missing.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL. skills/apex/apex-stripinaccessible-and-fls-enforcement exists and covers the REMOVE-and-continue tradeoff and getRemovedFields (8 files mention getRemovedFields). But `grep -rl enforceRootObjectCRUD skills/` = 0 — the third-argument CRUD gap is not documented anywhere. See coverage_verification[1].

practices.practice: Size synchronous Apex against the concurrent long-running Apex limit using the 5-second threshold and the license-scaled ceiling, not the flat '10' or the API-request '25 over 20 seconds' number — they are three different limits.
practices.why_it_matters: When the ceiling is hit, every new synchronous Apex request in the org is denied — users cannot open records or log in. Teams size for the wrong threshold (20s) and therefore never notice that a 6-second Lightning controller is the thing consuming slots.
practices.specifics: A synchronous Apex transaction begins counting against the org-wide limit once it exceeds 5 seconds. The ceiling is a ratio of 100 licenses to 1 concurrent long-running Apex transaction, with a minimum of 10 and a maximum of 50 (raised from a flat 10 in Spring '25). Asynchronous requests do not count. Diagnose with the `ConcurrentLongRunningApexLimit` Event Monitoring event type. The separate concurrent *API request* limit is 25 requests running longer than 20 seconds.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models conflate the Apex limit with the API limit and state '25 concurrent requests longer than 20 seconds' for Apex. They also treat the ceiling as a fixed 10 and never mention that it now scales with licenses, so capacity math for a large org is off by up to 5x in the wrong direction.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED BUT FACTUALLY WRONG. skills/architect/omnistudio-scalability-patterns/SKILL.md states 'Salesforce enforces a hard limit of **25 concurrent long-running Apex requests** … more than 20 seconds' — that is the API limit's numbers applied to Apex. `grep -rl ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn skills/` = 0. This is a correction, not a new skill. See coverage_verification[2].

practices.practice: Assume any SOQL executed inside a trigger against an object over ~200,000 rows must be selective or the transaction dies — the platform only enforces selectivity as a hard error inside trigger context.
practices.why_it_matters: The identical query runs fine in Execute Anonymous, in a batch, and in a Lightning controller, then throws the moment it is called from a trigger in production. Teams spend the debugging cycle looking for a governor-limit cause that does not exist.
practices.specifics: Exact error: `System.QueryException: Non-selective query against large object type (more than 200000 rows). Consider an indexed filter or contact salesforce.com about custom indexing.` The 200,000-row floor is the object size at which the check activates, not the number of rows returned. Selectivity thresholds that must be met: standard index < 30% of the first million rows and < 15% beyond, capped at 1,000,000 targeted rows; custom index < 10% of the first million and < 5% beyond, capped at 333,333 targeted rows.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models know the selectivity percentages but present non-selective queries purely as a performance concern ('the query will be slow'). They do not know that trigger context converts it into a thrown exception, so they will confidently tell you a query that passed in Developer Console is safe to move into a trigger.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE. `grep -rl 'Non-selective query against large object' skills/` = 0. skills/data/soql-query-optimization covers thresholds, LIKE '%x%', ORDER BY cost, soft-deleted rows, sandbox index copying, and null indexing — but never the trigger-only hard exception or its error string. See coverage_verification[3].

practices.practice: Do not use `@future` as the transaction-splitting mechanism inside Batch Apex — the allocation there is zero — but do use it inside a Queueable, where 50 are allowed.
practices.why_it_matters: The asymmetry decides the shape of an async design. Advising 'never call @future from async' pushes teams into unnecessary Queueable-chaining rewrites when a single `@future(callout=true)` from the Queueable would have been correct and simpler.
practices.specifics: Official per-transaction allocation for methods with the future annotation: 50 synchronous; '0 in batch and future contexts; 50 in queueable context'. Additional hard rules: `@future` methods must be `static`, must return `void`, accept only primitives / arrays of primitives / collections of primitives ('can't take sObjects or objects as arguments'), cannot be called from another `@future`, cannot be used in a Visualforce `getMethodName`/`setMethodName` or constructor, and execution order is not guaranteed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models compress the rule to 'you cannot call a future method from asynchronous context' and lump Queueable in with Batch. They also pass an sObject to a @future method and only catch it at compile time, and they assume two @future calls made in order execute in order.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED BUT PARTLY WRONG. skills/apex/governor-limits/references/gotchas.md #3 correctly covers the batch case. skills/apex/async-apex/references/llm-anti-patterns.md #3 is titled 'Calling a future method from a Batch or Queueable context' — the Queueable half contradicts the official allocation of 50. Correction needed. See coverage_verification[4].

practices.practice: Use `AsyncOptions.MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes` for retry back-off instead of building a Schedulable-based delay or claiming Apex cannot wait; and know that an explicit delay overrides the org-level default.
practices.why_it_matters: Retry-with-back-off is the single most common Apex integration requirement and the platform now has a first-class mechanism for it. Teams that believe no delay primitive exists build Schedulable dispatchers (100 scheduled jobs org-wide limit) or immediate-retry chains that hammer a failing endpoint.
practices.specifics: `AsyncOptions.MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes` accepts 0–10 minutes. The org-wide default is set in Setup → Apex Settings → 'Default minimum enqueue delay (in seconds) for queueable jobs', range 1–600 seconds, and applies only to enqueues that do not specify a delay. Read the effective value at runtime with `System.AsyncInfo.getMinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes()`. Passing a delay explicitly ignores the org-wide setting entirely.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models state flatly that 'Apex has no Thread.sleep() and no way to delay a job' and then generate a Schedulable wrapper that calls `System.scheduleBatch` or builds a CRON string. They have almost no exposure to AsyncOptions beyond MaximumQueueableStackDepth.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for delay. `grep -rl MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes skills/` = 0. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns and skills/apex/long-running-process-orchestration cover AsyncOptions.MaximumQueueableStackDepth only, and skills/integration/retry-and-backoff-patterns/SKILL.md asserts Apex 'cannot introduce delay'. See coverage_verification[5].

practices.practice: De-duplicate queueable enqueues with `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature` and catch `DuplicateMessageException`, rather than a static Set guard — and understand the signature is released when the job is dequeued, not when it finishes.
practices.why_it_matters: Static guards only cover one transaction. A trigger firing across ten separate Data Loader batches enqueues ten identical recalculation jobs; the signature mechanism is the only thing that dedupes across transactions.
practices.specifics: Build with `QueueableDuplicateSignature.Builder().addId(...).addString(...).addInteger(...).build()`, assign to `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature`, pass to `System.enqueueJob(job, options)`. The exception is `DuplicateMessageException` with the exact message `Attempt to enqueue job with duplicate queueable signature`. The signature is removed from the registry when the job is dequeued for execution — 'This removal guarantees that at least one job instance for a given signature runs' — so a job that is already running does not block a fresh enqueue.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models solve duplicate-enqueue with `private static Boolean enqueued = false;`, which is per-transaction and therefore useless for the cross-batch case that actually causes the problem. They have essentially no knowledge of QueueableDuplicateSignature, and if asked they will invent a custom-object-based lock table.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE. `grep -rl QueueableDuplicateSignature skills/` = 0. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns covers MaximumQueueableStackDepth re-setting on every enqueue but not deduplication. See coverage_verification[5].

practices.practice: Before designing around the 250,000/day async ceiling, check whether the org has enabled elastic async limits (Summer '26 Beta) — it changes the failure mode from a hard exception to throttling and doubles the ceiling.
practices.why_it_matters: The classic mitigation for approaching the daily async limit is an architectural rewrite (batch consolidation, event-driven fan-in). If elastic limits are on, jobs past the licensed limit are queued and processed slowly instead of rejected, which is an operational problem, not an architectural one — a completely different remediation.
practices.specifics: Enable at Setup → Apex Settings → 'Use elastic limits for asynchronous Apex jobs (Beta)'. The elastic ceiling is 2× the org's licensed daily limit; the licensed limit itself is '250,000 or the number of applicable user licenses multiplied by 200, whichever is greater'. New OrgLimits keys: `DailyAsyncApexElasticExecutions` and `DailyAsyncApexProcessed`, readable via `System.OrgLimits.getMap()`. The Apex Jobs page in Setup shows a banner with jobs processed in the past 24 hours against both limits.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models state the 250,000 figure as immutable and describe exceeding it as an unconditional failure. They will not ask whether elastic limits are enabled, and they do not know `DailyAsyncApexElasticExecutions` exists, so any monitoring code they generate reads only `DailyAsyncApexExecutions` and reports a misleading utilisation percentage.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE. `grep -rl DailyAsyncApexElasticExecutions skills/` = 0. skills/architect/limits-and-scalability-planning and skills/architect/org-limits-monitoring cover the static 250K limit and OrgLimits keys but predate elastic limits. See coverage_verification[6].

practices.practice: Never assert full-dataset results in a Batch Apex test — only one `execute()` invocation runs per test — so size the test data to a single scope and assert on that scope.
practices.why_it_matters: A test that inserts 250 records and asserts all 250 were processed fails with a 200-vs-250 mismatch that looks like a bug in the batch logic. Developers then add records, change scope size, or add a second `Test.stopTest()`, none of which fix it.
practices.specifics: Documented behaviour: 'When testing your batch Apex, you can test only one execution of the execute method.' Default scope is 200; maximum scope for a `Database.QueryLocator` start method is 2,000 (iterables have no documented cap). 'In a running test, you can submit a maximum of 5 batch jobs.' Org-wide, 'Maximum number of batch Apex job start method concurrent executions: 1' — so a start method that runs long serialises every other batch job in the org, while their execute methods still run in parallel.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models generate batch tests that insert 500+ records to 'prove bulk safety' and then assert on all of them. When it fails they rationalise it as an async-timing problem and add sleeps or extra Test.stopTest() calls. They also never mention that start methods are globally serialised, so they recommend 'split into more batch jobs' as a scaling fix when the start method is the bottleneck.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL. skills/apex/apex-batch-chaining covers 'Test.stopTest() Only Executes One Synchronous Chain Level' (chained jobs, not chunks within one job). `grep -rl 'only one execution of the execute method' skills/` = 0 and `grep -rl 'batch Apex job start method' skills/` = 0. skills/apex/batch-apex-patterns has no single-chunk-in-test gotcha. See coverage_verification[7].

practices.practice: In a `Database.Stateful` batch, keep accumulated state in instance members only — static members are reset between chunk transactions even when the class is Stateful.
practices.why_it_matters: A static error collector or static recursion guard in a Stateful batch produces a silently truncated result: only the last chunk's entries survive into `finish()`, so a summary email reports 3 failures out of 50,000 records instead of 300.
practices.specifics: 'When using Database.Stateful, only instance member variables retain their values between transactions. Static member variables don't retain their values and are reset between transactions.' Each `execute()` is a discrete transaction: 'If the first transaction succeeds but the second fails, the database updates made in the first transaction aren't rolled back.'
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models understand that Stateful preserves state but do not distinguish static from instance. They frequently write `private static List<String> errors` inside a Stateful class — a pattern that compiles, passes a single-chunk unit test, and loses data only at production volume.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL. skills/apex/batch-apex-patterns/references/llm-anti-patterns.md #1 covers 'Accumulating state in instance variables without implementing Database.Stateful' (the inverse error), and skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns covers statics not surviving between chained Queueables. `grep -rl 'static member variables' skills/` = 0 — the static-vs-instance distinction *inside* Stateful is not stated. See coverage_verification[8].

practices.practice: Bound Finalizer-driven retries at 5 or fewer — the platform allows a failed Queueable to be successively re-enqueued exactly five times by a transaction finalizer before the chaining limit stops it, and the counter resets on a successful completion.
practices.why_it_matters: Choosing MAX_RETRIES = 10 produces a retry loop that dies at attempt 6 with a chaining error rather than the designed give-up path, so the compensation logic (write failure record, publish a DLQ event) never runs.
practices.specifics: One finalizer per Queueable job (`System.attachFinalizer(Finalizer)` inside `execute`). A failed Queueable 'can be successively re-enqueued five times by a transaction finalizer'; the counter resets when a job completes successfully. `FinalizerContext.getResult()` returns `ParentJobResult.SUCCESS` or `ParentJobResult.UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`; `getException()` carries the cause. The finalizer runs in a separate Apex and database transaction from the job and does not consume additional daily async Apex executions. Synchronous limits apply inside the finalizer except heap size, System.enqueueJob count, and future-method count, which stay asynchronous.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models pick an arbitrary MAX_RETRIES (usually 3 or 10) with no reference to a platform ceiling, and they describe the finalizer as running 'in the same transaction' as the job — which leads them to expect the job's DML rollback to also roll back the finalizer's logging insert. It does not, and that separation is precisely why finalizer logging works.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL. skills/apex/apex-transaction-finalizers exists and prescribes 'MAX_RETRIES (typically 3–5)' and 'the ONE allowed enqueue from a Finalizer', but never states the platform's own five-successive-re-enqueue ceiling or that the counter resets on success. See coverage_verification[9].

practices.practice: When diagnosing repeated automation, check whether the record is in a recursive save before adding a recursion guard — Salesforce already skips steps 9 through 17 of the order of execution on a recursive save, and workflow field updates re-fire before/after update triggers exactly once more.
practices.why_it_matters: Guard code written for a failure the platform already prevents adds a static flag that later suppresses legitimate second-pass work (the workflow-field-update re-fire), converting a non-bug into a real one.
practices.specifics: 'During a recursive save, Salesforce skips steps 9 (assignment rules) through 17 (roll-up summary field in the grandparent record).' For workflow field updates the platform 'Executes before update triggers and after update triggers, regardless of the record operation (insert or update), one more time (and only one more time).' Roll-up summary recalculation is steps 16–17; Criteria Based Sharing evaluation is step 18, after roll-ups and before commit. Record-triggered flows run at step 3 (before-save) and step 14 (after-save).
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models present the order of execution as a flat numbered list and never mention the recursive-save skip range or the 'one more time (and only one more time)' bound on workflow re-firing. Asked why a trigger ran twice, they default to 'add a static Boolean guard' rather than identifying the workflow field update as the documented, bounded, second pass.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL. skills/apex/order-of-execution-deep-dive enumerates the steps and skills/admin/workflow-field-update-patterns covers the overlap, but `grep -rn 'recursive save\|skips steps' skills/apex/order-of-execution-deep-dive/` = 0 hits. The skip range and the exactly-once re-fire bound are absent. See coverage_verification[10].

practices.practice: Stop attributing `System.LimitException: Apex CPU time limit exceeded` to slow queries — database execution time for SOQL, SOSL and DML and callout wait time are all excluded from the CPU clock.
practices.why_it_matters: The wrong diagnosis leads to index requests and query rewrites that cannot move the number. The real consumers are loops over collections, Map/Set construction, string concatenation, JSON serialization, describe calls, and formula-field evaluation triggered by DML.
practices.specifics: Verbatim: 'Application server CPU time spent in DML operations is counted towards the Apex CPU limit. Operations that don't consume application server CPU time aren't counted toward CPU time. For example, the portion of execution time spent in the database for DML, SOQL, and SOSL isn't counted, nor is waiting time for Apex callouts.' Limits: 10,000 ms synchronous, 60,000 ms asynchronous, with a separate 10-minute maximum transaction execution time. `System.LimitException` cannot be caught: 'If some Apex code exceeds a limit, the associated governor issues a runtime exception that can't be handled.'
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to fix a CPU-time exception, models reliably recommend 'optimize your SOQL' and 'add selective filters' — advice for a limit that excludes query time. They also generate `try { … } catch (LimitException e) { … }` recovery scaffolding around bulk loops, which never executes.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/apex-limits-monitoring ('CPU Time and Callouts', '`System.LimitException` Is Uncatchable'), skills/apex/apex-performance-profiling (gotcha 5 + anti-pattern 5), skills/apex/governor-limit-recovery-patterns, skills/apex/common-apex-runtime-errors. See coverage_verification[11] and [12].

practices.practice: When the running user's identity matters to a platform-event subscriber, set it explicitly via `PlatformEventSubscriberConfig` and lower `batchSize` from the default 2,000 — a PE trigger's batch is ten times a normal trigger's.
practices.why_it_matters: A subscriber written and tested against 200 events hits 101 SOQL / 151 DML / CPU limits the first time production delivers a real burst, and it fails as the Automated Process user, which has no assigned permission sets, so any FLS-enforced query in it returns nothing.
practices.specifics: Default platform-event trigger batch is 2,000 event messages versus 200 for an sObject trigger. `PlatformEventSubscriberConfig` (Metadata API / Tooling API) sets `batchSize` from 1 through 2,000 and overrides the running user, which otherwise defaults to Automated Process.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models write platform-event triggers with the same bulkification instincts as record triggers and state the batch is 200. They also never mention the Automated Process running user, so their `WITH USER_MODE` query inside a PE trigger silently returns an empty list in production.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/apex-event-bus-subscriber cites 'platform event subscriber 2000 events governor limit' and 'PlatformEventSubscriberConfig' in its trigger scenarios; 7 files reference PlatformEventSubscriberConfig. See coverage_verification[13].

practices.practice: Choose exactly one platform-event retry mechanism per trigger: `setResumeCheckpoint(event.ReplayId)` OR `EventBus.RetryableException` — combining them reprocesses already-checkpointed events.
practices.why_it_matters: The hybrid is the intuitive design (checkpoint on success, retry on failure) and it is the one that produces duplicate side effects, because RetryableException refires the whole original batch regardless of the checkpoint.
practices.specifics: A trigger runs at most 10 times — the initial run plus 9 retries — after which it moves to the error state and stops processing new events. Guard with `EventBus.TriggerContext.currentContext().retries`; the docs' own sample caps at `< 4`. RetryableException may only be thrown before `setResumeCheckpoint` has been called in that invocation. If the exception recurs after retries are exhausted, the first event is skipped and the loop continues from the next event.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models write the hybrid — checkpoint after every success and throw RetryableException in the catch — because both appear in the docs and each looks like defensive programming. They also throw RetryableException unconditionally with no `retries` check, which walks the trigger straight into the error state where it stops consuming events entirely.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/apex-event-bus-subscriber: SKILL.md 'Three retry strategies and when to use each', gotchas.md 'Gotcha 3: RetryableException reprocesses already-checkpointed events', llm-anti-patterns.md 'Anti-Pattern 4: Mixing checkpoint and RetryableException'. See coverage_verification[13].

practices.practice: Use the `Assert` class for new tests, and remember that `Assert.isInstanceOfType` inverts the argument order used by every other method in the class.
practices.why_it_matters: An inverted expected/actual pair still compiles and still passes or fails correctly on equality, but produces a backwards failure message that sends the next developer looking at the wrong side of the comparison.
practices.specifics: `Assert` was added in Winter '23 (API 56.0). `Assert.areEqual(Object expected, Object actual, String message)` — expected first. `Assert.isInstanceOfType(Object actual, Type expected, String message)` — actual first. Docs note: 'Assert method isInstanceOfType accepts the first parameter as the actual type, followed by the expected type and then the custom message. While for the rest of the Assert methods, the first parameter is the expected result followed by the actual result.' Other members: isTrue, isFalse, isNull, isNotNull, areNotEqual, isNotInstanceOfType, fail.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models emit `System.assertEquals(actual, expected)` — reversed from the correct `(expected, actual)` — because natural reading order puts the thing under test first. They also generate `Assert.isInstanceOfType(Account.class, record)` by analogy with areEqual, which is the exact inversion the docs warn about.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/test-class-standards: SKILL.md '### Prefer The `System.Assert` Class For Assertions' naming Winter '23 / API 56.0, examples.md 'Example 3: Same Test Written With The System.Assert Class', gotchas.md '`Assert` Messages Must Be Strings'; isInstanceOfType appears in SKILL.md. See coverage_verification[14].

practices.practice: Route Apex performance triage through ApexGuru's runtime profiles before hand-profiling, but confirm the org qualifies first — it is gated behind Scale Center, which requires Unlimited Edition production/Full Copy sandbox or a Signature Success Plan.
practices.why_it_matters: A recommendation to 'enable ApexGuru' in an Enterprise Edition org with a Premier plan is dead on arrival, and the team wastes a cycle raising a case. Conversely, orgs that do qualify usually have not turned it on and are hand-profiling work the platform already did.
practices.specifics: Activation path: Setup → Scale Center (enable) → ApexGuru Insights → accept the ApexGuru Agreement. It analyses via the Einstein Trust Layer using runtime profiles rather than static analysis. Insight categories: Code Recommendations (critical/major/minor), SOQL/DML analysis, Expensive Methods (critically expensive ≥ 5% of CPU time; expensive 2–5%), and Unused Classes and Methods from the most recent production deployment. Separately, Salesforce Code Analyzer v5 bundles PMD 7.5 for static Apex/Visualforce rules and now surfaces ApexGuru findings in the VS Code extension.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models do not know ApexGuru exists at all — it postdates most training corpora and has thin blog coverage. Asked to find Apex performance hotspots they will always propose manual `Limits.getCpuTime()` instrumentation or PMD, never the runtime-profile tool. When they do mention it they omit the edition/success-plan gate, which is the first thing that determines whether the advice is actionable.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE. `grep -rl ApexGuru skills/` = 0, `grep -rl 'Scale Center' skills/` = 0, `grep -rl 'Signature Success' skills/` = 0. Code Analyzer is mentioned in 24 files but not ApexGuru integration. See coverage_verification[15].

practices.practice: Keep mocking callouts with `HttpCalloutMock` for unit tests; reach for `@IntegrationTest` only in scratch orgs with the `ApexIntegrationTests` feature, and only for Agentforce / Data 360 flows that genuinely cannot be asserted against a mock.
practices.why_it_matters: `@IntegrationTest` makes real callouts and commits data mid-transaction. Used casually it produces tests that mutate a shared org, cannot run in a deployment validation, and fail non-deterministically when the remote service is down.
practices.specifics: Summer '26, Developer Preview, scratch orgs only. Requires `ApexIntegrationTests` in the scratch org definition `features` array. Enables live callouts, mid-transaction commits via `IntegrationTest.commitTestOnly()`, and cleanup in a `@TearDown` method. Standard unit tests still cannot make callouts — attempting one raises `Methods defined as TestMethod do not support Web service callouts`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models do not know the annotation exists and, when asked how to test a real integration, either say it is impossible or invent `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)` plus a Named Credential as a workaround. Conversely, once told it exists, a model will over-apply it to ordinary REST callout tests where HttpCalloutMock is the correct answer.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for @IntegrationTest. `grep -rl 'IntegrationTest' skills/` returns only a class name inside a sfdx CLI example. skills/apex/test-class-standards and skills/apex/apex-http-callout-mocking cover mocking thoroughly. See coverage_verification[16].

practices.practice: Enqueue chained Queueables with an explicit `AsyncOptions.MaximumQueueableStackDepth` re-set on every link in the chain, and design chains to terminate within 5 levels if the code must run in Developer Edition or a Trial org.
practices.why_it_matters: A chain that works in a sandbox dies in a Developer Edition scratch org or a Trailhead Playground with 'Maximum stack depth has been reached', which is usually the first environment a package is tested in.
practices.specifics: 'For Developer Edition and Trial organizations, the maximum stack depth for chained jobs is 5, which means that you can chain jobs four times.' 'When chaining jobs with System.enqueueJob, you can add only one job from an executing job.' Per transaction: 50 jobs may be added synchronously, 1 asynchronously. `AsyncOptions.MaximumQueueableStackDepth` is not inherited down the chain — it must be re-supplied at each `enqueueJob` call.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models generate unbounded self-chaining Queueables ('enqueue the next batch until no records remain') with no depth cap and no Developer Edition caveat, and they assume a depth limit set on the first enqueue governs the whole chain.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns/references/gotchas.md '`MaximumQueueableStackDepth` Must Be Re-Set On Every Enqueue Call In The Chain'; skills/apex/long-running-process-orchestration also covers AsyncOptions and attachFinalizer. See coverage_verification[5].

practices.practice: Do not use a static Boolean as a trigger recursion guard; use a static `Set<Id>` of processed record IDs, and remember neither survives a rollback.
practices.why_it_matters: A static Boolean set on the first 200-record chunk suppresses every subsequent chunk in the same transaction, so records 201+ are silently skipped — the defect appears only at Data Loader volume and produces no error.
practices.specifics: Trigger batch size is 200 records per invocation. Recursive trigger stack depth is capped at 16 ('Maximum trigger depth exceeded'). `Database.rollback(savepoint)` resets `Limits` counters for DML and queries but does not reset static variables — a guard set before a rollback stays set.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The static Boolean guard is the single most reproduced Apex snippet on the internet and models emit it unprompted. They also assume a rollback restores static state, so a guard-plus-savepoint retry pattern they generate silently no-ops on the retry.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/recursive-trigger-prevention (llm-anti-patterns #1 'Using a single static Boolean guard that blocks ALL re-entry', Set<Id>-based guard section), skills/apex/order-of-execution-deep-dive (anti-pattern 4), skills/apex/trigger-framework examples, skills/apex/governor-limit-recovery-patterns ('Static Variables Are Not Reset on Rollback'). See coverage_verification[17].

practices.practice: Filter on a field whose index actually exists and is selective, and check for null-filter and formula-field traps — index tables exclude null rows by default and non-deterministic formula fields cannot be indexed at all.
practices.why_it_matters: `WHERE Status__c = null` on a 5M-row object is a full table scan no matter how many custom indexes exist, and a custom index request on a cross-object formula field is rejected, so teams wait weeks on a support case that was never going to help.
practices.specifics: Standard-indexed by default: Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp/LastModifiedDate, RecordTypeId, Division, Email (Contact/Lead), and all lookup/master-detail foreign keys. Custom indexes cannot be created on: text area (long), text area (rich), non-deterministic formula fields, encrypted text. External IDs auto-index and are allowed only on Auto Number, Email, Number, Text. 'By default, index tables exclude null records' — Support can enable null-inclusive custom indexes on request. Soft-deleted (recycle bin) rows count toward the selectivity denominator.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models recommend 'add a custom index on that field' for any slow query without checking field type, and they treat `!= null` / `= null` filters as ordinary predicates. They also assume a custom index created in production exists in every sandbox.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/data/soql-query-optimization SKILL.md '**Null handling:** By default, index tables do not include null-value records…', gotchas.md covers per-field thresholds, leading-wildcard LIKE, ORDER BY cost, soft-deleted rows inflating denominators, and custom indexes only copying to Full sandboxes; check_soql_query_optimization.py flags null filters on custom fields. skills/data/custom-index-requests also exists. See coverage_verification[18].

practices.practice: Treat `Database.getQueryLocator` outside Batch Apex as a 10,000-row ceiling, not an unbounded cursor; only a Batch `start()` method gets the 50 million row allowance.
practices.why_it_matters: Code that uses a QueryLocator in a Visualforce StandardSetController or a Queueable to 'avoid the 50,000 row limit' hits a lower limit, not a higher one, and fails at a volume that looks arbitrary.
practices.specifics: Per-transaction: 'Total number of records retrieved by Database.getQueryLocator: 10,000' versus 'Total number of records retrieved by SOQL queries: 50,000'. 'Maximum number of records returned for a Batch Apex query in Database.QueryLocator: 50 million.' SOQL for-loop list batch size is 200.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models present `Database.getQueryLocator` as the generic answer to 'too many query rows', without distinguishing batch from non-batch context — inverting the actual limits (10,000 vs 50,000).
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/governor-limits SKILL.md limits table; 78 files reference Database.getQueryLocator and 21 reference the 10,000-row figure. See coverage_verification[11].

practices.practice: Write tests against a data factory and treat `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)` as a defect, not a shortcut — and use `Test.startTest()`/`Test.stopTest()` to both reset governor limits and force async work to execute before assertions.
practices.why_it_matters: SeeAllData tests pass in the org they were written in and fail in a scratch org, a fresh sandbox, and any CI pipeline; they also silently couple the test suite to production data that changes.
practices.specifics: `Test.startTest()` grants a fresh set of governor limits for the code between the markers; all asynchronous work started inside the block runs synchronously at `Test.stopTest()`. Unit tests cannot make callouts — `Methods defined as TestMethod do not support Web service callouts` — so `Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock)` is mandatory. `@IsTest(isParallel=true)` opts a class out of the org-wide test-parallelism setting, which matters when tests contend on the same setup objects and produce UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models assert immediately after `Database.executeBatch` or `System.enqueueJob` without a `Test.stopTest()` and then explain the failure as 'async timing'. They also add `SeeAllData=true` as the fix for any test that fails on missing reference data (pricebooks, record types).
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/test-class-standards (llm-anti-patterns #3 'Not using Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() for async operations'; well-architected anti-patterns list SeeAllData), skills/apex/test-data-factory-patterns, skills/apex/apex-test-setup-patterns, skills/apex/apex-http-callout-mocking, skills/apex/apex-mocking-and-stubs, skills/apex/async-apex ('Async Tests Pass Only After Test.stopTest()'). 48 files mention SeeAllData, 49 mention Test.setMock. See coverage_verification[16] and [19].

practices.practice: Split callouts away from DML rather than reordering them — a callout after any uncommitted DML in the same transaction throws, and the fix is an async boundary, not a rearrangement.
practices.why_it_matters: Reordering to put the callout first works until a trigger upstream performs DML, at which point the same error returns from a code path that was never touched.
practices.specifics: Exact error: `You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out.` It is raised by any DML earlier in the transaction, including DML performed by a trigger the caller did not write. Remedies: `@future(callout=true)` (0 allowed from batch/future context, 50 from queueable), a Queueable implementing `Database.AllowsCallouts`, or splitting the DML into a finalizer/second transaction. Per transaction: 100 callouts, 120 seconds cumulative timeout.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models 'fix' this by moving the callout above the insert in the method they were shown, which does not address DML performed by triggers or by callers, and they omit `Database.AllowsCallouts` from Queueable classes that make callouts.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. 55 files reference 'uncommitted work pending'; skills/apex/callout-and-dml-transaction-boundaries is a dedicated package; skills/integration/callout-limits-and-async-patterns covers @future vs Queueable for callouts. See coverage_verification[4].

practices.practice: Consolidate to one trigger per object delegating to a handler with an externally controllable bypass, so automation can be disabled for a data load without a deployment.
practices.why_it_matters: Multiple triggers on an object have no guaranteed execution order, and without a bypass switch a 2-million-row migration either runs every trigger (blowing the async budget and CPU) or requires deploying commented-out code to production.
practices.specifics: Trigger batch size is 200 per invocation regardless of the API batch size — a Bulk API batch of 10,000 fires the trigger 50 times. Recursive trigger stack depth is capped at 16. Bypass is conventionally driven by a hierarchy Custom Setting or Custom Metadata Type checked in the handler's entry point.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models write logic directly in the trigger body, or generate a handler with no bypass hook, and they claim trigger execution order can be controlled by naming convention or alphabetical order — Salesforce guarantees no order among multiple triggers on the same object.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED. skills/apex/trigger-framework (with templates/trigger_handler.cls), skills/apex/apex-trigger-bypass-and-killswitch-patterns, skills/apex/feature-flags-and-kill-switches, skills/apex/apex-trigger-context-variables, plus the /consolidate-triggers runtime agent. See coverage_verification[17].

practices.practice: Re-assign the field to trigger a re-render; add @track ONLY for plain objects/arrays, and never expect @track to observe a Date, Set, Map, or class instance.
practices.why_it_matters: A component silently shows stale data with no error in the console — the mutation succeeded in memory, so nothing looks broken. Teams then add @track to a Map and ship a permanently stale UI.
practices.specifics: reactivity-fields.html: changes are detected "by comparing the value identity using `===`"; "When manipulating complex types like objects and arrays, you must create a new object and assign it to the field for the change to be detected"; @track "observes mutations made to plain objects and arrays in a recursive fashion, including nested objects, nested arrays" — but "the framework doesn't observe mutations made to complex objects, such as objects inheriting from `Object`, class instances, `Date`, `Set`, or `Map`." Fix pattern: `this.items = [...this.items, row]`, `this.rec = { ...this.rec, Name: v }`, and for Map/Set `this.myMap = new Map(this.myMap).set(k, v)`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Two failures, in sequence. First it writes `this.items.push(row)` (React/Vue muscle memory). When told the UI doesn't update, it 'fixes' it by adding `@track` — which works for `[]`/`{}` and therefore reinforces the wrong mental model. It then applies the same fix to a `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, or a class instance (`this.selection = new Set(); @track selection;`) where @track does nothing at all, and confidently asserts the bug is fixed. It also still emits `@track` on primitives, which has been unnecessary since Spring '20.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-performance (gotchas.md Gotcha 1 is exactly the Date/Set/Map case) and lwc/lwc-reactive-state-patterns. search_knowledge.py returns `lwc/lwc-performance (1.373)` and `lwc/lwc-reactive-state-patterns (0.805)` — COVERED, no gap.

practices.practice: Diagnose 'my property changed but nothing re-rendered' against the read-set rule, not the @track rule: LWC re-renders only if a property that was ACCESSED during the previous rendering cycle changes.
practices.why_it_matters: Explains the class of staleness bugs that survive after @track is correctly applied — a property first read inside a getter that was short-circuited, or inside an `lwc:if` branch that was false last render, will not schedule a re-render when it changes.
practices.specifics: reactivity-fields.html: "A component rerenders only if a property accessed during the previous rendering cycle is updated, even when the object is annotated with `@track`." And: components rerender when "a field's value changes, and the field is used in a template or in a getter of a property that's used in a template." Corollary: a getter with an early `return ''` that never touches `this.x` de-registers `x` from the read-set for that cycle.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: When a re-render doesn't happen, an LLM reaches for exactly three fixes in order: add @track, deep-clone with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))`, or force a re-render by toggling a dummy boolean. It never diagnoses the read-set: it does not know that LWC tracks which properties were *read* during render, so it cannot explain why an identical mutation re-renders in one branch and not another. The `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` suggestion additionally destroys `Date` values and drops `undefined` keys.

practices.practice: Copy wire-provisioned data before mutating it; the wire service emits a read-only (frozen) proxy.
practices.why_it_matters: `this.wiredRows.data.push(x)` throws `Invalid mutation: Cannot set "0" on "[object Object]". "[object Object]" is read-only.` in dev mode and no-ops in production, which is worse.
practices.specifics: Wire service "provisions an immutable stream of data"; the runtime error text is `Invalid mutation: Cannot set "<prop>" on "[object Object]". "[object Object]" is read-only.` Fix: `this.rows = [...result.data]` or a per-row spread; a shallow copy of the array is NOT enough if you mutate a row object — you must spread the row too.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes `this.data.forEach(r => r.selected = false)` or `data.map(r => { r.x = 1; return r; })` — the `map` form looks immutable but mutates each frozen row and throws on the first element. It also commonly 'fixes' the read-only error with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(data))`, which works but silently converts every date field to a string and inflates heap for large result sets.

practices.practice: Distinguish undefined from null in a `$`-prefixed reactive wire config: undefined suppresses the call entirely, null issues the call with a null argument.
practices.why_it_matters: The undefined case is a silent no-request failure (no network entry, no error, no data); the null case is a real server round-trip that can throw a server-side NPE or return the wrong result set. They need opposite fixes and are indistinguishable in the UI.
practices.specifics: apex-wire-method.html: "If a parameter value is `null`, the method is called. If a parameter value is `undefined`, the method isn't called." Diagnostic: filter DevTools Network by `/aura?...ApexActionController` or `/ui-api/` — zero requests means undefined; a request with `"param":null` means null. Common cause of the undefined case: `@api recordId` is undefined on the first render of an App Builder-placed component.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It states 'the wire won't fire if the parameter is null or undefined' as one rule, then recommends the param-nulling hack (`this.filter = null; this.filter = value;`) as a way to force a wire re-run — which actually fires a real Apex call with null and can blow up server-side. It also adds a defensive `if (!this.recordId) return;` inside a wired *function*, which does nothing because the adapter was never invoked in the first place.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/wire-service-patterns (1.450) covers the undefined half explicitly ('If a required reactive parameter is `undefined`, the wire adapter is not evaluated') and its llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 6 covers it. The `null` DOES call the method half is the delta.

practices.practice: Store and pass the entire wire-provisioned result object to refreshApex(), not its `.data`.
practices.why_it_matters: `refreshApex(this.rows.data)` resolves without error and refreshes nothing — the classic 'refresh does nothing' ticket.
practices.specifics: apex-result-caching.html: "The parameter you refresh with `refreshApex()` must be an object that was previously emitted by an Apex `@wire`." So capture it in a wired function: `@wire(getRows) wiredRows(result) { this._wired = result; ... }` and call `refreshApex(this._wired)`. refreshApex returns a Promise whose resolved value is meaningless — use `.then()`/`await` only for sequencing.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Because the destructured `@wire(getRows) wired({data, error})` form is the one it has seen most, it has no handle on the raw result and passes `this.rows`, `this.data`, or the imperative Apex return value. It also calls `refreshApex()` after an *imperative* Apex call that was never wired, where it is a guaranteed no-op.

practices.practice: Call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable with an array of OBJECTS `[{ recordId }]`, await the returned Promise, and know it only refreshes records already in the LDS cache.
practices.why_it_matters: Passing bare ID strings silently refreshes nothing. Not awaiting means the follow-on UI work runs before LDS has re-emitted.
practices.specifics: reference-notify-record-update.html: the argument is "An array of objects with an object shape of `{ recordId: string }`", the ID "can be either 15 or 18 characters long", it returns "A Promise object that is resolved when Lightning Data Service has completed its processing", it "refreshes those records that are in the LDS cache", and "Values are not re-emitted to wires whose data has not changed, per the usual semantics of `@wire`." It does NOT refresh Apex wires — use refreshApex for those. `getRecordNotifyChange(recordIds)` is deprecated; it "isn't suitable for use with multiple adapters that return data of the same type".
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable([this.recordId])` — a plain string array — roughly as often as the correct object form, because the deprecated `getRecordNotifyChange` examples it memorised are ambiguous in prose. It also still emits `getRecordNotifyChange` for new code, and expects notifyRecordUpdateAvailable to refresh an Apex `@wire` or a related-list component.

practices.practice: Never state or design around a specific client-side cache duration for `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`.
practices.why_it_matters: A component built on 'the cache expires in N minutes' breaks when Salesforce retunes it, and the failure mode is stale data shown to a user after a write.
practices.specifics: apex-result-caching.html: "the default cache duration can change as we optimize the platform. When you design your Lightning web components, don't assume a cache duration." Also: "To set `cacheable=true`, a method must only get data, it can't mutate (change) data." If freshness matters per page visit, use a non-cacheable imperative call; if you need to invalidate, use refreshApex on the wired value.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It confidently quotes a number — '15 minutes', '5 minutes', 'the session' — because those figures circulate in blog posts. It also marks a method `cacheable=false` 'to force fresh data' in a `@wire`, which is invalid (the wire simply never fires), and marks a DML-performing method `cacheable=true`, which fails at runtime.
