practices.practice: Put any non-trivial boolean in a getter — `lwc:if` and `lwc:elseif` accept only property access with simple dot notation.
practices.why_it_matters: `lwc:if={items.length > 0}` is a compile error, not a runtime one, so it blocks the deploy; and `lwc:if={items.length}` (which compiles) silently renders on a truthy number rather than a boolean.
practices.specifics: reference-directives.html: "The expression passed in to `lwc:if` and `lwc:elseif` supports simple dot notation. Complex expressions like `!condition`, `object?.property?.condition` or `sum % 2 === 1` aren't supported." Also "The expressions and property getters are only accessed once per instance of an `lwc:if` or `lwc:elseif`" — versus chained `if:true`/`if:false`, which "are not as performant nor as lightweight" because each directive evaluates its own expression. `if:true`/`if:false` "are no longer recommended and may be deprecated and removed in the future."
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes React-style template expressions — `lwc:if={!isLoading}`, `lwc:if={records.length > 0}`, `lwc:if={status === 'ready'}` — all of which fail to compile. It also emits `if:true={x}` alongside `lwc:if` in the same file because its training data spans both eras, and pairs `lwc:if` with `if:false` (which is not a valid `lwc:else` partner).
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-conditional-rendering (gotchas.md Gotcha 7 'Complex Boolean Expressions Belong In Getters, Not The Template' lists exactly `lwc:if={a && b}`, `{items.length > 0}`, `{status !== 'error'}`). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-conditional-rendering (1.600)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Use `lwc:if` to lazily instantiate; CSS hiding constructs, wires, and runs the whole subtree.
practices.why_it_matters: A tab panel hidden with `class="slds-hide"` still fires its `@wire` adapters and Apex calls on page load, so the 'optimisation' costs a full server round-trip per hidden panel while showing nothing.
practices.specifics: Per Salesforce's LWC performance guidance, conditional rendering lazily instantiates part of the UI, whereas with CSS "the component and all of its children are created and rendered up front" and "if there is any event associated with it, then it would be executed." The trade-off: `lwc:if` flipping to false destroys the subtree, fires `disconnectedCallback`, and discards partially-entered user input — so use a CSS class deliberately when state must survive a toggle.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to 'improve page load performance', it recommends hiding off-screen components with CSS and asserts that hidden components 'do not impact performance'. Conversely, asked to build a wizard, it uses `lwc:if` per step and is surprised that step 1's inputs are blank on Back — it does not connect unmount to state loss.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/lwc-conditional-rendering SKILL.md covers 'Keep-State Toggle vs Reset-State Toggle' and '`lwc:if` unmounts — it does not hide'; admin/lightning-page-performance-tuning examples.md covers the wire-never-fires benefit. Retrieval on this phrasing surfaces admin/lightning-page-performance-tuning (1.200) first, not an LWC skill — a trigger-keyword gap more than a content gap.

practices.practice: Give every `for:each`/`iterator` item a stable business key — a string or number, never the loop index, never an object.
practices.why_it_matters: An index key makes LWC reuse the wrong DOM node when the list reorders or a row is deleted, so inline-edit values and focus jump to the wrong record — a data-integrity bug, not a cosmetic one.
practices.specifics: create-lists.html: "Every item in a list must have a `key`"; "The `key` must be a string or a number, it can't be an object"; "You can't use `index` as a value for `key`"; "The `key` in the template is used for performance optimization and isn't reflected in the DOM at run time" — so you cannot read it back with `event.target.key` or a `[key=...]` selector. Use `data-id={row.Id}` plus `event.currentTarget.dataset.id` instead.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It ports React's `key={index}` verbatim (`for:index="i"` + `key={i}`), which LWC rejects at compile time — and when that fails it generates a synthetic key by concatenating fields, producing a key that changes on every edit. It also tries to retrieve the key from the DOM in a click handler (`event.target.key`), which is always undefined because the key is never emitted to the DOM.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 5 covers a computed key that changes across re-renders, and lwc/lwc-conditional-rendering gotchas.md Gotcha 6 covers `lwc:if` inside `for:each`. But search_knowledge.py for 'for:each key must be unique string or number cannot use index' returns `architect/salesforce-shield-architecture (1.156)` and `data/external-id-strategy (0.461)` at the top — no LWC skill wins. Real retrieval gap; the 'key is not reflected in the DOM' fact is absent.

practices.practice: Dispatch custom events with the default `bubbles: false, composed: false` and re-dispatch at each level; reserve composed events for genuinely global signals.
practices.why_it_matters: `composed: true` events escape the shadow boundary and can be caught by any ancestor including platform containers, creating invisible coupling; and once retargeted, the listener cannot identify the real source.
practices.specifics: events-best-practices.html: "Use events configured with `bubbles: false` and `composed: false` because they're the least disruptive"; "Bubbling and composed events are not recommended because they bubble up the entire DOM tree, across shadow boundaries"; "When an event bubbles up the DOM, if it crosses the shadow boundary, the value of `Event.target` changes to match the scope of the listener" — so a parent's `event.target` is the child host element, not the inner button.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It defaults to `{ bubbles: true, composed: true }` on every CustomEvent because that is what makes cross-component demos 'just work'. Then, in the parent handler, it reads `event.target.dataset.recordId` expecting the originating button, gets the child host element, and papers over the undefined with optional chaining rather than moving the payload into `event.detail`.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/component-communication (llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 2 is exactly 'Dispatching custom events with bubbles: true, composed: true by default') and lwc/common-lwc-runtime-errors (Anti-Pattern 6 on event.target retargeting), lwc/lwc-custom-event-patterns (bubbles+composed truth table). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/component-communication (1.183)`, `lwc/lwc-custom-event-patterns (0.800)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Copy any object or array into a new instance before putting it on `event.detail`.
practices.why_it_matters: `detail` is passed by reference, so any listener anywhere can mutate the dispatcher's own state without its knowledge — and since the mutation is in-place, it will not even re-render the dispatcher.
practices.specifics: events-best-practices.html: "JavaScript passes all data types by reference except for primitives. If a component includes an object in its `detail` property, any listener can mutate that object without the component's knowledge." And: "Before you add data to the `detail` property, copy it to a new object or array." Prefer primitives outright: `detail: { recordId: this.record.Id }` over `detail: this.record`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes `detail: this.selectedRow` or `detail: { rows: this.rows }` as the idiomatic payload, treating detail like a React callback argument. It does not warn that the parent's `event.detail.rows.push(...)` will corrupt the child's array, and if the payload came from a `@wire` it will additionally throw the read-only Invalid mutation error in the parent — an error the LLM then misattributes to the parent's own code.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — the event-payload skills (lwc/component-communication, lwc/lwc-custom-event-patterns) surface on the bubbles/composed query but the returned chunks are about bubbles/composed and naming, not detail-by-reference. Likely a small content delta.

practices.practice: Name custom events as a single lowercase token, no `on` prefix, no camelCase, no hyphen.
practices.why_it_matters: A mis-named event binds to nothing and fails silently — no console error, the handler simply never runs.
practices.specifics: events-create-dispatch.html: "No uppercase letters", "No spaces", "Use underscores to separate words", and "Don't prefix your event name with the string `on`, because inline event handler names must start with the string `on`" — an event named `onmessage` would require the markup `<c-my-component ononmessage={handleMessage}>`. Template listeners are `oneventtype`, so event `previous` → `onprevious`. Because HTML attribute names are case-insensitive, `selectionChange` can never be bound from a template.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It generates camelCase event names (`new CustomEvent('rowSelect')` with `onrowselect={...}`) at a high rate because JS convention favours camelCase, and the mismatch produces zero diagnostics. It also occasionally names the event `onselect` and then writes `onselect={handler}` in the parent, which binds a *different*, never-fired event.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-custom-event-patterns (SKILL.md 'Event Naming Rules Are Non-Negotiable'; gotchas.md #5 'Naming an event with `on` prefix or camelCase silently breaks template binding'; check script has VALID_EVENT_NAME_RE) and lwc/component-communication gotchas.md 'Event Names Are Public API'. search_knowledge.py: `lwc/component-communication (1.314)`, `lwc/lwc-custom-event-patterns (1.171)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Default every boolean `@api` property to false, and never name a field or method `slot`, `part`, `dataset`, or anything matching `data[A-Z]`.
practices.why_it_matters: A boolean `@api` initialised to `true` can never be set to false from markup — the attribute-presence semantics of HTML booleans make it a one-way switch. The reserved names collide with native element APIs and fail at compile time or corrupt `this.dataset`.
practices.specifics: Salesforce's own eslint-plugin-lwc `valid-api` rule: "Fields and methods can't be named `slot`, `part` or `dataset`, as these names are reserved by LWC"; "Fields and methods can't start with `data[A-Z]`, as these are mapped to the reflected property `this.dataset.*`"; and boolean public properties "must be initialized with `false`" — "by initializing a public property to true, the consumer component can't set its value to false via the template." camelCase JS properties map to kebab-case attributes (`recordId` → `record-id`).
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes `@api isVisible = true;` or `@api showHeader = true;` to express a sensible default, producing a property the consumer can never turn off — and then, when asked to fix it, adds an `if (this.showHeader === undefined)` guard instead of flipping to a negative-sense property (`hideHeader = false`). It also freely declares `@api dataset` or `@api dataValue` for 'data attributes'.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-public-api-hardening (SKILL.md review checklist on @api coercion; check_lwc_public_api_hardening.py encodes BOOLEAN_NAMES/BOOLEAN_PREFIXES and flags boolean-shaped @api bare fields). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-public-api-hardening (1.517)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Treat renderedCallback as running after EVERY render, flowing child-to-parent, and never write a public property or a wire-config property inside it.
practices.why_it_matters: An unguarded write inside renderedCallback is an infinite render loop that pins a CPU core; a write to a wire config property re-fires the adapter on every render, generating an unbounded stream of server calls.
practices.specifics: create-lifecycle-hooks-rendered.html: "This hook flows from child to parent"; "Updating the state of your component in `renderedCallback()` can cause an infinite loop"; "Don't update a wire adapter configuration object property in `renderedCallback()`"; "Don't update a public property or field in `renderedCallback()`"; and for one-time work "use a boolean field like `hasRendered` to track whether `renderedCallback()` has been executed."
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It maps renderedCallback onto React's `useEffect(..., [])` and puts one-time initialisation there with no guard — chart library bootstrapping, `loadScript`, focus calls, imperative Apex. When shown the loop it adds a `hasRendered` guard but still leaves a public-property or wire-config assignment inside the guarded block on a later re-entry path. It also assumes the parent's renderedCallback runs before the child's, so it queries a child's internals from the parent and gets null.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-reactive-state-patterns (SKILL.md '4. The `renderedCallback` infinite-loop trap'; template has a `_hasRenderedOnce` audit), lwc/lifecycle-hooks (llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 3; gotchas.md), lwc/lwc-async-patterns gotchas.md Gotcha 3, lwc/aura-to-lwc-migration gotchas.md Gotcha 3. search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-reactive-state-patterns (1.350)` — COVERED. Delta: the child→parent ordering and the two explicit 'don't update' rules.

practices.practice: Scope errorCallback correctly: it catches errors in DESCENDANT components' lifecycle hooks and template-declared handlers only — not programmatically-added listeners, not promise rejections, not the boundary component's own render.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams ship an 'error boundary' that catches nothing, because the failures they actually see are rejected fetch/Apex promises and listeners registered with addEventListener.
practices.specifics: create-lifecycle-hooks-error.html: errorCallback "captures errors that occur in lifecycle hooks or during an event handler declared in an HTML template"; it captures errors in "all the descendent components in its tree"; "Errors from programmatically assigned event handlers are not caught by `errorCallback()`." Signature is `errorCallback(error, stack)` where "the `error` argument is a JavaScript native error object, and the `stack` argument is a string." Async work needs its own try/catch inside the callback, since try/catch "can handle exceptions in synchronous code only."
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It presents errorCallback as a general-purpose catch-all equivalent to React's componentDidCatch, and puts it on the SAME component whose code throws — where it does not fire, because the hook only sees descendants. It also promises it will catch `await getData()` rejections in connectedCallback, and forgets that `this.template.addEventListener('x', h)` handlers are outside its reach entirely.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-error-boundaries (gotchas.md Gotcha 1 'Async errors uncaught'), lwc/lwc-async-patterns (gotchas.md Gotcha 5, exactly this), lwc/common-lwc-runtime-errors (Anti-Pattern 7). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-async-patterns (1.327)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Never use `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`, or `for` across a shadow boundary — use aria-label, move both elements into one template, or switch that component to light DOM.
practices.why_it_matters: The IDREF resolves to nothing, so a screen reader announces an unlabelled control. There is no console warning and axe/Lighthouse frequently miss it because the attribute is present — this is the single most common silent a11y failure in LWC.
practices.specifics: create-components-accessibility-attributes.html: "In native shadow DOM, you can't link IDs and ARIA attributes between elements in separate templates" — the fix is to "use light DOM to place them in the same shadow root." Element IDs are scoped to their shadow root; LWC also rewrites template IDs at runtime, so hardcoding one is doubly unsafe. ARIA attributes map to camelCase accessors: `aria-label` → `ariaLabel`. Cross-root ARIA / Reference Target is a W3C AOM proposal Salesforce participates in, not a shipped capability.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It generates textbook-correct ARIA — a custom combobox with `aria-activedescendant`/`aria-controls` pointing at a listbox that lives in a child component — because the pattern is right for plain HTML. It has no model of shadow-scoped IDs, so it never flags the break, and it will also hardcode `id="error-msg"` in a template and reference it from a sibling component.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-shadow-vs-light-dom-decision (gotchas.md '2. `aria-describedby` and `aria-labelledby` do not cross shadow roots'; llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 6) and lwc/lwc-accessibility-patterns (SKILL.md 'Shadow DOM Blocks Cross-Component ARIA Relationships'). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-shadow-vs-light-dom-decision (1.750)`, `lwc/lwc-accessibility-patterns (0.650)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Reach for a base component before hand-rolling an interactive element, and supply the component-specific text attribute — `alternative-text` on lightning-icon/avatar/button-icon, `label` on every input.
practices.why_it_matters: Salesforce accessibility conformance is contractual for many customers; an icon-only `lightning-button-icon` with no alternative-text announces as an empty button and fails WCAG 4.1.2.
practices.specifics: base-components-accessibility.html: lightning-avatar and lightning-icon "Include an `alternative-text` attribute" and the avatar "passes down this description to the `alt` and `title` attributes"; lightning-input "appends the `aria-describedby` attribute to the `input` element when a validation error is displayed" (so do not hand-add your own describedby); lightning-accordion "toggles between `aria-hidden="true"` and `aria-hidden="false"`"; lightning-breadcrumbs supplies `aria-label="Breadcrumbs"`, `role="navigation"`, `role="list"`, `role="listitem"`. Use `variant="label-hidden"` to visually hide a label while keeping it for AT — never omit the label.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It emits `<lightning-button-icon icon-name="utility:delete" onclick={handleDelete}>` with no alternative-text (the attribute is optional in the signature, so nothing complains), and it hand-builds clickable `<div onclick=...>` elements with a manually added `role="button"` but no `tabindex` and no keydown handler. It also duplicates ARIA the base component already manages, e.g. adding `aria-describedby` to a lightning-input.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-accessibility (SKILL.md 'Base-Component Replacement For Custom Click Targets'; llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 5 'Missing labels on icon-only buttons'; gotchas.md 'Icon-Only Actions Need Text Equivalents'). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-accessibility (1.450)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Size lightning-datatable to Salesforce's published envelope: 1,000 rows × 5 columns, ≤50 rows per fetch, and <20 columns once past 250 rows.
practices.why_it_matters: These are the documented cliffs. A 5,000-row table is not 'slow because of the user's laptop' — it is outside the tested envelope, and no amount of Apex tuning fixes it.
practices.specifics: data-table-performance.html: "Datatable performance is best with a maximum of 1,000 rows and 5 columns"; "Adding more rows or columns can degrade performance"; "Load a maximum of 50 rows at a time. For example, use `LIMIT` to specify no more than 50 rows"; "If your datatable has more than 250 rows, use fewer than 20 columns to reduce the amount of data presented"; "The more columns that enable inline editing, the slower the datatable performs." For paging, set `enable-infinite-loading` + `onloadmore`, place the table in a container with an explicit height (otherwise loadmore fires in a loop), and tune `load-more-offset` (default 20px from the bottom).
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked for 'a table of all Contacts', it writes `LIMIT 10000` and binds the whole array to lightning-datatable with 12 columns, offering no limits at all. When it does add `enable-infinite-loading`, it omits the fixed-height container, which makes onloadmore fire recursively and hammer Apex. It also never mentions that inline-edit columns carry a per-column cost.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists (gotchas.md Gotcha 3 '`lightning-datatable` degrades past 1,000 rows × 5 columns' and Gotcha 4 'For tables > 250 rows, keep columns < 20'; SKILL.md Pattern A with enable-infinite-loading). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists (1.288)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: For lists in the 50–5,000-item range on Summer '26+ orgs, evaluate the platform virtualization components before hand-rolling a windowing algorithm.
practices.why_it_matters: Hand-built virtual lists are where LWC accessibility goes to die (lost aria-rowcount/aria-rowindex, broken keyboard nav, focus stranded on recycled nodes). The platform components ship that behaviour.
practices.specifics: Summer '26 introduces `lightning-dynamic-list-container` and `lightning-dynamic-list-item` (Developer Preview): they render "only the rows in the viewport and stream the rest in as you scroll", target 50–5,000 items, and include built-in virtualization plus accessibility. Developer Preview means not supported in production — record that status rather than presenting it as GA.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Its knowledge of the base-component catalogue is frozen well before Summer '26, so it will always hand-roll an IntersectionObserver/scroll-offset virtual list, and that hand-rolled version reliably omits `aria-rowcount`/`aria-rowindex` and assumes fixed row height. It also has no concept of Developer Preview vs Beta vs GA and will assert production readiness.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the new components. lwc/virtualized-lists (1.413) and lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists (0.975) cover hand-rolled virtualization and datatable infinite loading well, but search_knowledge.py returns no chunk mentioning `lightning-dynamic-list-container`. Genuine gap (release-recency).

practices.practice: Call loadScript/loadStyle from a guarded one-time path, and defend against the two known de-duplication failures.
practices.why_it_matters: `loadStyle` has de-dup logic that can leave its Promise permanently pending, so every `.then()` after it — including the code that actually initialises your chart — never runs, with no error. Users see an empty container only after navigating away and back.
practices.specifics: lightning/platformResourceLoader: "Both methods create and return promises"; invoke them "in `renderedCallback()` on the first render" behind a guard. Known issue (salesforce/lwc #2062): "if a CSS style already exists on a page ... loadStyle will never call resolve()", so `await loadStyle(...)` hangs on the second visit to the page. Separately, if an Aura component loads the same URL via `ltng:require`, "the script duplication is not detected and the script is loaded twice" — the library itself must guard on a global. Static resource size cap is 5 MB per resource / 250 MB per org.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes `Promise.all([loadScript(this, X), loadStyle(this, X_CSS)]).then(() => this.initChart())` in connectedCallback (where the container element does not exist yet) or in an unguarded renderedCallback (re-loading on every render). It never mentions that loadStyle can hang, so when the user reports 'the chart works on first load but is blank when I navigate back', the LLM misdiagnoses it as a lifecycle/timing issue and adds setTimeout.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/static-resources-in-lwc (SKILL.md '`loadScript` And `loadStyle` Need A Real Lifecycle', llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 4) covers the lifecycle and the forgotten-CSS case. search_knowledge.py for 'loadStyle promise never resolves ... navigate back' returns `lwc/lightning-navigation-dead-link-handling (1.191)` on top — the never-resolving-promise silent failure is NOT covered. Gap.

practices.practice: Leave LMS subscriptions at the default scope; add `{ scope: APPLICATION_SCOPE }` only when the subscriber genuinely lives outside the active navigation item, and always release on disconnect.
practices.why_it_matters: APPLICATION_SCOPE makes every background console tab react to a message meant for the foreground tab — cross-talk that shows up as 'the wrong record loaded in tab 3'.
practices.specifics: lightning/messageService: "By default, communication over a message channel can occur only between Lightning web components, Aura components, or Visualforce pages in an active navigation tab, an active navigation item, or a utility item." `subscribe(messageContext, messageChannel, listener, subscriberOptions)` returns a Subscription used by `unsubscribe()`. `MessageContext` must be obtained via `@wire(MessageContext) messageContext;`. `releaseMessageContext()` "Releases a MessageContext object ... and unsubscribes all associated subscriptions." LMS spans LWC, Aura, and Visualforce on the same Lightning page, plus utility bar items and Open CTI softphones. The message must be a serializable JSON object.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It adds `{ scope: APPLICATION_SCOPE }` to every subscribe call by default, because tutorial code does, and treats it as boilerplate rather than a deliberate widening. It also imports MessageContext and instantiates it directly instead of wiring it, and omits `unsubscribe` in disconnectedCallback so subscriptions leak across console tab churn.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/message-channel-patterns (llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 2 'Using APPLICATION_SCOPE by default'; template comments 'Remove if default (active tab)') and lwc/component-communication llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 6. search_knowledge.py: `lwc/message-channel-patterns (1.550)`, `lwc/lwc-pubsub-patterns (0.700)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Generate client-side file downloads with `blob:` object URLs, not `data:` URIs — LWS blocks data: URIs as of Summer '26.
practices.why_it_matters: The classic CSV/PDF export snippet (`a.href = 'data:text/csv;charset=utf-8,' + encodeURIComponent(csv)`) stops working on Summer '26 orgs, and the failure surfaces as a download that simply does nothing.
practices.specifics: Summer '26 secure downloads (GA): "LWS now blocks `data:` URIs" — use `URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([csv], {type:'text/csv'}))` instead, and revoke it afterwards. The related LWS distortions are on `Element.getAttribute`, the `innerHTML`/`outerHTML` getters, and `MutationObserver.observe`. Wider LWS context: LWS "is enabled by default for all orgs created in Winter '23 and later", and "As of Summer '23, LWS for Lightning web components and Aura components is generally available for all orgs." Unlike Locker, LWS permits same-origin iframe content access, custom elements, and third-party web components.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The data: URI download is the single most-reproduced LWC snippet in its training data, so it emits it near-universally for 'export to CSV'. It also still describes Locker Service restrictions (no custom elements, wrapped DOM objects, no iframe access) as current, and cannot say which LWS distortion is responsible when a third-party library breaks.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/lightning-out-2-embedding SKILL.md notes LWS blocks HTML insertion, lwc/lwc-security llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 6 covers CSP for third-party scripts. search_knowledge.py for 'LWS blocks data URI download use blob object URL' returns `lwc/lightning-out-2-embedding (1.418)` — the Summer '26 data:→blob: rule is NOT covered. Gap.

practices.practice: In Jest, flush the microtask queue before asserting the DOM and remember that lightning-* stubs never fire events.
practices.why_it_matters: LWC re-rendering is asynchronous; assertions written immediately after setting a property pass or fail based on timing, producing intermittent CI failures that get 'fixed' with sleeps.
practices.specifics: unit-testing-using-jest-patterns.html: "Wait for the component to rerender by returning a `Promise.resolve()` value"; "Use a `Object.assign()` statement to set an attribute before the `appendChild` call"; and of the sfdx-lwc-jest lightning-stubs: "No events are fired from these mocks but you can call `dispatchEvent()` against them." Mock wire adapters with `createTestWireAdapter` / `createApexTestWireAdapter` from `@salesforce/wire-service-jest-util` and drive them with `.emit(value)` / `.error(body, status, statusText)`; mock imperative Apex with `jest.mock('@salesforce/apex/Cls.method', () => ({ default: jest.fn() }), { virtual: true })`. Override a stub via `moduleNameMapper` in jest.config.js.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It asserts synchronously right after `element.recordId = '001x'`, then, when the test flakes, reaches for `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 100))` rather than a microtask flush. It also writes tests that expect a real `lightning-input` to emit a change event when its value is set — the stub never will — and mocks wire adapters with a bare `jest.fn()` instead of `createTestWireAdapter`, so `.emit()` does not exist.

practices.practice: Verify UI API / LDS object and field support before choosing lightning-record-form or a getRecord wire — the holes are specific and silent.
practices.why_it_matters: An unsupported object throws `Object <Name> is not supported in UI API` at runtime, and unsupported FIELDS on a supported object simply do not render, so the form looks fine in review and loses data in production.
practices.specifics: lightning-record-edit-form documentation: "External objects are not supported. The `InformalName` field is not supported for editing"; "This component doesn't support all Salesforce standard objects. This limitation also applies to a record that references a field that belongs to an unsupported object"; "This component supports the Task object but `Task.IsRecurrence` and `Task.IsReminderSet` fields don't render even when requested" — same for `Event.IsRecurrence`, `Event.IsRecurrence2`, `Event.IsReminderSet`. LDS "supports all custom objects and all the standard objects that User Interface API supports" but "Custom metadata types are not supported." `lightning-input-field` "doesn't support client-side custom validation" — use lightning-input if you need it. Confirm support at runtime with `/ui-api/object-info`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It presents lightning-record-form as universally applicable and will happily generate one for Task, Event, a custom metadata type, or an external object. Worse, on Task it includes `IsReminderSet` in the field list — the deploy succeeds, the form renders without that field, and no one notices reminders stopped being set. It also attaches custom validation logic to `lightning-input-field`, which ignores it.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/lwc-lightning-record-forms (gotchas.md Gotcha 3 preventDefault, Gotcha 4 record types) and lwc/lwc-forms-and-validation (1.600, covers the input-field vs input validation split) and lwc/lwc-base-component-recipes cover the component well. search_knowledge.py for the UI API support query returns `admin/dynamic-forms-and-actions (1.282)` first — the specific Task/Event field-level render holes and the external-object exclusion are the delta.

practices.practice: When overriding lightning-record-edit-form's onsubmit, call event.preventDefault() before re-submitting programmatically.
practices.why_it_matters: Without it, the form submits twice — once with your mutated payload and once with the original — producing a duplicate save or a last-write-wins overwrite of the field you just set.
practices.specifics: lightning-record-edit-form: "If you capture the submit event and submit the form programmatically, use `event.preventDefault()` to cancel the default behavior of the event. This prevents a duplicate form submission." Pattern: `handleSubmit(e){ e.preventDefault(); const fields = e.detail.fields; fields.OwnerId = this.ownerId; this.template.querySelector('lightning-record-edit-form').submit(fields); }`. Server-side errors arrive on `event.detail.output.fieldErrors`, keyed by field API name.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes an onsubmit handler that mutates `event.detail.fields` and calls `.submit(fields)` without preventDefault — the pattern is subtly wrong rather than broken, so it passes a quick manual test and produces intermittent duplicate records under load.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-base-component-recipes (llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 6 'Overriding onsubmit without calling event.preventDefault()') and lwc/lwc-lightning-record-forms (gotchas.md Gotcha 3 and examples.md Example 3). search_knowledge.py: `lwc/lwc-base-component-recipes (1.300)`, `lwc/lwc-lightning-record-forms (1.100)` — COVERED.

practices.practice: Parse LDS/wire errors against the FetchResponse shape and branch on whether `body` is an array or an object.
practices.why_it_matters: `error.body.message` is correct for Apex and network errors but undefined for UI API READ errors, where body is an array — so the user sees a toast that literally says 'undefined'.
practices.specifics: data-error.html: the error is a FetchResponse with `body` ("Object or Array"), `ok` (Boolean), `status` (Number — "404 if a resource is not found or 500 for an internal server error"), and `statusText` (String — "`NOT_FOUND` for a status code of 404"). "UI API read operations (e.g. `getRecord`) return `error.body` as an array of objects"; "UI API write operations (e.g. `createRecord`) return `error.body` as an object, often with object-level and field-level errors"; "Apex operations return `error.body` as an object"; "Network errors return `error.body` as an object." Reference reducer: trailheadapps/lwc-recipes `ldsUtils.reduceErrors`. LDS write rejections carry `{ body: { output: { errors: [...], fieldErrors: {...} } }, status, statusText }`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes one handler — `message: error.body.message` — for every error source, so getRecord failures render 'undefined' and network failures render '[object Object]'. Its alternative is `JSON.stringify(error)`, which dumps a raw payload into a toast. It rarely distinguishes object-level from field-level errors, so validation-rule messages are never surfaced next to the offending field.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — lwc/lwc-toast-and-notifications (llm-anti-patterns.md Anti-Pattern 4 is exactly the JSON.stringify toast), lwc/lwc-lds-writes SKILL.md documents the write-error shape, and lwc/lwc-imperative-apex ships a reducer template. The array-vs-object split by API type is the delta. search_knowledge.py top skill: `lwc/lwc-toast-and-notifications (1.100)`.

practices.practice: Pin an explicit `<apiVersion>` in every .js-meta.xml and know the floor: LWC treats anything below 58.0 as 58.0.
practices.why_it_matters: Component-level versioning freezes runtime semantics per component. A component with no apiVersion drifts with the org's default each release, so a reactivity or template behaviour change can land in production without any code change.
practices.specifics: create-version-considerations.html: "Versioning support began with API version 58.0"; "If you use an `apiVersion` that's earlier than 58.0, LWC uses 58.0"; "If you set an `apiVersion` that's later than the latest version available, you'll receive an error." From the versioning announcement: "Starting with Winter '24, all API versions of 58.0 and below will be treated by LWC as version 58.0 (aka Summer '23) ... some bug fixes and performance improvements will only be available for components using API version 59.0 and above." Current cycle: LWC API 67.0 ships with Summer '26.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It conflates three different version knobs — `sourceApiVersion` in sfdx-project.json, the `<version>` in package.xml, and the component's own `<apiVersion>` — and asserts that setting one of the first two changes runtime behaviour. It also scaffolds js-meta.xml files with whatever apiVersion appeared in its training data (often 57.0 or 59.0) with no comment on the consequence, and cannot explain why an identical component behaves differently in two orgs.

BUT search_knowledge.py for 'LWC component level API version 58 frozen bug fixes only 59 and above' returns literally `Coverage: NONE — no skill meets the confidence threshold.` The 58.0 floor and the 59.0+ bug-fix boundary are absent.

practices.practice: For state shared across a component tree on Summer '26+ orgs, use platform State Managers (`@lwc/state`) rather than pub/sub, prop drilling, or a bundled third-party store.
practices.why_it_matters: It removes the three worst LWC state workarounds at once — prop drilling through intermediate components, an LMS channel used as a state bus (which leaks across console tabs), and a vendored Redux clone that cannot be tree-shaken and breaks in LWS.
practices.specifics: `@lwc/state` exposes `defineState`, and the setup function receives `atom`, `computed`, and `setAtom`. "A `computed` is a lazily-evaluated derivation that recalculates only when its dependencies change"; "Multiple `setAtom` calls in the same tick are batched into a single notification cycle." Consumers use `fromContext`: `import { fromContext } from '@lwc/state'; shopState = fromContext(createShopStateManager);` — "no prop drilling, no event handling, and no pub/sub plumbing." Constraint: "state managers are available in Lightning Experience, but not yet supported in Experience Cloud." They are plain JS modules, so Jest can unit-test them "without mounting a component." Platform-supplied managers exist as `lightning/stateManagerRecord` and siblings.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked for LWC state management, it produces one of three obsolete answers: a hand-rolled `pubsub.js` singleton (which breaks across Lightning console tabs), an LMS message channel repurposed as a store, or a recommendation to install Redux/MobX inside the bundle. It has no knowledge of `@lwc/state`, `fromContext`, or the Experience Cloud exclusion, and if it hears the name it will guess a `@wire`-based consumption API.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the platform module. lwc/lwc-reactive-state-patterns (1.671) is the top hit and its llm-anti-patterns.md #5 correctly rejects Redux/Pinia/MobX, but no returned chunk mentions `@lwc/state`, `defineState`, `atom`, `computed`, `setAtom`, or `fromContext`. Genuine gap (release-recency).

practices.practice: Drive the Agentforce side panel from an LWC with the `lightning/accApi` module rather than embedding a chat UI.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams currently rebuild an agent surface inside a custom component because they do not know a headless control API exists, duplicating Trust Layer and conversation-state handling that the native panel already provides.
practices.specifics: Summer '26 (GA): `lightning/accApi` is a "headless module [that] lets your LWC components drive the native Agentforce side panel", with three async methods — `open(botId?)`, `close()`, and `execute(utterance, botId)`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It has no model of this module and will instead propose an iframe, a custom chat component calling an Agent API endpoint from JS (which leaks credentials and violates the platform's callout model), or a Messaging for In-App embed — none of which integrate with the native panel's conversation state.

practices.practice: Audit for the native-shadow-DOM behaviour deltas before enabling `static shadowSupportMode = 'native'` or migrating an org off synthetic shadow.
practices.why_it_matters: Synthetic shadow lets global styles leak IN; native does not. A component that inherits corporate CSS today renders unstyled after the switch, and the breakage list extends well past CSS.
practices.specifics: "In synthetic shadow, styles cannot leak out, but they can leak in. Whereas in native shadow, styles cannot leak in either direction" — replace global stylesheet reliance with `@import` in the component CSS. Also breaking: cross-boundary CSS selectors (`.parent .child`); `aria-labelledby`/`for` across trees; slot creation order changes from lazy to eager; `innerText`, `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, and `textContent` behave differently; form elements no longer auto-associate with an enclosing `<form>`; XPath selectors in WebDriver tests change. Opt in per component with `static shadowSupportMode = 'native';` (Spring '24). Light DOM is the escape hatch: `static renderMode = 'light'` + `<template lwc:render-mode="light">`, and then query with `this.querySelector`, not `this.template.querySelector`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: It writes `this.template.querySelector` in a light-DOM component (returns null, since the template is not a shadow root) and `this.querySelector` in a shadow-DOM component. It treats shadow vs light as purely a styling choice and never raises the ARIA, slot-timing, or form-association consequences. It also cannot say which shadow mode an org is running, so it gives advice valid in one mode and silently wrong in the other.
practices.already_covered_by: lwc/lwc-shadow-vs-light-dom-decision (gotchas.md '1. research.domain: Salesforce Data & Migration — data model, external IDs and upsert idempotency, load ordering, Bulk API selection and throughput, lock contention, skinny tables and custom indexes, LDV thresholds, deferred sharing calculation, data skew, deduplication at scale, archival, and the storage model

practices.practice: When an upsert key field has External ID checked but Unique unchecked, the calling user must hold "View All Data" or the upsert call itself fails — regardless of whether any duplicate actually exists.
practices.why_it_matters: Integration users are routinely provisioned with a least-privilege permission set that deliberately excludes View All Data. The migration works in the sandbox (admin runs it) and fails in production (integration user runs it), and the failure looks like a data problem, not a permission problem.
practices.specifics: SOAP API upsert(): "If you're upserting a record for an object that has a custom field with both the External ID and Unique attributes selected (a unique index), you don't need any special permissions, because the Unique attribute prevents the creation of duplicates. If you're upserting a record for an object that has the External ID non-unique index) your client application must have the permission 'View All Data' to execute this call." The permission is required to *execute the call*, not per-record. Standard objects can substitute any field whose `idLookup` describe property is true (e.g. Contact.Email, Account.Name is not) for a custom External ID.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to design an integration user's permission set for an upsert-based sync, an LLM lists object CRUD + FLS on the External ID field and stops. It never connects the Unique checkbox to a *system permission* requirement, because that coupling exists nowhere in the mental model of "upsert = insert-or-update". It will also confidently say "External ID alone is enough for upsert" — true syntactically, false operationally.

practices.practice: State External ID case behaviour as two separate rules: uniqueness enforcement vs upsert matching. Upsert matching is case-INSENSITIVE only when the field has BOTH the Unique attribute AND the "Treat 'ABC' and 'abc' as duplicate values (case insensitive)" option; in every other configuration, including a non-Unique External ID, matching is case-SENSITIVE.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the single most common cause of silent duplicate creation in an idempotent-by-design sync. An ERP that emits `sap-000123` on Monday and `SAP-000123` on Tuesday creates two Accounts, and the reconciliation count still looks plausible because both loads reported 100% success.
practices.specifics: Exact doc text: "Matching by external ID is case-insensitive only if the external ID field has the Unique attribute and the Treat \"ABC\" and \"abc\" as duplicate values (case insensitive) option selected... If these options are selected, 'ABC123' is matched with 'abc123.'" Note the option label is phrased as *duplicate values*, not the *different values* phrasing used elsewhere in the field-creation UI — the two labels are opposite polarity and are easy to invert.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM collapses uniqueness and matching into one property and picks a side. Worse, the two most common answers are both defensible-sounding and mutually exclusive: "Text External IDs are case-sensitive because strings are case-sensitive" (programming-language prior) or "Salesforce Text uniqueness is case-insensitive by default" (half-remembered field-creation UI). It never says "it depends on Unique + the checkbox, and the two behaviours differ".

practices.practice: Name the exact upsert failure surface per API: SOAP/Bulk returns StatusCode `DUPLICATE_EXTERNAL_ID`; REST sObject-rows-by-External-ID returns HTTP 300 with a list of matching record URLs (not a normal error body). Never write retry logic that treats a 300 as a transient error.
practices.why_it_matters: A generic HTTP client library classifies 3xx as a redirect and either follows it or retries it. A 300 from Salesforce means "your external ID is not unique" — a permanent data defect that retrying will never resolve, and following the redirect silently updates one arbitrary duplicate.
practices.specifics: `DUPLICATE_EXTERNAL_ID`: "A user-specified external ID matches more than one record during an upsert." REST PATCH /sobjects/{obj}/{extIdField}/{value}: 201 when a record is created, 200 when a record is updated in API v46.0+ (204 No Content in v45.0 and earlier — a real version boundary for old clients that check for 204), 300 when the external ID matches multiple records, 404 with `"errorCode": "NOT_FOUND"` when the field named in the URL is not actually an External ID field. Duplicate external IDs *within a single request* are a separate case: "those records are marked as errors in the UpsertResult file. The records are neither created."
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Given "handle upsert errors", the LLM writes `if (status >= 400) { retry }` and never enumerates 300. practices.practice: When upserting a child and linking it to its parent by the parent's External ID, the parent record must already exist — upsert() will not create it. Plan self-referencing and circular loads as two passes; the External ID relationship column does not defer the reference.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams choose External ID relationship columns specifically to avoid a two-pass load, then discover on the Account.ParentId / Contact.ReportsTo / CPQ option-group pass that half the rows fail because the referenced parent is later in the same file.
practices.specifics: SOAP API upsert(): "Unlike create(), the parent record must currently exist when using upsert() to create or update a child record related by a foreign key." CSV header syntax for the reference is `RelationshipName.IndexedFieldName` (custom: replace the child field's `__c` with `__r`, e.g. `Mother_Of_Child__r.External_ID__c`). Constraints: child-to-parent only (no parent-to-child), no grandparent chaining (`A__r.B__r.C__c` is rejected), and the parent field must be indexed — External ID checked for custom fields, `idLookup = true` for standard fields.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM presents `Parent__r.Ext_Id__c` as a general-purpose forward reference and says "order doesn't matter because Salesforce resolves the External ID". practices.practice: Treat a dirty file as a throughput problem, not just a data-quality problem: any error inside a Bulk batch causes Salesforce to fall back to single-row processing for that batch. Validate and cleanse before the load rather than relying on partial-success semantics.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the mechanism behind the classic "the load was fine in sandbox and took 14 hours in production" post-mortem. A 2% bad-row rate does not cost 2% of throughput; it collapses the batch from set-based to row-by-row processing.
practices.specifics: LDV best practices, Loading Data from the API: "Ensure that data is clean before loading when using the Bulk API 2.0. Errors in batches trigger single-row processing for that batch, and that processing heavily impacts performance." Same table: operation cost ordering is "insert() is fastest, update() is next, and upsert() is next after that. If possible, also break upsert() into two operations: create() and update()" — i.e. an idempotent upsert is deliberately trading throughput for safety, and splitting it is a documented optimisation.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM says "Bulk API 2.0 supports partial success, so failed rows just land in failedResults — no problem". It models errors as isolated per-row events with no batch-level side effect, and therefore recommends "load everything and fix the failures afterward" as a *faster* strategy than pre-validating. It also never states the insert < update < upsert cost ordering.

practices.practice: Bulk API v1 does not fail a lock-contended batch immediately. It waits, then requeues. Read the requeue mechanics before concluding that a load "succeeded" — a requeued batch does not retry the rows it already marked failed.
practices.why_it_matters: A job can report Completed with a batch that was internally requeued nine times and permanently dropped rows on each pass. If your reconciliation only checks job state, you ship a silently incomplete migration.
practices.specifics: "The Bulk API doesn't generate an error immediately when encountering a lock. It waits a few seconds for its release and, if it doesn't happen, the record is marked as failed. If there are problems acquiring locks for more than 100 records in a batch, the Bulk API places the remainder of the batch back in the queue for later processing. When the Bulk API processes the batch again later, records marked as failed aren't retried... it's placed back in the queue and reprocessed up to 10 times before the batch is permanently marked as failed." Error code `TooManyLockFailure` may be returned mid-batch. `Sforce-Disable-Batch-Retry: TRUE` suppresses retries; the default retry count is 10 for bulk uploads and 15 for bulk queries. Bulk API 2.0 differs: batch fails after 5 minutes, retried up to 20 times, then the whole ingest job moves to Failed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM recommends "add exponential backoff and retry the failed rows" as client-side logic without knowing the platform already requeues 10 times, and it never mentions that requeued batches skip already-failed rows — so its retry advice double-counts platform behaviour while missing the actual data loss. It also has no knowledge of `Sforce-Disable-Batch-Retry`, so it cannot advise the one lever that bounds a chronically timing-out batch.

practices.practice: Sort the CSV by parent Id before a parallel Bulk load of child records, and treat sorting as the primary mitigation — serial mode is the fallback, not the default.
practices.why_it_matters: Serial mode is often reached for first because it "obviously" fixes locking, at a large throughput cost. Sorting by ParentId places all children of a parent in one batch and removes the contention without giving up parallelism.
practices.specifics: Bulk API 2.0 guide, Organize Data to Minimize Lock Contention: "When an AccountTeamMember record is created or updated, the corresponding Account for this record is locked during the transaction... organize your CSV data files by AccountId." The four operations explicitly named as likely to cause lock contention and to warrant serial mode are: creating users, updating ownership for records with private sharing, updating user roles, and updating territory hierarchies. Salesforce's own guidance: "Avoid processing data in serial mode unless you know that parallel mode would otherwise result in lock timeouts and you can't reorganize your batches to avoid locks." There is also a non-GA "Bulk API 2.0 Automatic Record Lock Handling Pilot" — do not design around it.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM's first and often only answer to `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW` is "switch to serial mode" or "reduce batch size". It also recommends setting `concurrencyMode: Serial` on a Bulk API 2.0 job, which is not a v2.0 capability at all.

practices.practice: In a master-detail relationship, updating a child locks the parent as well as the child. Sequence threads so that no two concurrent threads touch children of the same parent, and never run a parent update pass and a child update pass at the same time.
practices.why_it_matters: Practitioners assume locking is scoped to the rows in their DML. The parent lock is invisible in the payload, so a load that never mentions Account still serialises on Account rows.
practices.specifics: DRAES: "for objects with a master-detail relationship, when you update child records, the system locks the parent and the child records to prevent inconsistencies... two situations in particular pose a risk of producing locking errors: Updates to parent records and their children are being processed simultaneously in separate threads. Updates to child records that have the same parent records are being processed simultaneously in separate threads." Mitigation ladder: retry logic for occasional errors; "Sequence operations on parent and child objects by ParentID and ensure that different threads are operating on unique sets of records" for frequent ones.

practices.practice: Budget the Bulk daily allocation as batches, not jobs, and remember the 15,000-batch allocation is shared across Bulk API v1 and Bulk API 2.0. It also treats 150 MB as the raw CSV budget and generates chunking code that produces 150 MB files, which fail after base64 expansion.
