research.domain: Salesforce Security & Sharing (platform security, record access, encryption, monitoring, secure coding)

practices.practice: Correct the library's claim that Shield Platform Encryption respects a "View Encrypted Data" permission. It does not — that permission belongs to Classic Encryption only. Under Shield, any user with field-level read access sees plaintext; masking is a key-availability signal, not an access control.
practices.why_it_matters: skills/security/platform-encryption currently instructs practitioners to grant a permission that does not gate Shield data, and to 'verify integration users have View Encrypted Data' — a step that will silently do nothing while the team believes encrypted fields are access-controlled. It also implies encryption substitutes for FLS, which is the exact reasoning error that leaves PII readable by every user on the object.
practices.specifics: Official wording: "Encryption prevents outsiders from using your Salesforce data even if they manage to get it. It is not a way to hide data from authenticated users. User permissions are the only way to control data visibility for authenticated users. Encryption at rest is about logins, not permissions." and "With Shield Platform Encryption, if a user is authorized to see a given set of data, that user sees that data whether it's encrypted or not." The `View Encrypted Data` permission exists ONLY for Classic Encryption (the 175-character `Text (Encrypted)` custom field type). Shield's masking values are troubleshooting signals, not redaction. Wrong text in repo: skills/security/platform-encryption/references/gotchas.md:57 ("Shield encryption respects the View Encrypted Data permission — users without it see masked values rather than plaintext"), plus SKILL.md:114 and SKILL.md:171.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/254/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf (Salesforce Security Guide, "Why Isn't My Encrypted Data Masked?", p.116)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models conflate Classic Encryption with Shield Platform Encryption because both are called 'encrypted fields' in Setup. Asked "how do I stop non-privileged users seeing the encrypted SSN field?", an LLM confidently answers "remove the View Encrypted Data permission from their profile" — which has zero effect under Shield. The deeper error is treating encryption as an authorization layer at all; the model produces a security design where encryption is listed as the control that restricts users, rather than FLS/sharing.
practices.already_covered_by: security/platform-encryption — COVERED BUT INCORRECT. Search returns it as top skill (1.529) for encryption masking queries, and grep confirms gotchas.md:57 asserts the false claim.

practices.practice: When Shield encryption or its key is unavailable, encrypted fields render reserved sentinel values — and writing one of those sentinels into an encrypted field silently saves a blank instead. Add these five strings to any incident runbook and never use them as test data.
practices.why_it_matters: An admin seeing `?????` in a Contact Phone assumes data corruption or a bad load, and starts a data-restore that overwrites good ciphertext. Worse: a data-migration that happens to contain the literal date 07/07/1777 or a `?????` placeholder writes empty fields with no error row in the Bulk API result file.
practices.specifics: Destroyed key → Email/Phone/Text/Text Area/Text Area (Long)/URL display `?????`; Custom Date displays `08/08/1888`; Custom Date/Time displays `08/08/1888 12:00 PM`. Service unavailable → `!!!!!`; Custom Date `01/01/1777`; Custom Date/Time `01/01/1777 12:00 PM`. Official: "Notification values such as ????? and 01/01/1777 are strings reserved for masking notifications and can't be used as data values in encrypted fields. While you aren't restricted from saving a record with one of these reserved masking notification strings into an encrypted field, the field is saved with a blank value."
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to diagnose `?????` in an encrypted field, an LLM invents a field-level-security explanation or says 'the value literally contains question marks'. It has no notion that the platform reserves sentinel strings, and it will never warn that writing them is a silent no-op — so generated data-load or test-data scripts happily use `?????` as an anonymisation placeholder against encrypted fields.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — search_knowledge for 'Shield Platform Encryption reserved masking notification strings destroyed key question marks field saved blank' returns security/platform-encryption (1.529) but only generic SKILL.md/template chunks; `grep -rn '?????\|01/01/1777\|08/08/1888' skills/security/platform-encryption/ skills/architect/salesforce-shield-architecture/` returns zero hits.

practices.practice: Budget encrypted-field capacity in BYTES, not characters. Encrypting a field cuts its usable length for non-ASCII data by up to ~45%, and the failure is a save error in production only for CJK/accented records.
practices.why_it_matters: An org encrypts Contact.LastName, passes UAT with Latin names, then Japanese or Korean records over 70 characters fail on save after go-live. Because the API length is still reported as 80, no validation rule or integration mapping predicts it.
practices.specifics: Published caps (API length / byte length / non-ASCII characters): Last Name (Contact, Lead) 80 / 240 / 70; Email (Contact, Lead) 80 / 240 / 70; Name (Custom Object) 80 / 240 / 70; Name (Opportunity) 120 / 360 / 110; Title (Contact, Lead) 128 / 384 / 126; First/Middle Name, City, Phone, Fax (Account/Contact/Lead) 40 / 120 / 22; Assistant Name (Contact) 40 / 120 / 22; Site (Account) 80 / 240 / 70; Subject (Email Message, probabilistic or case-sensitive deterministic) 2207 / 3000 / 1000; Address To/CC/BCC (Email Message) 2959 / 4000 / 1333. Salesforce recommends enforcing these with validation rules. Separately, Email-to-Case text can carry `￾` and `￿`, which Shield cannot encrypt at all.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/254/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("Field Limits with Shield Platform Encryption", p.214)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked "does encrypting Last Name change the field length?" says no — encryption is transparent, the field is still 80 characters. It has no concept of the ciphertext expansion budget and will never produce the validation rule Salesforce explicitly recommends. It also won't connect a 'value too long' save failure in a Japanese-locale org to the encryption policy.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — search_knowledge for 'encrypted field length limit non-ASCII characters Japanese Chinese Korean byte length last name 70' returns "Coverage: NONE — no skill meets the confidence threshold".

practices.practice: Before encrypting the standard User.Email field, stop: it silently severs Salesforce's own operational email to your admins and can lock users out via Login Discovery.
practices.why_it_matters: Org-migration and service-degradation notices from Salesforce stop arriving with no error and no setting to indicate why. If the org uses Login Discovery (email-as-username identity flows), encrypting User.Email breaks the handler lookup and blocks logins — a self-inflicted outage discovered only at login time.
practices.specifics: Official: "If the Email field on the User object is encrypted with field-level encryption, you don't receive critical Product & Service Notifications, including emails about org migrations, from Salesforce." "Login Discovery Handler lookups that rely on emails don't work if the email field is encrypted, which can block user logins." Also: Lightning Sync and Einstein Activity Capture duplicate User.Email into a second database column that is stored UNENCRYPTED for any user in a sync configuration; and Einstein Conversation Insights video calls require User.Email under case-insensitive deterministic encryption, not probabilistic.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/254/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("General Shield Platform Encryption Considerations — User Email", p.205)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to build an encryption policy for a GDPR/PII programme, an LLM enumerates 'all fields containing personal data' and puts User.Email at the top, because it is textbook PII. It has no model of the platform's internal dependencies on that specific field, and will not flag that the encryption creates an unmonitored copy of the same data via Einstein Activity Capture — i.e. the compliance control is defeated at the same moment it is applied.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — search_knowledge for 'encrypting the User Email field breaks product and service notifications login discovery handler list view sorting' returns architect/hipaa-compliance-architecture (1.100) and lwc/experience-cloud-authentication (0.469), neither about this.

practices.practice: Never let a paused Flow or a Wait element carry an encrypted field value in a variable — the serialized flow interview writes it to the database unencrypted.
practices.why_it_matters: This is a compliance hole that no encryption-statistics report will reveal: the field shows 100% encrypted while plaintext copies of the same values sit in the flow-interview store for as long as the interview is paused.
practices.specifics: Official: "Paused flow interviews can cause data to be saved in an unencrypted state. When a flow or process is waiting to resume, the associated flow interview is serialized and saved to the database. The flow interview is serialized and saved when: users pause a flow; flows execute a Wait element; processes are waiting to execute scheduled actions. If the flow or process loads encrypted fields into a variable during these processes, that data isn't always encrypted at rest." Also from the same page: you cannot reference encrypted fields for filtering or sorting in Flow Builder's Get Records, Delete Records, Update Records, Record Choice Set, or condition requirements.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/254/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("General Shield Platform Encryption Considerations — Flows and Processes", p.205)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM designing a screen flow that collects and holds an encrypted SSN across a Pause element sees no problem — it reasons that encryption is 'at the field level, applied on save'. It has no representation of the flow-interview serialization store as a separate persistence surface, so it produces designs that leak the exact data the customer bought Shield to protect.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — search_knowledge for 'paused flow interview serialized encrypted field data stored unencrypted wait element' returns flow/pause-elements-and-wait-events (1.418), whose gotchas cover version invalidation, not the encryption leak.

practices.practice: When a SOQL filter against an encrypted field is malformed, expect `INVALID_FIELD`, not `MALFORMED_QUERY` — do not let the error code send you field-hunting.
practices.why_it_matters: Integration error handling keyed on `MALFORMED_QUERY` won't catch it, and an admin reading `INVALID_FIELD` will start checking FLS and field API names on a field that exists and is accessible.
practices.specifics: Official: "When you query encrypted data, invalid strings return an INVALID_FIELD error instead of the expected MALFORMED_QUERY." Pair this with the probabilistic restrictions on the same page: fields encrypted probabilistically cannot appear in aggregate functions (`MAX()`, `MIN()`, `COUNT_DISTINCT()`), `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, or `ORDER BY`. Deterministic encryption permits exact `WHERE` matching only — no `LIKE`, no `STARTS WITH`, no `ORDER BY`, no `GROUP BY`. Probabilistic encryption is not supported at all on the Contact Email field (use deterministic to avoid duplicate accounts at self-registration).
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/254/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("Tradeoffs and Limitations — SOQL and SOSL", p.206; "How Deterministic Encryption Supports Filtering", p.136)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Given `INVALID_FIELD` on a query, an LLM's first move is always 'check the field API name / add the __c suffix / check field-level security' — the same misdiagnosis it makes with WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED. It does not know encryption rewrites the error class. On the deterministic side, models routinely generate `WHERE Email LIKE '%@acme.com'` against a deterministically encrypted field and assert it works because 'deterministic encryption supports filtering'.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — search_knowledge for 'querying encrypted field with invalid string returns INVALID_FIELD error instead of MALFORMED_QUERY' returns apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis (0.650) with only INVALID_ID_FIELD chunks; deterministic-vs-probabilistic filtering IS covered by security/platform-encryption (gotchas.md:39, llm-anti-patterns.md:8), but the error-code substitution and the Contact.Email probabilistic carve-out are not.

practices.practice: Learn the real shape of restriction rules before recommending them: 2 or 5 per object depending on edition, EQUALS-only criteria, no formulas, no AND/OR, and a hard bypass for View All / Modify All.
practices.why_it_matters: Restriction rules are the only subtractive record-access control on the platform, so they get proposed for 'hide these records from these users' requirements they cannot satisfy. Designing around them and discovering the operator limit or the admin bypass at build time costs a sprint.
practices.specifics: Up to 2 active restriction rules per object in Enterprise and Developer editions, 5 in Performance and Unlimited. Available only for custom objects, external objects, contracts, events, quotes, tasks, time sheets, and time sheet entries — NOT Account/Contact/Opportunity/Case. Only the EQUALS operator; AND and OR are unsupported; formulas are unsupported; supported criteria data types are boolean, date, dateTime, double, int, reference, string, time, single picklist. Only one restriction OR scoping rule per object may evaluate true for a given user. Reference 15-character IDs, not 18. Record criteria cannot reference the object's parent (e.g. a Task rule cannot reference Activity fields). Applied to Links, List Views, Lookups, Records, Related Lists, Reports, Search, SOQL, SOSL. A rule on a parent does NOT restrict its child objects.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked "how do we stop the contractor role from seeing high-value Opportunities?" reaches for a restriction rule — an object it isn't available on — and writes criteria with AND plus a formula, neither of which the feature supports. It also states restriction rules 'work like inverse sharing rules and apply to everyone', missing the View All / Modify All bypass entirely.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — search_knowledge for 'restriction rule filter records users can see custom object contract task event limit two per object' returns apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis (1.136) with a 3-line note, and security/record-access-troubleshooting has an anti-pattern about forgetting restriction rules. `grep -rn 'EQUALS\|two restriction\|five restriction\|System Mode' skills/security/record-access-troubleshooting/ skills/apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis/references/security-sharing.md` returns no matches for any limit, operator, or bypass fact.

practices.practice: Treat restriction rules as invisible to your two main diagnostic tools: they are not enforced for code running in system mode, and `UserRecordAccess` does not reflect them.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the single most confusing failure mode in the feature. `UserRecordAccess` says HasReadAccess = true, the sharing debug tool agrees, and the user still gets an error opening the record. Meanwhile an Apex/Flow layer running in system mode happily returns the very records the rule was written to hide, so a 'restriction rule' security control is defeated by any @AuraEnabled controller without an access-mode declaration.
practices.specifics: Official: "Restriction rules aren't applied for code executed in System Mode." and "The UserRecordAccess object doesn't consider whether a user's access is blocked due to a restriction rule. If a user's access is blocked even though query results state that they should have access, check to see if a restriction rule on the object prevents the user's access." Also: after a rule is applied, previously-viewed records still appear in the search-shortcut list and Recently Viewed, and clicking them produces an access error; Open Activities / Activity History related lists cap at 50 rows BEFORE the rule is applied, so users see fewer than 50 activities they do have access to; users cannot clone a record with a lookup to a restriction-hidden record.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM's standard record-access triage script is: query UserRecordAccess, then check OWD → hierarchy → sharing rules → shares. Restriction rules are absent from that chain, and because UserRecordAccess reports access as granted, the model concludes the user's problem must be FLS or a page-layout issue and sends the admin down a dead end. Conversely, when asked to enforce data segregation, it recommends a restriction rule without mentioning that Apex in system mode ignores it.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for these two facts — see the grep in the previous entry; security/record-access-troubleshooting SKILL.md:152 documents a different UserRecordAccess caveat (the querying user needs View All Data) but not the restriction-rule blind spot.

practices.practice: Design sharing rules against the published ceilings: 300 total per object with a 50-rule sub-limit for criteria-based rules, and know the supported increase path before you architect around them.
practices.why_it_matters: Guest user sharing rules are themselves criteria-based, so an Experience Cloud build quietly consumes the same 50-rule budget as the internal sharing model. Teams hit the wall mid-build and have to redesign toward public groups or Apex managed sharing.
practices.specifics: 300 total sharing rules per object; of those, a maximum of 50 may be criteria-based. Salesforce Support can raise these to 500 total and 200 criteria-based. Salesforce's performance guidance is tighter than the hard limit: keep ownership-based rules under 100 and criteria-based under 50 per object. Guest user sharing rules are a special type of criteria-based sharing rule and count against the 50.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM designs one criteria-based sharing rule per region/product/segment value and produces 80+ rules without comment, because it has no numeric ceiling in mind. It also never mentions that guest user sharing rules draw from the criteria-based pool, so an Experience Cloud design and an internal-sharing design that were each 'fine' collide.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the numbers — search_knowledge for 'sharing rules limit 300 per object 50 criteria based increase by support' returns data/sharing-recalculation-performance (1.300) about recalculation cost, and `grep -rn '300 sharing\|300 total sharing\|50 criteria' skills/` matches only an unrelated WCAG line in admin/digital-storefront-requirements.

practices.practice: Sequence OWD and sharing-rule changes around the platform's share locks: while any object's sharing recalculation is running you cannot change org-wide defaults, and touching Account/Contact/Opportunity/Case recalculates all four.
practices.why_it_matters: A release plan that batches 'tighten Account OWD, then adjust Opportunity sharing rules' in one window stalls — the second change is refused until the first finishes, which on a large org is hours. Knowing the Background Jobs subtype names lets you tell an in-progress recalculation from a stuck one instead of raising a case.
practices.specifics: Official: "If sharing rules are recalculated for accounts, cases, contacts, or opportunities, sharing rules are also recalculated for the other three objects." "You can't modify the org-wide defaults when a sharing rule recalculation for any object is in progress. Similarly, you can't modify sharing rules when recalculation for an org-wide default update is in progress." Background Jobs subtypes to watch: `Account — Extra Parent Access Removal`, `Account — Parent Access Grant`, and `Object — Access Cleanup` (emitted when a sharing rule is deleted and stale share rows are removed). "When sharing is recalculated, Salesforce also runs all Apex sharing recalculations." You get an email on completion; monitor on the Background Jobs page or View Setup Audit Trail.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/260/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("Automatic Recalculation of Org-Wide Defaults and Sharing Rules", p.65)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked for a cutover plan, an LLM sequences OWD and sharing-rule edits as ordinary metadata deployments with no waiting state, because it models Setup changes as synchronous. It never names the Background Jobs subtypes, so its 'how to verify' step is 'check that the change was saved' rather than 'confirm Account — Parent Access Grant has completed'. It also does not know that Apex sharing recalculation classes are re-run as a side effect.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — search_knowledge for 'cannot change organization-wide defaults while sharing rule recalculation in progress share lock background jobs parent access grant' returns data/sharing-recalculation-performance (1.482) and security/record-access-troubleshooting; the recalculation cost model and the queued-processing banner are covered, but the share-lock rule and the three Background Jobs subtype names are not in the returned chunks.

practices.practice: Use the Spring '25 `View All Fields` object permission deliberately: it grants read on every field of the object AND auto-grants every field created afterwards.
practices.why_it_matters: It is a genuinely useful replacement for hand-maintaining hundreds of field permissions on an analyst permission set — and a genuinely dangerous permission to hand out, because a future field holding regulated data is exposed on creation with no review step. Any FLS audit that enumerates field permissions will miss holders of this permission entirely.
practices.specifics: `View All Fields` is an object-level permission (Spring '25, API v63.0), available for all standard and custom objects that support field permissions, granting read access to all fields and field data for that object. Assignees are automatically granted access to any new fields created for the object. It is distinct from `View All` (all records of one object), `View All Data` (all records of all objects), and from `Modify All` / `Modify All Data`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models' knowledge of Salesforce object permissions stops at Read/Create/Edit/Delete/View All/Modify All. Asked "how do I give the audit team read access to every field on Case?", an LLM enumerates field permissions one by one or tells the admin to grant View All Data — over-privileging at the org level to solve an object-level problem. When asked to audit FLS, it never checks for View All Fields, so its audit under-reports exposure.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — `grep -rln "View All Fields" skills/` returns zero files; search_knowledge for 'View All Fields object level permission grants access to all fields including new fields created later' returns admin/custom-field-creation (1.267) about new fields being hidden by default, which is the opposite behaviour.

practices.practice: Do not propose a LoginEvent Transaction Security Policy as a brute-force or credential-stuffing control — LoginEvent policies do not fire on failed login attempts, and the MFA action is silently downgraded to Block for API logins.
practices.why_it_matters: A security team believes it has a lockout control that has never evaluated a single failed login. And an 'require MFA from this country' policy that reads as a soft control actually hard-blocks every API and middleware call from that country the moment it activates.
practices.specifics: Official LoginEvent policy considerations: "LoginEvent policies aren't triggered by invalid login attempts such as incorrect passwords." "Multi-factor authentication isn't supported for Lightning Login (passwordless login) users or for API-based logins. For API-based logins, the action is upgraded to Block." Also: if both an Apex policy and a Condition Builder policy exist on the same event with the same action, the Apex policy executes first and `PolicyId` reflects the LAST policy executed; the same Apex class cannot be reused across policies on the same event. With action = None, the event still populates `EvaluationTime`, `PolicyOutcome = NoAction`, and `PolicyId = null`. In ApiEvent, `RowsProcessed = 0` with an empty `QueriedEntities` means the query ran and returned nothing — possibly because of missing row permissions.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/260/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("Considerations for Using Real-Time Event Monitoring", p.100; "LoginEvent Policies — Policy at a Glance", p.117)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to detect credential stuffing, an LLM writes a LoginEvent policy counting logins per user per minute — reasonable-looking Apex against an event stream that only ever contains successful logins. (Salesforce's actual control is the separate CredentialStuffingEvent threat-detection event.) It also treats the MFA action as universally available and never warns that API clients get hard-blocked instead.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — search_knowledge for 'transaction security policy block login from country LoginEvent not triggered by failed login attempts wrong password' returns security/transaction-security-policies (1.493) with strong coverage of policy construction, ISO country codes, and monitor-mode validation; `grep -rn 'invalid login\|failed login\|incorrect password\|brute\|upgraded to Block\|API-based logins' skills/security/transaction-security-policies/` returns zero hits.

practices.practice: When consuming ReportEvent or ListViewEvent for exfiltration detection, correlate chunks by `ExecutionIdentifier` and accept that only the first 1000 events carry record data — never treat one event as one report run.
practices.why_it_matters: A SIEM rule that counts ReportEvent rows massively over-counts (one export becomes N events with duplicated field values), while a rule that reconstructs 'what was exported' from the `Records` field silently under-reports anything past the first 1000 events. Both failures are invisible until an actual investigation.
practices.specifics: Chunking repeats most field values across events; the exceptions are `Records`, `Sequence`, and `EventIdentifier`. `Sequence` is 1-based and increments per chunk. `ExecutionIdentifier` is identical across all chunks of one execution and is the correlation key. `EventIdentifier` is unique per chunk. Official: "When a report executes, we provide the first 1000 events with data in the Records field. Use the ReportId field to view the full report." Applies to ReportEvent, ReportEventStream, ListViewEvent, ListViewEventStream. Object availability is not uniform: only ApiEvent, ListViewEvent, LoginEvent and ReportEvent can back a Transaction Security policy; UriEvent/UriEventStream are Salesforce Classic only; LightningUriEvent/LightningUriEventStream are Lightning Experience only.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/260/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("How Chunking Works with ReportEvent and ListViewEvent", p.108; "Recommended Usage of Event Objects", p.100)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM writing an event-monitoring query treats each ReportEvent row as one report execution and aggregates `COUNT()` by user — producing alert thresholds that are wrong by an unknown multiple. It has no awareness of `ExecutionIdentifier`/`Sequence` and never mentions the 1000-event data ceiling, so its 'reconstruct what the user exported' recipe is quietly lossy.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — search_knowledge for 'ReportEvent chunking first 1000 events ExecutionIdentifier Sequence field event monitoring report data' returns "Coverage: NONE — no skill meets the confidence threshold"; the only hits are raw chunks in knowledge/imports/platform-events.md.

practices.practice: Escape Visualforce formula expressions yourself — `{!$Request.*}` and all `{!...}` formula tags are rendered server-side and are NOT escaped, and the correct escaping differs by where the value lands in the page.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the one XSS vector on Visualforce that the platform's own anti-XSS filters do not cover, and it cannot be fixed client-side because the substitution happens on the server before the browser sees it. It is also the vector AppExchange security review fails packages on.
practices.specifics: Official: "An important feature of these expressions is that data isn't escaped during rendering. Because expressions are rendered on the server, it's not possible to escape rendered data on the client using JavaScript or other client-side technology." The documented server-side defense is nested `SUBSTITUTE()`: `{! SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE($Request.title,"<","<"),">",">")}`. Context matters: a value landing inside a JS string literal that will be used in a link needs the double quote escaped as `%22`, not `"` — otherwise `?retURL=foo%22%3Balert('xss')%3B%2F%2F` yields `<script>var ret = "foo";alert('xss');//";</script>`. Separately: `<apex:includeScript value="{!$CurrentPage.parameters.userInput}" />` lets an attacker load arbitrary remote JavaScript. Standard `<apex:*>` components ARE escaped unless `escape="false"`. Custom JavaScript and `<apex:includeScript>` bodies have no platform protection at all.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM auditing a Visualforce page checks for `escape="false"` and stops — that is the pattern it has memorised. It reports a page using `{!$Request.title}` inside a `<title>` tag or `{!$Api.Session_ID}` in a link as safe, because no `escape` attribute is present. It also proposes client-side sanitisation (DOMPurify, manual JS escaping) for a value that was already interpolated server-side, which cannot work.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — search_knowledge for 'Visualforce formula expression Request parameter not escaped SUBSTITUTE server side escaping escape false outputText' returns lwc/visualforce-to-lwc-migration (1.314) and security/secure-coding-review-checklist, both of which cover `escape="false"` well; `grep -rn '\$Request\|SUBSTITUTE(' skills/security/visualforce-security-and-modernization/ skills/security/xss-and-injection-prevention/` returns zero hits — the formula-tag vector and the `%22`-vs-`"` context rule are absent.

practices.practice: For Connected Apps and External Client Apps, the four controls that became mandatory on 11 May 2026 are not optional hardening — and two of them are one-way doors.
practices.why_it_matters: Enabling PKCE or Refresh Token Rotation cannot be undone, so a team that flips them without first shipping client-side support for `code_verifier` and for capturing rotated refresh tokens permanently breaks its own integration. Non-compliance carries de-listing and suspension, not just a warning.
practices.specifics: Deadline 11 May 2026. (1) OAuth PKCE — client must generate a `code_verifier`, derive `code_challenge` via SHA256 + BASE64URL, and send both; once enabled, PKCE cannot be disabled. (2) Refresh Token Rotation — old tokens are invalidated when a new access token is issued; clients must persist the new refresh token and handle race conditions; once enabled, RTR cannot be disabled. (3) "Limit Idle Refresh Token Time-to-Live (TTL) to 30 Days" — idle refresh tokens auto-invalidate after 30 days, TTL resets on each use. (4) "Enforce Refresh Token IP Allowlist" — maximum 256 addresses total; not applicable to localhost, Salesforce org, or custom URL scheme callbacks. Non-compliance may result in AgentExchange de-listing and/or temporary or permanent suspension of interoperation. Related current state: OAuth Device Flow has been removed with "no exceptions or extensions", uninstalled connected apps are blocked for users lacking `Approve Uninstalled Connected Apps` or `Use Any API Client`, and Spring '26 disabled creation of new legacy Connected Apps.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM writing a Salesforce OAuth integration guide presents PKCE and refresh-token rotation as best-practice options with a 'consider enabling' framing, and never states that they are irreversible per app. Its refresh-token handling code stores the original refresh token once and reuses it forever — which works under the old model and fails on the second call under RTR. It also has no model of the 30-day idle TTL, so its 'long-lived background integration' design breaks after a month of inactivity.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — security/connected-app-security-policies covers PKCE deeply (including the real mutual-exclusion with "Require Secret for Web Server Flow") and admin/integration-admin-connected-apps covers the uninstalled-app blocking; `grep -rln "May 11, 2026" skills/` returns zero files and `grep -rn "Refresh Token Rotation\|refresh token rotation" skills/security/ skills/admin/connected-apps-and-auth/ skills/admin/integration-admin-connected-apps/` returns zero hits.

practices.practice: State the Apex security default by API version, not as a timeless rule: at API 67.0 (Summer '26) database operations run in user mode by default, classes without a sharing declaration default to `with sharing`, and `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` is removed.
practices.why_it_matters: Every pre-2026 Apex security guide on the internet says the opposite ('Apex runs in system mode and ignores CRUD/FLS by default'). Repeating it now produces code that is either over-permissive on old API versions or that mysteriously loses records after a routine API-version bump.
practices.specifics: API v67.0: SOQL, SOSL, DML and `Database` methods run in user mode by default, enforcing the running user's sharing rules, field-level security and object permissions unless code explicitly opts into system mode; classes compiled at v67.0+ default to `with sharing`; `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` is removed — use `WITH USER_MODE`. Triggers always run in system mode and cannot declare sharing or access modes. Note the still-current Security Guide text (v66.0, Spring '26) says the opposite — "When using an Apex class, the built-in user permissions and field-level security restrictions aren't respected during execution" — so cite the version explicitly.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models trained on the pre-v67 corpus emit `public class Foo` with no sharing keyword and then add a comment saying it runs without sharing — wrong for v67+. Conversely they still generate `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` as the recommended clause, which no longer compiles at v67. The failure is not the fact but the missing version qualifier: the model states one absolute truth where the platform has two.
practices.already_covered_by: apex/apex-security-patterns — COVERED. search_knowledge for 'Apex database operations run in user mode by default API version 67 WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED removed' returns the chunk "## The Default Sharing Mode Changed In API 67.0 — A class that used to run without enforcing sharing suddenly enforces it after an API-version bump, and records that were previously visible disappear" (gotchas.md, 0.433), plus apex/apex-security-patterns SKILL.md on triggers-and-user-mode-DML.

practices.practice: Read `System.QueryException: No such column 'X' on entity 'Y'` from a `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` query as a field-level-security denial, not a typo — and migrate to `WITH USER_MODE`, which names the real problem.
practices.why_it_matters: The `No such column` wording sends every engineer to check the field API name and the `__c` suffix on a field that exists and is spelled correctly. It also hides which field failed when several are inaccessible.
practices.specifics: `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` surfaces an FLS failure as `No such column 'AnnualRevenue' on entity 'Account'`. `WITH USER_MODE` (API 58.0+) instead throws `Insufficient permissions: secure query included inaccessible field`, checks object-level and field-level security, honours polymorphic fields, and enforces security on ALL fields in the query — not only those after `SELECT` and `FROM`. User-mode DML raises the correct `DmlException` rather than a security exception as of API v58.0. For graceful degradation instead of an exception, use `Security.stripInaccessible()` — but note it enforces FIELD access only; record-level visibility still requires the class sharing declaration or an explicit `AccessLevel`.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Given the `No such column` error, an LLM's top three suggestions are always: check the API name, add `__c`, verify the field exists in the org. It reaches FLS only after several rounds. Separately it presents `stripInaccessible` as a complete security solution, omitting that it silently drops fields — so a generated `stripInaccessible(AccessType.UPDATABLE, records)` followed by `update` writes partial records with no error and no log line.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge returns admin/salesforce-object-queryability gotcha 4 ("A query with WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED that hits a field the running user can't see returns INVALID_FIELD for the field, not INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS_OR_READONLY", 0.211) and apex/soql-security + apex/apex-dynamic-soql-binding-safety ("WITH USER_MODE (API 58+) is preferred and is enforced at parse time on the field list").

practices.practice: Never present `String.escapeSingleQuotes()` as SOQL-injection protection for anything that is not a quoted string literal — field names, object names, ORDER BY, LIMIT and operators need an allowlist, and bind maps need `Database.queryWithBinds`.
practices.why_it_matters: escapeSingleQuotes is the single most over-trusted API in Apex security review. It cannot defend a dynamically-composed `ORDER BY` or field list because those positions contain no quotes to escape.
practices.specifics: `String.escapeSingleQuotes()` adds a backslash before every single quote so the value cannot terminate the string literal — that is its entire scope. Structural injection points (SELECT field list, FROM object, WHERE field name, ORDER BY, LIMIT, operator) must be validated against `Schema.getGlobalDescribe()` / `getDescribe().fields.getMap()` or a hard-coded allowlist. `Database.queryWithBinds(query, bindMap, accessLevel)` (API v57.0, Spring '23) resolves `:key` references from a `Map<String, Object>` rather than from Apex variables in lexical scope — which also removes the class of bugs where a bind silently resolves to the wrong in-scope variable. Salesforce's own documented first choice remains static SOQL with binding.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to make a dynamic query safe, an LLM wraps every interpolated value — including a sort column and a field list — in `String.escapeSingleQuotes()` and declares the code secure. It has learned the function as a general-purpose sanitiser by analogy to `mysqli_real_escape_string`, and does not model where the quotes actually are.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge returns apex/soql-security (1.369) with the chunk "String.escapeSingleQuotes() only prevents injection through quoted string values. It does nothing when user input appears in: Field names…", plus security/xss-and-injection-prevention and security/secure-coding-review-checklist gotcha 3.

practices.practice: Grant record access to unauthenticated guest users through guest user sharing rules only — they are Read Only, criteria-based, count against the 50 criteria-based rules per object, and no other sharing mechanism works.
practices.why_it_matters: Every other route an engineer would reach for (add the guest user to a public group, insert a share row from Apex, manual share) fails, and the failures are configuration-time or silent rather than a clear error. Since Winter '21 these policies cannot be disabled.
practices.specifics: Guest user sharing rules are the only way to grant record access to unauthenticated guest users, grant Read Only at most, and are a special type of criteria-based sharing rule counting toward the 50 criteria-based sharing rules per object; only the label, rule name, criteria filters, and access level are editable. Guest users cannot be added to queues or public groups, cannot receive access through manual sharing or Apex managed sharing, cannot own records (new records are reassigned to a configured default owner), and cannot hold update or delete object permissions. The Winter '21 settings "Secure guest user record access", "Assign new records created by guest users to the default owner", and the Sites equivalent are permanently on.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM designing a public Experience Cloud form writes an Apex trigger that inserts an `Account__Share` row for the guest user, or tells the admin to add the guest user to a public group used in an existing sharing rule. Both are impossible. It also writes `record.OwnerId = guestUserId`, which the platform overrides.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge for 'guest user sharing rule read only criteria based cannot be in public group or queue Experience Cloud' returns security/guest-user-security-audit (1.564) and admin/experience-cloud-guest-access (0.886), with an example finding on exactly this rule shape.

practices.practice: Do not assume `View All` on a child object grants the implicit read-up to its parent Account — the implicit share is skipped for View All in both directions.
practices.why_it_matters: An access design that gives a support team `View All` on Case and expects them to open the parent Account produces users who can read every Case but cannot open the Account it belongs to. The reverse also fails: `View All` on Account does not carry the account owner's implicit access to child records.
practices.specifics: Salesforce's Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale states, for Parent implicit sharing (read-only access to the parent account for a user with access to a child case, contact, or opportunity, when sharing on the child is not controlled by its parent): "Not granted by the View All permission on the child object." For Child implicit sharing (access to child case/contact/opportunity records for the owner of the parent account, controlled by the account owner's role child access settings): "Not granted by the View All permission on the parent object." Also documented there: Experience Cloud Site sharing, High Volume sharing (sharing-set share group), and High Volume Parent sharing.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM reasons transitively: 'View All Cases means you see all Cases; implicit sharing means Case access grants Account read; therefore they see the Accounts.' It composes two rules it knows individually and misses the documented exception, because the exception is a single bullet in a doc that reads like a feature description.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge for 'implicit sharing parent account child case contact opportunity read access not granted by View All permission' returns security/record-access-troubleshooting (1.367) whose gotchas name `RowCause = 'ImplicitChild'` and the four hardcoded pairs (Contact/Opportunity/Case/Order → Account), plus knowledge/imports/draes.md carrying the literal "Not granted by the View All permission on the child object".

practices.practice: Use a custom Apex sharing reason (custom RowCause) for programmatic shares — `RowCause = 'Manual'` rows are deleted on ownership change and on sharing recalculation.
practices.why_it_matters: Access granted by a trigger disappears at the first record transfer or the next OWD/sharing-rule recalculation, with no error anywhere. The bug surfaces weeks later as 'the junction-based access randomly stopped working'.
practices.specifics: Manual-row-cause shares are wiped whenever the record's owner changes or sharing recalculation runs. A custom Apex sharing reason (Object Manager → [Custom Object] → Apex Sharing Reasons, available only on custom objects) produces shares the platform treats as owned by your code and preserves across transfer and recalculation. Deletion permissions also differ: `RowCause = 'Manual'` shares can be deleted by any user with Modify All Data; custom-row-cause shares require the specific reason to be granted.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to share a record from Apex, an LLM writes `new AccountShare(ParentId=..., UserOrGroupId=..., AccessLevel='Edit', RowCause='Manual')` because Manual is the value it has seen most often, and because it does not model share rows as having a lifecycle tied to ownership. It also frequently targets a standard object, where custom Apex sharing reasons are not available at all.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge for 'Apex managed sharing custom sharing reason RowCause survives owner change manual shares deleted' returns security/record-access-troubleshooting (1.267) anti-pattern 5 and apex/apex-managed-sharing (1.058) anti-pattern 1, plus data/sharing-recalculation-performance example 2.

practices.practice: Distinguish profile Login IP Ranges (a hard login deny) from org-wide Trusted IP Ranges (only skips identity verification) — recommending the wrong one gives an org a control it does not have.
practices.why_it_matters: 'We restricted admin logins to the office network' is one of the most common false beliefs in Salesforce security reviews, and it is created by putting the office range into Network Access instead of the profile.
practices.specifics: Profile → Login IP Ranges: any login from outside the range is denied for users on that profile. Setup → Security → Network Access (Trusted IP Ranges): logins from inside the range skip the device-activation verification code; logins from outside are still permitted after email/mobile verification. Profile login IP ranges are evaluated before trusted IPs. Connected apps add a third layer: "Relax IP restrictions" on an app conflicts with the org setting "Enforce login IP ranges on every request" — with both enabled, users cannot access the app in some circumstances, and this applies to all OAuth-enabled connected apps including mobile.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Because 'Trusted IP Ranges' sounds like an allowlist, an LLM asked to restrict logins by IP names Network Access first. It then describes the effect as 'users outside the range cannot log in', which is precisely wrong.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge for 'profile login IP ranges deny login versus trusted IP ranges network access skip identity verification' returns security/network-security-and-trusted-ips (1.600) with anti-pattern 1 "Conflating Trusted IP Ranges with Login IP Ranges", plus security/org-hardening-and-baseline-config anti-pattern 3.

practices.practice: Match the forensic source to the investigation window and licence before promising an answer: LoginEvent 6 months, EventLogFile 30 days (1 day without the add-on), LoginHistory 6 months — and each requires a different permission.
practices.why_it_matters: An incident opened 45 days after the fact cannot be answered from EventLogFile at all. Knowing which store still holds the evidence, and which permission the responder needs, is the difference between an investigation and a shrug.
practices.specifics: LoginEvent (Login Forensics): 6 months, API only, requires `View Real-Time Event Monitoring Data`, extensible via the `AdditionalInfo` field, needs the Event Monitoring add-on or Real-Time Event Monitoring. EventLogFile Login event type: 30 days, API download plus the Event Monitoring Analytics app, requires `View Event Log Files`, add-on only, not extensible. LoginHistory: 6 months, Setup UI and API, requires `Manage Users`, included in all orgs. Hourly EventLogFile granularity requires full Salesforce Shield; the standalone Event Monitoring add-on gives 30-day retention and all event types for DAILY logs only.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/260/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("How Does LoginEvent Compare to Login Log Lines and Login History?", p.118)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM answers 'query EventLogFile' for any historical login question regardless of window, and asserts 30-day retention in orgs that have no add-on (where it is 1 day). It rarely names the required permission, so its runbook step fails for the responder who has Manage Users but not View Event Log Files.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge for 'EventLogFile 30 day retention LoginEvent 6 months LoginHistory View Event Log Files permission' returns security/security-incident-response (1.327) with a Forensic Evidence Sources table ("EventLogFile | 1 day (free) / 30 days (add-on/Shield)"), security/event-monitoring (0.527), and security/login-forensics on the LoginHistory 6-month purge; event-monitoring/references/gotchas.md:76 covers the hourly-vs-Shield distinction.

practices.practice: Muting permission sets subtract only within their own permission set group — they cannot remove anything granted by a profile, a standalone permission set, or another PSG, and muting a parent permission cascades to its dependents.
practices.why_it_matters: Least-privilege designs built on muting fail silently in orgs that still carry feature permissions on profiles: the mute is configured, the audit shows it, and the user keeps the permission. Conversely, muting Read on an object unexpectedly removes five other permissions in the group.
practices.specifics: If a user holds the same permission via a profile, a directly-assigned permission set, or a different permission set group, the muting permission set has no effect. Profiles are entirely outside the scope of muting. Within the group, muting a dependency cascades: muting Read on an object also mutes Create, Edit, Delete, View All Records, and Modify All Records. A muting permission set cannot be assigned directly to a user — it only takes effect as a muting entry inside a PSG. Related runtime behaviour: `PermissionSetGroup.Status` cycles Updated / Outdated / Updating / Failed, and during Updating assigned users retain the permissions from the last completed recalculation.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked to remove Delete on Opportunity from one team proposes a muting permission set without asking where the permission comes from — and permission sets being 'additive only' is a fact it knows, so it presents muting as the general-purpose subtractive tool. It also never predicts the dependency cascade, so its 'mute Read only' recommendation removes far more than intended.
practices.already_covered_by: COVERED — search_knowledge for 'muting permission set cannot mute permission granted by profile or another permission set group muting Read cascades' returns architect/zero-trust-salesforce-patterns (1.200) gotcha 4 "Muting Permission Sets do not mute Profile-granted permissions", security/permission-set-groups-and-muting (0.933), and admin/permission-sets-vs-profiles anti-pattern 3; PSG status/recalculation is covered by security/privileged-access-management and admin/permission-set-group-composition.

practices.practice: Do not put an encrypted field in a criteria-based sharing rule, a Unique/External ID custom field under probabilistic encryption, or on Custom Metadata Types — and understand that destroying a key does not clear the search index.
practices.why_it_matters: These are configuration-time hard blocks and one post-hoc surprise. The search-index residue in particular defeats the 'destroy the key to make the data unrecoverable' story that key destruction is usually sold on.
practices.specifics: Official: "You can't use encrypted custom fields in criteria-based sharing rules." Custom fields that cannot be encrypted include fields with the Unique or External ID attributes (probabilistic scheme only), fields on external data objects, and fields used in an account contact relation. You cannot create an encrypted custom field via Schema Builder. Shield Platform Encryption does not work with Custom Metadata Types. Search: "If you encrypt fields with a key and then destroy the key, the corresponding search terms remain in the search index. However, you can't decrypt the data associated with the destroyed key." Data copied from an encrypted Contact field into a Quote field is not encrypted. If a legacy portal created before 2013 is still enabled, standard fields cannot be encrypted at all.
practices.official_source_url: https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/254/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_security_impl_guide.pdf ("Tradeoffs and Limitations of Shield Platform Encryption", pp.206–207)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to design a right-to-erasure ('crypto-shredding') process, an LLM confidently proposes destroying the tenant secret and calls the data irrecoverable, with no mention of the retained search terms or the unencrypted Quote copies. On the config side, it will happily encrypt a field that an existing criteria-based sharing rule depends on and predict no impact.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — the criteria-based sharing rule constraint IS covered: `grep -rn 'criteria-based sharing' skills/security/platform-encryption/` hits SKILL.md:96, examples.md:95, llm-anti-patterns.md:64 and the checker script (check 2 detects fields in both an encryption policy and a criteria-based sharing rule). The search-index residue after key destruction, the Custom Metadata Types exclusion, the Unique/External-ID probabilistic block, the Quote-copy leak and the legacy-portal block are not present.

practices.practice: Treat the Pub/Sub API gRPC error code as the routing key for recovery, not the gRPC status. Build a decoder table keyed on the `sfdc.platform.eventbus.grpc.*` string pulled from the exception Trailers via `getTrailers()`, because the same `UNAVAILABLE`/`INTERNAL` gRPC status maps to at least four different recovery actions.
practices.why_it_matters: Clients that branch on gRPC status alone retry a permanently-fatal condition forever. `...topic.not.found` (bad topic name) and `...service.protection.triggered` (back off) both surface as generic RPC failures; retrying the first is an infinite loop, and NOT retrying the second drops events.
practices.specifics: Codes arrive in gRPC Trailers, retrieved with `getTrailers()`; the RPC ID for Salesforce support is prefixed `rpcId:` in the message. Key codes: `sfdc.platform.eventbus.grpc.subscription.fetch.replayid.corrupted` (replay ID invalid or past the 72-hour window), `...subscription.fetch.replayid.validation.failed` (replay_preset=CUSTOM with no replay_id supplied), `...subscription.limit.exceeded` (24-hour delivery allocation gone — wait for the next 24-hour period, retrying will not help), `...subscription.fetch.overflow` (client requested more events than it drained — process before the next FetchRequest), `...concurrent.client.limit.exceeded`, `...service.protection.stream.limit.triggered`, `...service.auth.error` (also fires on IP session locking and across Salesforce release windows), `...topic.not.found`, `...schema.meta.permission`, `...publish.stream.sweeper.timeout` (no publish request in 1,800 seconds), `...publish.auth.refresh.invalid` (refresh token illegally present in the *initial* publish request), `...managed.subscription.already.active`, `...managed.subscription.config.stopped` (state must be RUN). `io.grpc.StatusRuntimeException: UNAVAILABLE: RST_STREAM closed stream.` is the normal long-lived-connection recycle and must be retried, not alerted on.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to write a resilient Pub/Sub subscriber, an LLM produces a single `try/except` that catches `grpc.RpcError`, logs `e.code()`, and retries with a fixed backoff. It never calls `getTrailers()`, so it never sees the Salesforce-specific code, and it therefore retries `topic.not.found` and `subscription.limit.exceeded` in a tight loop. It also treats `UNAVAILABLE: RST_STREAM` as an outage and pages on-call, when it is routine stream recycling. Models also confidently invent plausible-but-nonexistent codes like `SFDC_REPLAY_ID_EXPIRED`.

practices.practice: On `...replayid.corrupted`, do NOT resubscribe with EARLIEST as a reflex. Choose LATEST plus an out-of-band reconciliation, because EARLIEST replays up to 72 hours of events and can itself blow the 24-hour delivery allocation.
practices.why_it_matters: The documented recovery lists both LATEST and EARLIEST. Picking EARLIEST on a high-volume CDC channel replays three days of traffic against a delivery allocation of 25,000/day (Enterprise), which trips `...subscription.limit.exceeded` and takes the subscriber down for the rest of the 24-hour window — converting a recoverable gap into a full-day outage.
practices.specifics: ReplayPreset enum values are LATEST, EARLIEST, CUSTOM. Retention is 72 hours and is explicitly not guaranteed — purge 'may occur later', so older events can transiently still be there and then vanish. Replay IDs are opaque, are NOT guaranteed contiguous for consecutive events, and are NOT unique across org migration/maintenance; to uniquely identify an event message use the event `id` field, not the replay ID. Org migration to a new instance can reset the retained stream, making prior events permanently inaccessible.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write `replay_preset=EARLIEST` as the 'safe' fallback ('replay everything so we lose nothing'), and they build deduplication keyed on `replay_id` because it looks like a monotonic sequence number. Both are wrong: replay IDs are non-contiguous and can repeat after a maintenance migration, so replay-ID-keyed dedup silently drops or double-processes events. Models also assume replay IDs can be arithmetically compared or incremented.

practices.practice: Correct the repo's stated cause of CDC overflow events. `GAP_OVERFLOW` is emitted when a single transaction exceeds 100,000 changes — it has nothing to do with subscriber lag or the retention window.
practices.why_it_matters: An operator told that GAP_OVERFLOW means 'the subscriber fell behind' will scale up consumers and tune replay position, which fixes nothing. The real trigger is a publisher-side bulk operation or cascade delete, so the fix is upstream batching or a reconciliation job — a completely different remediation.
practices.specifics: Threshold is exactly 100,000 changes per transaction: the first 100,000 changes generate normal change events, and everything beyond generates one overflow event per entity type. Weighting is asymmetric — a create, delete, or undelete counts as 1 change, but an update counts 1 change per modified field, so a 3-field update on 34,000 records crosses the line. The overflow event's `changeType` is `GAP_OVERFLOW`, it carries no record fields, and `recordIds` contains the placeholder `000000000000000AAA` rather than real IDs. `changedFields`, `nulledFields`, and `diffFields` are all empty. Common real causes: cascade deletes and recurring-event expansion with many attendees.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs conflate 'gap event' with 'I missed events because I was offline', because that is the intuitive reading of the word gap. They then write handlers that respond to GAP_OVERFLOW by re-subscribing from an earlier replay ID — which returns the same overflow event again. They also write `for (String id : event.recordIds) fetchRecord(id);` and get a 'malformed id' or empty-result path against `000000000000000AAA`, and unlike normal gap events (which DO carry real record IDs) there is no per-record recovery available at all.

practices.practice: Size the platform-event *delivery* allocation against the API subscriber fan-out only. Apex triggers, Flows, and Process Builder do not consume it; every additional Pub/Sub, CometD, empApi, or Event Relay subscriber multiplies consumption of the same event.
practices.why_it_matters: Delivery allocation is per-subscriber, not per-event. Adding a second Pub/Sub consumer to an existing channel doubles daily consumption with no code change and no warning, and Enterprise only gets 25,000/day. Teams size capacity from the publish rate and are blindsided when the ceiling is a function of subscriber count.
practices.specifics: Daily delivery allocation (rolling 24h), no add-on: Performance/Unlimited 50,000; Enterprise 25,000; Developer 10,000. Add-on license adds 100,000/day (3 million/month) with grace allowances. Delivery counts ONLY for Pub/Sub API, CometD, the empApi Lightning component, and Event Relays. The allocation is shared between high-volume platform events and Change Data Capture. Exceeding it disconnects subscriptions: CometD receives `403::Organization total events daily limit exceeded`; Pub/Sub API receives `sfdc.platform.eventbus.grpc.subscription.limit.exceeded`. Concurrent CometD clients: 2,000 (Performance/Unlimited), 1,000 (Enterprise), 20 (Developer).
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked 'will 30,000 events/day fit in our Enterprise org?', an LLM answers yes by comparing 30,000 to the *publish* limit (250,000/hour) and never mentions the delivery allocation at all, or it applies the delivery allocation to Apex trigger subscribers and wrongly warns that a purely in-org event design will hit the cap. Models also assume the allocation is per-channel rather than org-wide and shared with CDC.

practices.practice: Distinguish the hourly *publish* allocation from the daily *delivery* allocation and know that exceeding publish drops the event entirely — it is not queued for later.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams build burst-tolerant publishers assuming Salesforce buffers overflow. It does not. A batch job that publishes 300,000 events in an hour on Enterprise loses the excess permanently, with a per-call error the calling code usually ignores because `EventBus.publish` returns SaveResult rather than throwing.
practices.specifics: Hourly publish allocation without add-on: Performance/Unlimited 250,000, Enterprise 250,000, Developer 50,000, Professional (with API add-on) 250,000. Add-on license adds 25,000/hour. On breach the publish call fails with the `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` error and 'the events aren't published or queued'.

practices.practice: Add Composite Graph to the Composite resource decision set. It is the only Composite resource that gives per-unit atomicity across 500 nodes; `/composite/` caps at 25 subrequests and `/composite/batch/` gives no rollback at all.
practices.why_it_matters: The repo's composite skill enumerates four resources and omits the fifth. A practitioner who needs atomic multi-object graphs at scale is currently routed to `/composite/` with allOrNone, hits the 25-subrequest ceiling, and hand-rolls compensating logic that Composite Graph provides natively.
practices.specifics: `/composite/graph`: up to 500 nodes per graph, up to 75 graphs per payload, maximum graph depth 15. allOrNone is implicit — each graph is its own transactional unit that fully commits or fully rolls back, and one graph failing does not block the others in the same request; the per-graph `isSuccessful` boolean in the response is the thing to branch on. Contrast `/composite/batch/`: 25 subrequests, runs sequentially, each commits as it goes with NO rollback of earlier commits, and the whole batch times out at 10 minutes with remaining subrequests unexecuted.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs default to `/composite/` for every multi-step write and describe `/composite/batch/` as 'like composite but faster', omitting that batch has no atomicity and no `@{referenceId}` resolution. Asked for an atomic 200-record parent/child load they produce a 25-subrequest `/composite/` call and then invent a nonexistent 'batchSize' parameter, or they claim Composite Graph shares the 25-subrequest limit. They also miss the 10-minute `/composite/batch/` timeout entirely.

practices.practice: Use `Crypto.verifyHMac()` for webhook signature verification. Do not compute the HMAC and compare with `String.equals()` — Apex `String.equals` short-circuits on first differing character and is not constant-time.
practices.why_it_matters: A short-circuiting comparison leaks the expected signature one byte at a time under timing measurement, letting an attacker forge a valid signature for an unauthenticated public endpoint. The repo currently ships code that does exactly this and labels it 'Constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks', which is worse than no comment — a reviewer reads the comment and stops looking.
practices.specifics: `Crypto.verifyHMac(algorithmName, input, privateKey, macToVerify)` returns Boolean and performs the comparison safely; supported algorithms are HMACMD5, HMACSHA1, HMACSHA256, HMACSHA512. The signature must be computed over the raw request body bytes (`RestContext.request.requestBody`), never over re-serialized parsed JSON, because key order and whitespace change the bytes. Pair with a signed timestamp header and reject outside a bounded skew window for replay protection.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: This is the single most reliable LLM failure in this domain: models generate `Crypto.generateMac(...)`, hex-encode it, compare with `==` or `.equals()`, and then add the comment 'constant-time comparison' — they know the requirement exists and believe stating it satisfies it. They almost never emit `Crypto.verifyHMac`, and they frequently HMAC a re-serialized `JSON.serialize(parsedBody)` instead of the raw body, producing an implementation that fails against every real sender.

But skills/integration/webhook-inbound-patterns/SKILL.md:104-111 implements it as `// Constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks` followed by `return expected.equals(signature);`. `grep -rn "Crypto.verifyHMac" skills/` returns zero matches repo-wide. Also note integration/webhook-signature-verification is a stub: references/llm-anti-patterns.md is 229 bytes.

practices.practice: Publish the exact Salesforce Connect / external-object ceilings up front, because they are absolute per-org caps that no amount of adapter tuning moves.
practices.why_it_matters: Salesforce Connect is chosen precisely to avoid storing data, and teams then discover the design is capped at 100 external objects org-wide and 4 joins per query — architectural limits that only surface after the OData service is already built. The 2,000-row report fetch quietly truncates reports rather than erroring.
practices.specifics: Maximum external objects per org: 100. Maximum joins per query across external objects and other object types: 4. OData callouts: 20,000 per hour (Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited). Maximum page size for server-driven paging: 2,000 rows. A report that includes an external object fetches up to 2,000 records for the primary object regardless of object type. Maximum length of an OAuth token issued by the external system: 4,000 characters. Separately, callouts to external objects are NOT excluded from the long-running-Apex limit (a known issue), so external-object rendering competes with the 25-concurrent-long-running-request budget.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked whether Salesforce Connect scales, LLMs answer 'yes, because data is not stored in Salesforce there are no storage limits' — technically true and completely misleading. They omit the 100-object cap, invent an SOQL-like unlimited join model, and describe external-object reporting as equivalent to standard reporting. They also never mention the 4,000-character OAuth token cap, which is the actual failure when an external IdP issues a large JWT.

practices.practice: For inbound mTLS, name the exact three-part configuration: the `Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication` user permission on an API-only user, the CA-signed client certificate uploaded to the org truststore, and port 8443 on the endpoint. Omitting any one produces an authentication failure that looks like bad credentials.
practices.why_it_matters: mTLS is usually a compliance requirement with a hard deadline, and the failure mode is indistinguishable from an OAuth problem. Teams spend days re-issuing tokens because nothing in the error says 'you posted to port 443 instead of 8443' or 'this user lacks the mutual-auth permission'.
practices.specifics: Inbound: assign the `Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication` user permission to the API-only user; the client presents its certificate to Salesforce on port 8443 (not the standard 443); Salesforce accepts only a CA-signed client certificate, and that certificate must be uploaded to the org's truststore (the repository of accepted mTLS certificates) — self-signed will not work inbound. Outbound is a separate mechanism: Salesforce acts as client, and the client certificate is referenced from the Named Credential / callout configuration, where a Salesforce-generated self-signed cert IS acceptable if the counterparty trusts it.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs collapse inbound and outbound mTLS into one procedure, which is the core error — they tell you to generate a self-signed certificate in Setup > Certificate and Key Management and 'use it for mutual authentication', which works outbound and is rejected inbound. They omit port 8443 entirely (the single most common cause of a failed inbound mTLS rollout) and rarely name the `Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication` permission, instead suggesting a generic 'API Enabled' or 'Modify All Data'.

But `grep -ril "Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication" skills/` = 0 and `grep -ril "truststore" skills/` = 0. practices.practice: State the API-version retirement timeline with the calendar dates and the distinguishing HTTP status. Retired versions return `410 GONE`, which is how you tell 'this version was retired' from 'this endpoint path is wrong' (404).
practices.why_it_matters: Integration owners cannot plan remediation from a policy statement ('minimum 3 years'); they need the two live deadlines. And on the day it breaks, the 410-vs-404 distinction is what routes the incident to 'upgrade the client' instead of 'the URL is malformed'.
practices.specifics: Versions 21.0–30.0 (plus Streaming API 23.0–36.0) retired in Summer '25 (June 2025). Versions 31.0–40.0 are deprecated now and retire in Summer '28 (June 2028) — integrations must be on 41.0 or later. Separately, SOAP `login()` in API versions 31.0–64.0 retires in Summer '27, which breaks every username/password SOAP authentication regardless of the version-retirement schedule. Retired versions return `410:GONE` from REST API. Summer '26 ships API version 67.0.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recite the 3-year end-of-life policy and stop, or they give a stale cutoff. They also generate example endpoints pinned to whatever version dominated their training data (`/services/data/v58.0/`) while the surrounding prose claims 'use the latest version', shipping code that is already several releases behind. Critically, they almost never distinguish the SOAP `login()` retirement (Summer '27) from the version retirement (Summer '28) — these are separate deadlines that break different integrations.

practices.practice: Before any API-version retirement, identify the actual callers from `ApiTotalUsage` EventLogFile rows using CLIENT_NAME, CONNECTED_APP_ID, USER_ID and CLIENT_IP — do not rely on the org's own metadata API versions.
practices.why_it_matters: The versions in your Apex classes and Flow definitions say nothing about what external systems are calling. The population that breaks on retirement is external clients you may not own, and ApiTotalUsage is the only free telemetry that names them.
practices.specifics: `ApiTotalUsage` events are free (no Event Monitoring / Shield license required) and cover SOAP, REST, and Bulk API requests. Access via Setup > Security > Event Monitoring > Event Log Browser (Summer '24+) to browse and download CSV, or query `SELECT Id, LogFile, EventType, CreatedDate FROM EventLogFile WHERE EventType IN ('ApiTotalUsage')`. Trace each legacy call using CONNECTED_APP_ID, CLIENT_NAME, USER_ID, CLIENT_IP.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked 'how do I find integrations on old API versions', LLMs suggest grepping the codebase for `<apiVersion>` in metadata, or they recommend the paid `ApiEvent`/`ApiEventStream` (Event Monitoring add-on) without noting that `ApiTotalUsage` is free. Neither answer finds the external SOAP client from 2016 that is the actual risk. They also often invent a Setup page like 'API Usage by Version' that does not exist.

practices.practice: When designing bulk child-record loads, note that Bulk API 2.0 has no serial ConcurrencyMode — that option exists only in Bulk API 1.0. Mitigate parent-row lock contention by sorting the input by parent ID instead.
practices.why_it_matters: The standard published remedy for `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW` on bulk child loads is 'enable serial mode'. That advice is unexecutable on Bulk 2.0, so a team following it either wastes a sprint or is forced back to the deprecated 1.0 API. Sorting by parent ID is the remedy that actually works on 2.0.
practices.specifics: Bulk API 2.0 exposes no `concurrencyMode: Serial` on job creation; it is a Bulk API 1.0 concept and is an open IdeaExchange request. Salesforce row locking is pessimistic with a non-configurable 10-second timeout. Updating a child of a master-detail relationship locks the parent for the transaction, so two parallel internal batches touching children of the same parent collide. Sorting input by parent ID keeps a parent's children inside one 10,000-record internal batch, which removes cross-batch contention.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs reliably answer `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW` with 'set the job to serial mode' and then emit a Bulk 2.0 `POST /jobs/ingest` body containing a `concurrencyMode` field — a parameter the 2.0 endpoint does not accept. They also recommend client-side retry loops without noting the 10-second lock timeout means the retry usually collides again unless the ordering is fixed.

Confirming coverage, not proposing new work.

practices.practice: Do not size Bulk API 2.0 uploads from the 150 MB figure. 150 MB is the post-base64 ceiling; base64 inflates payload by roughly 50%, so the practical raw-CSV chunk is about 100 MB.
practices.why_it_matters: A 140 MB raw CSV is under the documented number and still fails, because it becomes ~210 MB encoded. The arithmetic is invisible unless someone states it.
practices.specifics: Per-job / per-upload-request cap is 150 MB of base64-encoded content; Salesforce notes conversion 'can increase the data size by approximately 50%' and advises uploading data not exceeding 100 MB raw. Daily ingest cap 150,000,000 records per rolling 24 hours. One internal batch per 10,000 records. Per-field maximum 131,072 characters; per-record maximum 400,000 characters. The API auto-retries; more than 20 retries on ingest (15 on query) means the file is too large / the filter too broad, not a transient fault. Query jobs have a separate 10,000-per-day submission limit and do not consume batch allocations.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs quote '150 MB per job' verbatim with no base64 caveat, and they frequently transplant Bulk API 1.0 concepts — 10,000 records per batch as a *user-supplied* parameter, 10,000 batches per day — into 2.0 where batching is automatic. They also invent a per-job record cap for 2.0, which does not exist.

Only the 131,072-char field / 400,000-char record caps are absent (`grep -ril "400,000 characters" skills/` = 0).

practices.practice: Recognise that the concurrent-request ceiling counts only requests running longer than 20 seconds, and that its remedy is making calls faster or serialising the slow ones — not throttling total call volume.
practices.why_it_matters: `REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` is emitted for two structurally different conditions (24-hour total exhausted vs concurrent long-running exceeded) with different fixes. Confusing them leads teams to throttle a healthy high-volume integration while the actual culprit — one slow report query — keeps failing.
practices.specifics: Concurrent long-running limit: 25 (production orgs and sandboxes), 5 (Developer Edition and trial orgs), counted only for requests in flight longer than 20 seconds. Internal limit name surfaced in errors is `ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn`; HTTP 403 with exception code `REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. Separately: REST API returns `QUERY_TIMEOUT`, SOAP API returns `REQUEST_RUNNING_TOO_LONG`. Total 24-hour allocations: Developer Edition 15,000; Enterprise/Professional/Unlimited/Performance base 100,000 plus per-license (1,000/user on EE, 5,000/user on UE/PE); Full sandbox 5,000,000.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat 25 as a hard cap on simultaneous API calls and design elaborate client-side semaphores limiting concurrency to 25 for sub-second requests — throttling throughput for no reason. They also read `REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` as always meaning the daily allocation and advise 'reduce your daily call count'.

practices.practice: Know that a Continuation resumes in a *new* Apex transaction with all governor limits reset — which is a correctness hazard, not just a performance note.
practices.why_it_matters: State accumulated before the callout (static variables, uncommitted DML intent, trigger-recursion guards) does not survive into the resume method. Code that assumes one continuous transaction produces duplicate DML or re-fires trigger logic it thought it had suppressed.
practices.specifics: Continuation limits: maximum 3 parallel callouts per continuation; maximum 3 chained continuations; 120-second timeout per continuation — and the timeout set in the autogenerated web-service stub or on the HttpRequest is ignored, only the Continuation timeout is enforced. Maximum HTTP response size 1 MB; maximum HTTP POST form size 1 MB with at most 500 keys; maximum Visualforce controller-state size 80 KB (distinct from the 170 KB view-state limit). Callouts inside one continuation run in parallel, so elapsed time is the longest callout, not the sum.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present Continuation as 'async callouts' and carry state in static variables across the callback boundary, which silently resets. They also set `new Continuation(180)` — above the 120-second maximum — and set a timeout on the HttpRequest expecting it to apply. And they claim the 1 MB response cap is the general Apex heap limit (6 MB sync), so they size responses wrongly.
