practices.practice: Assign External Credential Principal Access via permission set as a mandatory deployment step, and treat HTTP 401 from a Named Credential callout as a permission problem before touching the credential itself.
practices.why_it_matters: Enhanced Named Credentials split the endpoint (Named Credential) from the secret (External Credential), and access to the secret is gated by a permission-set assignment that has no default. The callout fails with a generic Unauthorized, so teams re-enter passwords and rotate keys against a problem that is purely an assignment.
practices.specifics: The assignment lives on the Permission Set under 'External Credential Principal Access' and must reference the named principal by its Parameter Name. Failure surfaces as HTTP 401 or `System.CalloutException: Unauthorized`. Guest User profiles and some custom profiles/permission sets additionally need explicit object permissions on `User External Credentials`. Only OAuth supports true per-user principals; Named Principal is the org-wide identity.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate the full Named Credential + External Credential setup and then jump straight to `req.setEndpoint('callout:My_API/path')`, omitting the permission-set step entirely — this is probably the most common LLM-authored Named Credential defect. They also assume the deploying admin's System Administrator profile implies access (it does not) and never mention the Guest User `User External Credentials` object permission.

HTTP 401 or throw System.CalloutException: Unauthorized', and skills/flow/flow-external-services/references/gotchas.md [0.267] '## Gotcha 4: External Credential Permission Set Assignment Is Required at Runtime, Not Just at Setup'. Confirming.

practices.practice: When a callout needs a secret inside a custom header or body, use Named Credential merge fields with the `{!$Credential.<ExternalCredential>.<ParameterName>}` syntax and enable 'Allow Merge Fields in HTTP Header/Body' — never read the secret into an Apex String.
practices.why_it_matters: Merge-field resolution happens at the callout boundary, so the secret never enters the Apex heap and cannot appear in a debug log, an exception stack, or a serialized retry payload. Any pattern that materialises the key in Apex defeats the entire point of External Credentials.
practices.specifics: Syntax is `{!$Credential.Container.ParameterName}` where Container is the External Credential and ParameterName is the principal's authentication parameter. The 'Generate Authorization Header' checkbox emits the standard Authorization header automatically — leave it on unless the API needs a non-standard header, in which case disable it and supply the header via merge field. The 'Allow Merge Fields in HTTP Header' and 'Allow Merge Fields in HTTP Body' checkboxes must be enabled on the Named Credential or the merge field is sent as a literal string.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: For an API-key service, LLMs write `req.setHeader('X-API-Key', ApiKeySettings__c.getInstance().Key__c)` — pulling the key from a Custom Setting into a String — or they store the key in a Custom Metadata field. Both put the secret in the heap and in debug logs. When they do use merge fields, they forget the 'Allow Merge Fields' checkboxes, and the callout ships the literal text `{!$Credential....}` to the vendor, producing a 401 with no obvious cause.

practices.practice: Serialise concurrent PATCH-by-external-ID requests per key. Upsert is idempotent for a *sequence* of calls but not for *simultaneous* ones — two in-flight upserts on the same external ID race and one fails with a duplicate-value error.
practices.why_it_matters: Idempotency is the usual justification for choosing upsert, and it holds only under serialisation per key. Event-driven producers that fan out in parallel hit this within days of go-live, and the error text ('duplicate value found') points at data quality rather than at concurrency, so teams chase phantom duplicates.
practices.specifics: When the external ID value matches more than one existing record the API returns HTTP 300 (Multiple Choices) and no records are created or updated. Under concurrency the failure is instead `duplicate value found: <field>__c duplicates value on record with id: <Id>` because the second request arrives while the first is still committing. The `updateOnly=true` query parameter suppresses record creation and is the correct guard when the caller must never insert. Permissions differ by field configuration: a custom field marked both External ID *and* Unique needs no special permission; External ID without Unique requires View All Data. Certain top-level domains that collide with file extensions (for example `.inc`) in an external ID value produce a spurious 404 — use a different external ID field or SOAP API.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs assert 'upsert is idempotent, so parallel retries are safe' and generate a `Promise.all` / parallel worker pool over the same key space. They also omit `updateOnly` entirely (it appears in zero of the repo's skills and rarely in model output), and they never mention the HTTP 300 response — they assume a multi-match returns 400 or silently updates the first record.

practices.practice: For platform-event Apex subscribers, budget the retry allowance as 10 total executions and use `setResumeCheckpoint()` so a partial failure does not re-process already-committed events.
practices.why_it_matters: Without a resume checkpoint, throwing RetryableException replays the entire batch, so events processed successfully before the failure are processed again — turning a retry mechanism into a duplicate-generation mechanism. And after the tenth execution the trigger enters an error state and stops consuming the channel entirely, which is a silent outage.
practices.specifics: A platform event trigger runs at most 10 times (initial run plus 9 retries) via `EventBus.RetryableException`; after that it moves to the error state and stops processing new events. Retry delay grows on successive attempts. `EventBus.TriggerContext.currentContext().setResumeCheckpoint(replayId)` marks the last successfully processed event so the retry resumes after it. `EventBus.TriggerContext.currentContext().retries` exposes the current attempt count. Trigger batch size is configurable up to 2,000 via Metadata API (default 2,000 for standard-volume, but the platform may deliver fewer).
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs throw `EventBus.RetryableException` for every failure including permanent ones (bad data, missing reference record), burning all 10 attempts and then poisoning the channel. They almost never emit `setResumeCheckpoint`, so their retry logic re-processes the whole batch. They also assume retries are unlimited, describing the mechanism as 'Salesforce will keep retrying until it succeeds'.

practices.practice: Never publish a platform event with 'Publish Immediately' from inside a transaction that can still roll back — the event survives the rollback and subscribers act on state that was never committed.
practices.why_it_matters: This produces the worst class of integration bug: an external system holds a record that does not exist in Salesforce, with no error anywhere. Savepoint rollback erases local DML only; it cannot recall a message already on the event bus.
practices.specifics: 'Publish After Commit' publishes only if the transaction commits and discards the event on rollback; 'Publish Immediately' publishes regardless of transaction outcome and cannot be undone by `Database.rollback()` or a savepoint. For Publish After Commit events each `EventBus.publish` counts as one DML statement against the Apex DML limit.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs pick Publish Immediately whenever the requirement mentions 'real time' or 'immediately', reading it as a latency setting rather than a transactional-semantics setting. They then wrap the publish in a try/catch with `Database.rollback(sp)` in the catch and describe the result as transactionally safe.

practices.practice: Cache the Pub/Sub Avro schema by schema_id and re-fetch via GetSchema whenever the schema_id on a FetchResponse or PublishResponse differs from the cached one — an admin adding a field rotates the ID.
practices.why_it_matters: A stale cached schema does not throw cleanly; it decodes the new binary payload against the old writer schema and yields garbage values in existing fields. The symptom is 'the data looks wrong', not 'decoding failed', so it is diagnosed as an upstream data problem.
practices.specifics: Every event definition change (including additive) changes the schema_id. Compare the schema_id on each PublishResponse/FetchResponse against the cached one and call the GetSchema RPC on mismatch. Avro schema resolution rules govern whether old and new coexist, so publish and subscribe continue working across resolvable differences — which is exactly why the failure is silent rather than fatal.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs hardcode the schema ID as a module-level constant after fetching it once at startup, because that is what every tutorial does. They also write the decoder with a single global schema object rather than a per-schema_id map, so a mid-stream rotation corrupts every subsequent event.

practices.practice: Design Outbound Message consumers as idempotent and order-agnostic, and return the exact SOAP `<Ack>true</Ack>` envelope — an HTTP 200 with any other body is treated as failure and triggers 24 hours of redelivery.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the classic 'the partner already has the data but Salesforce keeps resending' incident. The endpoint returns 200, the developer sees the record land, and Salesforce keeps retrying because it never got the acknowledgement it parses for.
practices.specifics: Salesforce waits up to 10 seconds for the acknowledgement. Retries use exponential backoff with intervals growing up to 2 hours, and messages are dropped from the queue permanently after 24 hours. Retried messages are delivered independently of their queue position, so ordering is not preserved. Up to 5 users can be registered to receive a daily notification listing outbound messages that have failed for at least 24 hours.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe Outbound Messages as 'fire and forget webhooks' and write receivers that return `200 OK` with an empty body or a JSON `{"status":"ok"}` — neither is the SOAP ack Salesforce parses. They also claim delivery is ordered and exactly-once, which leads to consumers that use the payload as an authoritative last-write.

practices.why_it_matters: The security argument has been available for years and has not moved these integrations. practices.specifics: Blocked by default for orgs created in Summer '23 or later; controlled by the 'Block Authorization Flows' setting. Full retirement for connected apps in Winter '27. Replacements: OAuth 2.0 JWT bearer flow (certificate-based, no user interaction) or OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with a designated Run-As user, both configured through External Client Apps; web server flow with PKCE for user-facing login.

practices.practice: Do not architect around Salesforce having a stable outbound IP address. On Hyperforce the callout egress IP is not a fixed value you can hand a partner for firewall allowlisting; use mTLS, OAuth, or Private Connect as the network-identity control instead.
practices.why_it_matters: Partner security teams routinely ask for 'the Salesforce IP' and integration owners supply one observed in a log. practices.specifics: Salesforce publishes Hyperforce outbound IP lists and an 'IP Addresses and Domains to Allow' article, but also publishes 'Preferred Alternatives to IP Allowlisting on Hyperforce' explicitly steering customers away from IP-based controls. practices.practice: Keep a long-lived Pub/Sub publish stream alive: an idle PublishStream is terminated after 1,800 seconds with `...publish.stream.sweeper.timeout`, so low-frequency publishers need a keep-alive or a reconnect-on-demand design.
practices.why_it_matters: A publisher that emits a few events per day looks correct in testing and then fails in production every time traffic pauses for 30 minutes. Because the error arrives on the stream rather than on a publish call, it is easy to log and ignore until events start disappearing.
practices.specifics: Exact code: `sfdc.platform.eventbus.grpc.publish.stream.sweeper.timeout`, documented cause 'No publish request received during 1,800 seconds'. Recovery is to resume publishing or reconnect the stream. Related trap: including an auth refresh token in the *initial* PublishRequest raises `sfdc.platform.eventbus.grpc.publish.auth.refresh.invalid` — the refresh belongs on subsequent requests only.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs open a PublishStream at application startup and hold it for the process lifetime with no idle handling, because the gRPC bidirectional-stream idiom they have learned from generic tutorials has no sweeper. They also put the auth refresh token in the first request 'so it's authenticated from the start', which is precisely the documented error case.

practices.practice: For ManagedSubscribe (server-side replay tracking), handle the commit-specific error set separately from the fetch error set — committing an older replay ID than the one already committed is an error, not a no-op.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams adopt ManagedSubscribe to stop managing replay IDs and then write commit logic that commits per-event in arrival order. Any out-of-order or duplicated commit produces an error the client usually ignores, and the server-side checkpoint silently stops advancing — so a restart replays a large backlog.
practices.specifics: ManagedSubscribe-only errors include `...managed.subscription.already.active` (another client holds the same subscription ID; wait for expiry), `...managed.subscription.config.stopped` (the configuration's state is STOP — set it to RUN before subscribing), `...managed.subscription.config.deleted`, `...managed.subscription.subscription.id.invalid` (ID must be 15 or 18 characters), `...managed.subscription.id.or.developer.name.empty` (supplying BOTH the ID and the developer name is an error — provide exactly one), `...managed.subscription.fetch.request.commit.request.restricted` and `...fetch.request.auth.request.restricted` (a CommitReplayRequest or auth refresh must not appear in the *initial* fetch request). Commit responses have their own error set: no replay ID supplied, replay ID outside the retention window, commit attempted before any event was delivered, and replay ID older than the already-committed one. ManagedSubscribe is Beta.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present ManagedSubscribe as strictly simpler than Subscribe and generate a client that commits after every single event with no error branch on the CommitResponse. They pass both subscription ID and developer name 'to be safe' (an error), and they put the CommitReplayRequest in the first fetch (also an error). They also do not flag the Beta status, so architecture decisions get made on it without a supportability caveat.

practices.practice: Treat `/composite/batch/` as explicitly non-transactional and bound by a 10-minute wall clock, and do not use it where partial commits are unacceptable.
practices.why_it_matters: `/composite/batch/` looks like a cheaper `/composite/`, but a mid-batch failure leaves earlier subrequests committed with no rollback and no compensating action. The 10-minute timeout silently abandons the remaining subrequests, so the caller sees a partial response and must reconcile which operations actually ran.
practices.specifics: Up to 25 subrequests, executed sequentially; each successful subrequest commits immediately and those commits are visible to later subrequests in the same batch. There is no rollback of earlier commits on a later failure. If the batch does not complete within 10 minutes it times out and the remaining subrequests are not executed. Each subrequest counts individually against rate limits. Supported resources include sObject, Query, QueryAll, Search, Connect, Chatter, Actions and Limits — but not sObject Blob or Rich Text Image retrieval.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend `/composite/batch/` for bundled writes and then add `"allOrNone": true` to the batch body — a field `/composite/batch/` does not support — believing they have made it atomic. They also assert that a composite call counts as a single API request against the daily allocation, when each subrequest is metered.

practices.practice: When an Apex transaction has uncommitted DML, a callout fails with `System.CalloutException: You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out` — restructure into DML-then-async-callout rather than reordering statements inside the same transaction.
practices.why_it_matters: The naive fix (move the callout above the DML) works in the trivial case and breaks as soon as the callout result must be persisted or a trigger performs DML earlier in the order of execution. The correct shape is a Queueable/@future callout invoked after commit.
practices.specifics: Exact message: `You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out`. Per-transaction callout limits: 100 callouts, cumulative timeout 120 seconds across all callouts in the transaction, default per-callout timeout 10 seconds, configurable via `HttpRequest.setTimeout()` between 1 ms and 120,000 ms.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs make callouts directly inside triggers and then, on being shown the error, simply reorder the callout before the `insert` — which fails again whenever a before-trigger or a prior DML in the same transaction has already occurred. They also set `req.setTimeout(300000)` (above the 120,000 ms ceiling) and treat the 120-second cumulative budget as per-callout.

practices.practice: When choosing between CDC and Platform Events for outbound change propagation, weigh that CDC shares the delivery allocation with high-volume platform events and gives you no control over what triggers an event — every qualifying field write publishes.
practices.why_it_matters: CDC is attractive because it needs no publisher code, but that is exactly its risk: a data-quality batch job or an unrelated integration writing to the same object floods the shared delivery allocation and starves the platform-event subscribers of an unrelated integration.
practices.specifics: The daily event delivery allocation is shared between high-volume platform events and Change Data Capture. CDC lets you filter with custom channels rather than the default `ChangeEvents` channel to receive only the entities you care about — this is the primary lever for controlling consumption. A single transaction over 100,000 changes degrades to one GAP_OVERFLOW event per entity type with no record data, so a large bulk job produces no usable CDC output at all.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend CDC as 'free, zero-code change propagation' with no mention of the shared allocation or the custom-channel lever, and they present it as suitable for bulk migration replication — the one workload where it degrades to content-free overflow events. They also assume CDC events are filtered by the subscriber, when the meaningful filtering is the channel definition on the publishing side.

absorb.practice: Two new gotchas. (a) 'Any element after a Custom Error silently commits the transaction.' When a record-triggered flow reaches a Custom Error element AND the path ends there, the record change is rolled back and the message renders as a pop-up or an inline field error. If any element (Assignment, Create Records, anything) sits after the Custom Error on the same path, the flow continues, the transaction COMMITS, the record is not rolled back, and the error message is never shown — with no log entry recording that the validation did not fire. The Custom Error element exists only in record-triggered flows (Winter '24); the screen-flow equivalent is Roll Back Records. (b) 'Create Records partial success still takes the fault path.' Flow DML defaults to allOrNone = true, so one bad row rolls back the whole collection for Update Records and Delete Records with no per-row result. Winter '25 added a partial-success option on Create Records only ('Process successful records' vs 'Process no records'); with it enabled the good rows persist AND the element is still marked failed and still routes down its fault connector — so a fault handler that logs 'the create failed' misreports what is actually in the database. Because Create Records supports upsert, it is also the only route to partial-success updates.
absorb.why_here: This package's own description already claims 'partial-commit pitfalls' and 'when rollback is appropriate vs catastrophic' as scope, and its 7 existing gotchas are all about what Rollback Records fails to undo (events, callouts, emails, files, approvals) — these two are the same shape and close the scope the description already promised. absorb.practice: REPLACE the three TODO placeholders with three real gotchas. (1) '$Record__Prior does not exist on a scheduled or asynchronous path.' Only flow paths that run immediately can reference prior values. A Decision comparing $Record.Stage to $Record__Prior.Stage on a scheduled path does not error — it takes the wrong branch, so the delayed automation silently does nothing. Asynchronous paths also do not support the Is Changed operator, including inside a Decision. Salesforce has stated no plan to support prior values on scheduled paths because they may fire months later. Entry-condition interlock: a scheduled path is only offered when the flow's entry condition is 'Only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements', and that option is itself incompatible with an Is Changed entry condition. Workaround: stamp the prior value onto a field on the triggering record from the immediate path so the delayed path can read it. Also note $Record__Prior is all-null on a create-only trigger. (2) 'Batch Size is a governor knob, not a throughput knob, and it batches per interval.' A scheduled path's Batch Size is settable 1-200 with default and maximum 200; batching is per time interval — with batch size 2 and seven records scheduled in the same interval, Flow Builder produces four batches. (3) 'A scheduled path is not a schedule-triggered flow.' Different context, different limits: schedule-triggered flow interviews are capped at 250,000 per 24 hours or user licenses x 200, whichever is greater, and 250,000 for any single schedule-triggered flow; Summer '26 added a configurable maximum batch size for schedule-triggered flows that overrides the 200 default — that knob does NOT apply to scheduled paths.

absorb.practice: New anti-pattern: 'Claiming Apex cannot delay a job, then building a Schedulable dispatcher.' What the LLM generates: 'Apex has no Thread.sleep() and no way to delay a job' followed by a Schedulable wrapper calling `System.scheduleBatch` or hand-building a CRON string. Why it happens: models have essentially no exposure to AsyncOptions beyond MaximumQueueableStackDepth, and the Thread.sleep absence is very heavily represented in training data. Correct pattern: `AsyncOptions opts = new AsyncOptions(); opts.MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes = 5; System.enqueueJob(job, opts);`. Why the generated fix is actively worse: Schedulable dispatchers consume the 100-scheduled-jobs-per-org limit, and immediate-retry chains hammer a failing endpoint. Detection hint: `System.schedule(` or a CRON literal appearing in retry/back-off code.
absorb.why_here: Retry-with-back-off is the single most common Apex integration requirement and three separate skills (integration/retry-and-backoff-patterns, apex/apex-callout-retry-and-resilience, this one) currently assume no delay primitive exists. The moat is the LLM entry, because the model will otherwise confidently talk the user out of the right answer.

absorb.practice: New gotcha: 'The duplicate signature is released at dequeue, not at completion.' `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature` (built via `new QueueableDuplicateSignature.Builder().addId(...).addString(...).addInteger(...).build()`, passed to `System.enqueueJob(job, options)`) dedupes enqueues ACROSS transactions — the thing a static guard cannot do. Attempting a duplicate throws `DuplicateMessageException` with the exact message `Attempt to enqueue job with duplicate queueable signature`. The non-obvious part: the signature is removed from the registry when the job is dequeued for execution, not when it finishes — per the docs, 'This removal guarantees that at least one job instance for a given signature runs' — so a job that is already running does NOT block a fresh enqueue, and you can still get two concurrent runs of the same logical work.
absorb.why_here: apex-queueable-patterns is the enqueue-API owner. `grep -rl QueueableDuplicateSignature skills/` = 0. The release-at-dequeue semantics are precisely a non-obvious platform behaviour, so gotchas rather than SKILL.md; the builder syntax belongs in examples.md.

absorb.practice: Two working snippets. (1) Retry-with-back-off using `AsyncOptions.MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes` computed from a retry counter (0/1/2/5/10, capped at the 10-minute ceiling), enqueued from a Finalizer. (2) Cross-transaction dedup: a trigger handler that builds a `QueueableDuplicateSignature` from the sObject type plus the parent Id, sets `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature`, and catches `DuplicateMessageException` as the success path — the case a static `Set<Id>` guard cannot cover because ten Data Loader batches are ten separate transactions.
absorb.why_here: Both are working code for rules added to SKILL.md and gotchas.md in the same wave. The Data Loader multi-batch framing is the concrete failure the static guard misses, and it is what makes the example non-generic.

absorb.practice: New anti-pattern: 'Deduplicating enqueues with a static Boolean.' What the LLM generates: `private static Boolean enqueued = false;` guarding `System.enqueueJob`. Why it happens: statics are the standard in-transaction recursion guard and models generalise them to cross-transaction deduplication; they have essentially no knowledge of QueueableDuplicateSignature and, if pressed, will invent a custom-object-based lock table with its own row-lock contention. Correct pattern: `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature` + catch `DuplicateMessageException`. Failure scenario to state explicitly: a trigger firing across ten separate Data Loader batches enqueues ten identical recalculation jobs; the static guard is reset in each transaction and stops none of them. Detection hint: a static Boolean or static Set whose only job is to gate `System.enqueueJob`.
absorb.why_here: apex-queueable-patterns/llm-anti-patterns.md already has AP1 (no depth guard) and AP5 (enqueue in a loop) — both in-transaction. The cross-transaction case is the gap and is the one that actually reaches production.

Adjacent hard numbers: default scope 200; maximum scope for a `Database.QueryLocator` start method is 2,000 (iterables have no documented cap); 'In a running test, you can submit a maximum of 5 batch jobs.'

absorb.practice: Add one bullet to the existing 'Governor Limits Are The Real Constraint At Large Data Volumes' list (which already carries the 5-concurrent, 250K/24hr, 50M QueryLocator and 2,000 scope ceilings): 'Maximum number of batch Apex job start method concurrent executions: 1' — org-wide. A start method that runs long therefore serialises every other batch job in the org, while their execute methods still run in parallel. The practical consequence: when the bottleneck is start(), 'split into more batch jobs' makes throughput worse, not better.

absorb.practice: New gotcha, place adjacent to the existing 'Database.Stateful Persists State, Not Good Judgment': 'Stateful preserves instance members, not statics.' Documented: 'When using Database.Stateful, only instance member variables retain their values between transactions. Static member variables don't retain their values and are reset between transactions.' A static error collector or static recursion guard in a Stateful batch produces a silently truncated result — only the last chunk's entries survive into finish(), so a summary email reports 3 failures out of 50,000 records instead of 300. Add the companion fact: each execute() is a discrete transaction, so 'if the first transaction succeeds but the second fails, the database updates made in the first transaction aren't rolled back.'
absorb.why_here: `grep -rl 'static member variables' skills/` = 0. apex-queueable-patterns covers statics not surviving between chained Queueables (a different mechanism); this skill's own llm-anti-patterns AP1 covers the inverse error (instance vars without Stateful). The static-vs-instance distinction INSIDE Stateful is the uncovered middle, and it is the one that compiles, passes a single-chunk unit test, and loses data only at production volume.

absorb.practice: Two new entries. Detection hint: a batch test inserting more than the scope size with an assertion count equal to the insert count. (b) 'Recommending more batch jobs when start() is the bottleneck': models never mention that start methods are globally serialised (concurrent executions: 1), so they prescribe fan-out as a scaling fix that adds contention. Detection hint: a scaling recommendation that splits one batch into N batches without any statement about start() cost. Place (a) immediately after the existing AP1 (instance vars without Stateful) so the Stateful static/instance pair reads together with the new gotcha.

absorb.practice: New gotcha: 'Which limits actually apply inside a Finalizer.' The Finalizer runs in a separate Apex AND database transaction from the job and does not consume additional daily async Apex executions. Synchronous limits apply inside it EXCEPT heap size, `System.enqueueJob` count, and future-method count, which stay on the asynchronous ceilings. This is the reason a Finalizer can safely do logging DML that the parent's rollback cannot undo, and also the reason a Finalizer doing heavy CPU work hits the 10-second synchronous CPU wall rather than the 60-second async one.
absorb.why_here: The existing gotchas cover abort, nested attach, parent-state inaccessibility and the single enqueue — the mixed sync/async limit profile is absent and is exactly the non-obvious behaviour that explains both why finalizer logging works and why finalizer CPU fails earlier than expected.

absorb.practice: New anti-pattern: 'Picking MAX_RETRIES with no reference to a platform ceiling.' What the LLM generates: `private static final Integer MAX_RETRIES = 10;` (or 3) in a Finalizer retry loop, justified by generic resilience-engineering convention. Why it happens: retry ceilings in general-purpose training data come from HTTP client libraries, not from Salesforce; the five-successive-re-enqueue rule appears only in the Apex Developer Guide. Correct pattern: bound at 5 or fewer and note that the counter resets on a successful completion, so a long-lived chain that intermittently succeeds gets a fresh budget. Detection hint: a MAX_RETRIES constant greater than 5 anywhere a Finalizer re-enqueues. Keep this entry narrow to the ceiling — the 'finalizer runs in the same transaction' misconception is already covered by SKILL.md Core Concepts and gotchas Gotcha 3, and restating it would be duplicate bulk.
absorb.why_here: llm-anti-patterns is the moat file; the existing entries cover Finalizer-instead-of-try/catch and nested attachFinalizer, neither of which touches retry bounding.

absorb.practice: Extend Gotcha 2 ('Workflow Field Update Re-Fire Is Exactly Once'). The skill's SKILL.md step 12 already states the re-fire runs before/after triggers once more and does not re-fire workflow rules — add the half it is missing: on a recursive save, the platform SKIPS steps 9 through 17 of the order of execution (assignment rules, auto-response rules, workflow rules, Process Builder, escalation rules, after-save flows, entitlement rules, roll-up summaries). This is why a guard written to stop 'the automation firing twice' often guards a failure the platform already prevents. NOTE FOR THE BUILD AGENT: the source research entry for this practice was truncated mid-sentence in the hand-off; re-fetch the full text and re-verify against the Triggers and Order of Execution doc before authoring, and scope the entry to the steps-9-to-17 skip plus the exactly-once field-update re-fire, both of which are verifiable from the current text.

absorb.practice: New anti-pattern: 'Adding a recursion guard for a re-entry the platform already suppresses.' What the LLM generates: a static Boolean guard prescribed for a symptom ('my automation is running twice') without first establishing WHERE the second pass comes from. Why it happens: 'trigger fires twice' → 'add a static flag' is one of the strongest associations in Salesforce training data. Correct pattern: identify the source first — a workflow field update re-fires before/after update triggers exactly once and skips steps 9–17, which is bounded and usually harmless; a roll-up summary update on a master-detail parent starts a FULL order of execution on the parent and is the case that actually needs guarding. A guard added for the former later suppresses legitimate processing in the latter. Detection hint: a proposed static guard in a diagnosis that never names the DML source of the second pass. Same caveat as the order-of-execution entry — re-fetch the truncated source text before authoring.

agent_upgrades.upgrade: Add a hard rule to the Constraints section: never raise `<apiVersion>` in a `.cls-meta.xml` as part of a refactor unless the user explicitly asked for a version bump. If the bump crosses 67.0, treat it as a security-behaviour change, not metadata hygiene — emit a required pre-flight inventory of every SOQL/SOSL and DML statement in the class, and state per statement whether elevated access was intentional (needs `WITH SYSTEM_MODE` / `AccessLevel.SYSTEM_MODE`) or not. Report the bump as a separate finding with its own confidence score; never bundle it into an unrelated refactor diff.

When scaffolding any new Apex class, emit the sharing keyword explicitly and state the target API version in the output header. Never rely on the version default in either direction. When generating async retry logic, default to `AsyncOptions.MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes` and only fall back to a Schedulable dispatcher when the required back-off exceeds 10 minutes — and say so in the Citations block.

Two behaviour changes. (1) Before reporting any `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` finding, read the target class's apiVersion from its meta.xml. At >=67.0 the clause does not compile, so the finding is a build break (Critical), not a hardening suggestion (Medium) — the severity and the recommended fix both change. (2) Every FLS remediation snippet the agent emits must include `catch (System.QueryException e)` + `e.getInaccessibleFields()`, and every `Security.stripInaccessible` snippet must use the three-argument overload with `enforceRootObjectCRUD = true` when the records come from an untrusted caller. Emitting the two-argument form on a user-supplied payload is itself a finding the agent should self-flag.

Add an explicit scoring rule: a change set whose only Apex delta is an apiVersion increase crossing 67.0 is NOT low risk. Score it as a data-access-semantics change and require the diff summary to list every affected class's queries and DML. Currently a meta.xml-only diff would score as near-zero churn, which is exactly the invisible-change failure mode.

When a review finds a static Boolean or static Set guarding `System.enqueueJob`, ask whether the duplicate source is cross-transaction (Data Loader batches, multiple integration calls) before accepting the guard. If cross-transaction, the correct answer is `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature`, not a bigger static. Likewise, when a review finds a static collection inside a `Database.Stateful` batch, flag it as data loss at volume rather than a style issue.

For Batch Apex targets, size generated test data to exactly one scope (default 200) and assert on that scope only — never generate a test that inserts more than the scope size and asserts on the full insert count, because only one execute() invocation runs per test. Cap generated batch submissions at 5 per test method. State the single-scope constraint in the generated test's header comment so the reader does not 'fix' it by adding records.

For the limits/scalability audit mode: before recommending any architectural remediation for daily-async-Apex pressure, ask whether Setup → Apex Settings → 'Use elastic limits for asynchronous Apex jobs (Beta)' is enabled. The remediation branches completely — elastic ON means jobs past the licensed limit queue and run slowly (an operational/throttling problem: monitor `DailyAsyncApexElasticExecutions` and `DailyAsyncApexProcessed`, tune scheduling), elastic OFF means jobs are rejected (an architectural problem: batch consolidation, event-driven fan-in). Recommending a rewrite without asking is a MEDIUM-confidence answer at best.

Add an execution-context question to the intake: where will this query run? If the answer includes trigger context and the target object exceeds ~200,000 rows, escalate the finding from performance to correctness — the platform throws `System.QueryException: Non-selective query against large object type` there and only there. Explicitly reject 'it ran fine in Developer Console / Execute Anonymous' as evidence of trigger safety, and say why in the output.

Stop quoting '25 concurrent long-running Apex requests over 20 seconds' in scalability output. The Apex threshold is 5 seconds and the ceiling scales with licences (100:1, floor 10, cap 50). Recompute any concurrency headroom estimate against those figures. This is the number the agent's own Mandatory Reads currently supply incorrectly — do not ship the agent change before the architect/omnistudio-scalability-patterns correction lands, or the agent will contradict its cited skill.

This is a routing criterion for 'should this be async at all' that the tree does not currently carry, and the 5-second threshold is far lower than the 20 seconds most agents assume.

absorb.practice: NEW Gotcha 7 — 'The read-set rule: a property that was not READ during the previous render will not schedule a re-render when it changes.' State the doc sentence verbatim: 'A component rerenders only if a property accessed during the previous rendering cycle is updated, even when the object is annotated with @track.' Then the two corollaries that make it diagnosable, which no source in the corpus states: (a) a getter with an early `return ''` / `return null` that short-circuits before touching `this.x` de-registers `x` from that cycle's read-set, so the next mutation of `x` is silently inert; (b) a property first referenced only inside an `lwc:if` branch that was FALSE last render is likewise unregistered — which is why an identical mutation re-renders in one branch and not the other. Fix: reference the property unconditionally (read it into a local at the top of the getter) or drive the branch from a property that IS in the read-set.
absorb.why_here: This is the reactivity skill and it is the ONLY package whose Core Concepts enumerate the reactivity contract field-by-field (§1 reassignment, §2 @track, §3 Date/Set/Map, §5 getter caching). The read-set rule is the missing §4 of that same contract — it is the rule that explains the staleness bugs that SURVIVE after §1–§3 are applied correctly. The only corpus mention is one clause in lwc/lwc-performance SKILL.md ('even with `@track`, LWC rerenders only when properties accessed during the previous render change') framed as a performance nicety, with no diagnostic. search_knowledge.py 'property accessed during the previous rendering cycle rerender read set' returns lwc/lwc-performance (1.163) and that single chunk at 1.100 — lwc-reactive-state-patterns surfaces only via its Trigger Scenarios block at 0.350, i.e. the skill that owns reactivity does not currently contain the rule.

absorb.practice: NEW Anti-Pattern 6 — 'The three reflex fixes for a re-render that did not happen.' In order, the LLM tries: (1) add `@track` (already refuted by existing AP1/AP2), (2) `this.x = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(this.x))`, (3) toggle a dummy boolean `this._tick = !this._tick` to force a render. Document why (2) and (3) are wrong: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` converts every `Date` to an ISO string, silently DROPS keys whose value is `undefined`, throws `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON` on proxied graphs, and doubles heap on large wire payloads; the dummy-boolean toggle only appears to work because it re-runs the whole template, which re-reads the property and re-registers it in the read-set — masking the actual bug for one cycle. Correct pattern: diagnose against the read-set (gotcha 7) and the Date/Set/Map rule, then reassign. Detection hint: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(` appearing anywhere OUTSIDE a `console.log(...)` argument, or a boolean field whose only reads are `!this._x` assignments.
absorb.why_here: llm-anti-patterns is the moat file and this is a sequenced failure mode, not a fact. Placement matters for a second reason: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` is currently RECOMMENDED nine times across lwc/lwc-debugging-devtools (SKILL.md L81/L115/L128/L151/L162, gotchas L21, well-architected L19, examples L50, and its checker script) as the LWS proxy-unwrapping idiom for console logging. That is correct for logging and wrong for state repair, and no package in the corpus draws the line. The entry must cross-reference lwc/lwc-debugging-devtools explicitly so the two do not read as contradictory.

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha — 'undefined suppresses the call; null MAKES the call.' Quote apex-wire-method.html verbatim: 'If a parameter value is `null`, the method is called. If a parameter value is `undefined`, the method isn't called.' Give the network-tab discriminator, which is the whole value of the entry: filter DevTools Network for `/aura?...ApexActionController` (Apex wires) or `/ui-api/` (UI API wires) — ZERO matching requests means an `undefined` reactive param and the adapter never ran; a request whose body contains `"param":null` means the call reached Apex with a null argument and any server-side NPE or wrong-result-set is a server bug, not a wiring bug. Add the corollary that a defensive `if (!this.recordId) return;` placed inside a wired FUNCTION is dead code in the undefined case — the adapter was never invoked, so the function body never ran. Most common origin of the undefined case: `@api recordId` is undefined on the first render of an App Builder-placed component.
absorb.why_here: wire-service-patterns is the correct retrieval winner already — search_knowledge.py 'wire parameter null calls the apex method undefined does not' returns `lwc/wire-service-patterns (1.538)` as the only skill above threshold. So this is a pure content delta with zero trigger work. It currently states only the undefined half, three times and identically: SKILL.md 'If a required reactive parameter is `undefined`, the wire adapter is not evaluated'; Gotchas 'An Undefined Reactive Parameter Looks Like A Silent Failure'; llm-anti-patterns AP6 'wire does not provision data until all reactive parameters have defined (non-undefined) values'. Nothing anywhere says null behaves oppositely, and nothing gives a way to tell the two apart from the browser. Package is 21,222 B / 49 chunks — the most headroom in the wire cluster.

absorb.practice: EXTEND existing Anti-Pattern 2 ('Param-null-then-restore hack') with the consequence paragraph. Current text justifies the ban only on style grounds — 'Param tricks are fragile and trigger extra re-renders.' Add: setting the reactive param to `null` does not pause the wire, it FIRES it with a null argument (per apex-wire-method.html), so the hack issues a real server round-trip that can throw a server-side NullPointerException, return an unfiltered result set, or burn an Apex call before the restore lands. Setting it to `undefined` instead is the only value that genuinely suppresses the call — and then the restore is what re-fires it, making the whole two-step redundant with `refreshApex`.
absorb.why_here: The ban already exists here and is also in this skill's SKILL.md ('Avoid forced re-render hacks like nulling params then restoring — tends to break and confuses framework caching') and its Review Checklist ('No param-null-then-restore hacks'). Adding a fourth restatement elsewhere would be pure retrieval waste. What is missing is the mechanism that turns 'fragile' into 'fires a real null call' — a ~450-byte upgrade to text that is already in the right place. Deliberately NOT filed as a new anti-pattern in wire-service-patterns, which would duplicate this one across two neighbouring skills that already compete for the same 'wire'/'refresh' tokens.

absorb.practice: NEW Anti-Pattern 6 — 'Passing bare ID strings to notifyRecordUpdateAvailable.' What the LLM generates: `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable([this.recordId])` or `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable(this.recordIds)`. Why it happens: the deprecated `getRecordNotifyChange` examples it memorised describe the argument in ambiguous prose, and a string array reads as the obvious shape. Consequence: no error, no network call, no refresh — a pure silent no-op. Correct pattern per reference-notify-record-update.html: the argument is 'An array of objects with an object shape of `{ recordId: string }`'; the id 'can be either 15 or 18 characters long'; it returns 'A Promise object that is resolved when Lightning Data Service has completed its processing' so it must be awaited before any dependent UI work; it 'refreshes those records that are in the LDS cache' only — a record never wired on this page is a no-op; 'Values are not re-emitted to wires whose data has not changed', which is why an identical-payload refresh looks like it failed; and it does NOT refresh Apex `@wire`s, which need `refreshApex`. Detection hint: `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable(` whose argument array contains anything other than object literals, or a call site with no `await` / no returned promise.
absorb.why_here: This skill is the retrieval winner for the query — search_knowledge.py 'notifyRecordUpdateAvailable array of objects recordId not string' returns `lwc/lwc-wire-refresh-patterns (1.183)`, `lwc/lwc-lds-writes (0.683)`. Its existing AP3 is about `getRecordNotifyChange` DEPRECATION and merely happens to show `[{ recordId }]` in the correct-pattern block; nothing labels the bare-string form as an error, and the checker's DEPRECATED_NOTIFY regex only catches the old import name. lwc/lwc-lds-writes also shows the correct shape twice but is scoped to write operations and is the larger package (36,913 B / 76 chunks). Package is 29,180 B / 61 chunks — comfortable.

absorb.practice: NEW Gotcha 8 — 'CSS hiding is not free: the hidden subtree is fully constructed, connected, and WIRED.' A panel hidden with `class="slds-hide"` or `display:none` still runs its constructor and `connectedCallback`, still fires every `@wire` adapter, and still executes any event handlers attached to it — per Salesforce's LWC performance guidance, with conditional rendering 'the component and all of its children are created and rendered up front' when you use CSS instead, and 'if there is any event associated with it, then it would be executed.' So a four-tab record page whose three inactive tabs are CSS-hidden pays three full Apex/UI-API round-trips on first paint for content nobody has asked for. `lwc:if` lazily instantiates and issues zero of them. Statement of the real trade-off: `lwc:if` costs you the subtree's state on toggle (existing Gotcha 1); CSS hide costs you a server round-trip per hidden wire on every page load. Choose CSS hide only when in-progress user input must survive the toggle, and when you do, hoist the wire out of the hidden child into the parent so the cost is paid once.
absorb.why_here: This skill actively RECOMMENDS CSS hide with no cost stated — SKILL.md 'Keep-State Toggle vs Reset-State Toggle' says 'keep the component mounted and toggle `display:none`', the Decision Guidance table row says the same, and the Review Checklist says 'Toggles that must preserve child state use CSS `display:none`, not `lwc:if`.' Adding the cost here corrects an existing recommendation rather than bolting on a fact, which is the strongest placement available. Verified absent: search_knowledge.py 'hidden component with CSS still fires its wire adapter on page load' returns lwc/lwc-dynamic-components (1.200) and lwc/commerce-lwc-components (0.650) — neither is about this, and the closest real chunk (lwc/lwc-performance-budgets gotcha 4, 0.300) says only that wires cost a round-trip, not that hidden ones still fire. Also add ONE trigger to SKILL.md frontmatter: 'does hiding an lwc with css stop its wire from firing' — the research flagged admin/lightning-page-performance-tuning winning this phrasing, which is a routing bug.

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha — 'Never design around a client-side cache duration for @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true).' Quote apex-result-caching.html verbatim: 'the default cache duration can change as we optimize the platform. When you design your Lightning web components, don't assume a cache duration.' Name the failure: a component built on a blog-sourced figure ('15 minutes', '5 minutes', 'the session') shows a user their own pre-write values after Salesforce retunes the client cache, and the bug reproduces only in the field. Prescription: if freshness matters per page visit, use a non-cacheable imperative call and own the data shape; if you need invalidation on a specific event, use `refreshApex` against the wired value; never write a comment or a test that asserts a duration. Second half of the same doc rule: 'To set `cacheable=true`, a method must only get data, it can't mutate (change) data.'
absorb.why_here: This is the cacheable-semantics skill — description says 'Covers import syntax, cacheable vs non-cacheable', it has a 'Cacheable Read' pattern, a decision-guidance row, and gotcha 2 on the DML-in-callstack runtime error. The duration rule is the one cacheable fact it lacks, and it is a genuine corpus hole: search_knowledge.py 'how long does cacheable true client cache last in lightning' returns 'Coverage: NONE — no skill meets the confidence threshold', with the top hit being raw `knowledge/imports/lightning.md`. lwc/lwc-wire-refresh-patterns gotcha 4 is adjacent ('cached by the Lightning client per the cache control headers') but frames it as a navigation-staleness story and never states the don't-assume rule. Because retrieval is currently NONE, this absorb MUST ship with a trigger in SKILL.md frontmatter: 'how long does cacheable true apex stay cached client side'. Package is 33,846 B / 73 chunks.

absorb.practice: REWRITE Gotcha 1. Two changes. (a) Name the exact dev-mode error string, which appears nowhere in the 1,027-package corpus: `Invalid mutation: Cannot set "0" on "[object Object]". "[object Object]" is read-only.` — and state that in production it degrades to a silent no-op, which is the worse failure. (b) Correct the fix, which is currently incomplete: a shallow array copy is NOT sufficient if you mutate a ROW. `this.rows = [...result.data]; this.rows[0].selected = true;` still throws, because the array is new but every row object inside it is the same frozen proxy. Show both the per-row spread `this.rows = result.data.map(r => ({ ...r, selected: false }))` and the trap form the LLM writes instead — `data.map(r => { r.x = 1; return r; })`, which looks immutable and throws on the first element. Add the negative: do not 'fix' this with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(data))` — it converts every date/datetime field to a string and doubles heap on large result sets.
absorb.why_here: lwc/lwc-datatable-advanced is the retrieval winner for wire-data mutation (research measured 1.250) and its Gotcha 1 already owns the topic — but the whole entry is four lines and its prescription is actively wrong for row mutation: 'Copy into `@track data = [...this.accounts.data]` and mutate the copy.' Following that advice reproduces the exact bug it claims to fix. This is the only absorb in the domain that is a correction rather than an addition. The ideal home for the error STRING would be lwc/common-lwc-runtime-errors (the symptom-to-error index), but that package is 54,408 B / 130 chunks — already failing hard gate G1 on bytes and 10 chunks from the chunk ceiling — so it cannot take new content until it is split. absorb.practice: NEW gotcha (single combined entry, both halves from Salesforce's own eslint-plugin-lwc `valid-api` rule). (a) Reserved member names: 'Fields and methods can't be named `slot`, `part` or `dataset`, as these names are reserved by LWC', and 'Fields and methods can't start with `data[A-Z]`, as these are mapped to the reflected property `this.dataset.*`' — so `@api dataUrl` or a helper named `dataSource` collides with `this.dataset` and either fails the lint/compile or corrupts dataset reads at runtime. (b) Boolean `@api` properties must be initialised to `false`: 'by initializing a public property to true, the consumer component can't set its value to false via the template', because HTML boolean-attribute semantics are presence-based — the consumer can add the attribute but cannot express its absence as an override. A boolean `@api` defaulted to true is a one-way switch; invert the name instead (`hideFooter = false`, not `showFooter = true`).
absorb.why_here: This is the @api-contract skill and it already owns the adjacent facts — gotcha 3 'Boolean attributes from HTML markup are *strings*, not booleans' and gotcha 6 'Kebab-case attribute / camelCase property mapping is not symmetric'. The reserved-name rule and the boolean-default-false rule are the two `valid-api` constraints it is missing, and neither appears anywhere else in the corpus (grep for `valid-api`, `eslint-plugin-lwc`, `data[A-Z]` across skills/ returns nothing). BUDGET WARNING — this target is the one absorb that cannot be additive: the package is already 52,531 B / 117 chunks, over hard gate G1's 50 KB byte ceiling and 23 chunks from the 140 ceiling. Ship this only as a budget-neutral swap: the weakest existing entry is llm-anti-patterns AP7 'Over-validating in `connectedCallback` and breaking unit tests' (~35 lines, and its substance is already carried by SKILL.md's 'Required-prop guard in connectedCallback' pattern). Cut AP7, add this gotcha, and the package nets ~1 KB smaller.

new_skills.rationale:
ONE new skill, and only because the `for:each` / `iterator:it` directive contract is explicitly disclaimed by every adjacent package and is unreachable by its natural query.

What it holds (all from create-lists.html, all verified absent from the corpus): the `key` must be a string or a number and 'can't be an object'; `for:index` as a key value is rejected at compile time; and the fact with the highest LLM-failure value — 'The `key` in the template is used for performance optimization and isn't reflected in the DOM at run time', so `event.target.key` is ALWAYS `undefined` and a `[key="..."]` selector never matches. The retrieval pattern for row identity is therefore `data-id={row.Id}` + `event.currentTarget.dataset.id`, never the key. Plus: why an index key is a data-integrity bug and not a cosmetic one (LWC reuses the wrong DOM node on reorder/delete, so inline-edit values and focus land on the wrong record), why a synthetic concatenated key is worse than no key (it changes on every edit, forcing full teardown), and the `iterator:it` surface (`it.value` / `it.index` / `it.first` / `it.last`) which appears exactly once in 1,027 packages — as a two-word exclusion clause in lwc-conditional-rendering's description.

Why nothing can absorb it: (1) lwc/lwc-conditional-rendering explicitly scopes it OUT — its description ends 'NOT for list rendering, which uses `for:each` or `iterator:it`'; (2) lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists is scoped to windowing above the 1,000-row × 5-column datatable ceiling and is 39,935 B / 74 chunks, too close to the byte gate to take a general directive contract; (3) lwc/lwc-performance frames keys purely as render cost ('Stable keys reduce DOM churn'), which is the wrong frame for a wrong-record bug, and it also fails hard gate G4 (its Recommended Workflow is the shared 149-package filler starting 'Gather context — confirm the org edition') so it needs its own repair pass before it takes new weight.

Scope guard, given the zero-sum window: cap at 22 KB / ~60 chunks and put hard NOT-FOR clauses in the description pointing at lwc-virtualized-lists (windowing/infinite scroll) and lwc-performance (render cost), so it competes on `for:each` / `key` / `iterator` tokens rather than on `list` / `rows` / `performance`.

agent_upgrades.upgrade: Add a fixed 'nothing re-rendered' triage ladder to the Render axis, executed in order and short-circuiting — this is procedure, not fact, so it belongs in the playbook rather than in lwc-reactive-state-patterns. (1) Is the field REASSIGNED or mutated in place? (2) Is its runtime type `Date` / `Set` / `Map` / a class instance? If yes, stop — no decorator helps. (3) Is the field wire-provisioned? If yes it is a frozen proxy and the mutation threw or no-opped, not failed to render. (4) Only now: was the property in the previous cycle's READ-SET — i.e. did a short-circuiting getter or a false `lwc:if` branch prevent it from being read last render? Pair it with an explicit prohibition: the agent must not propose `@track`, `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))`, or a dummy-boolean toggle as a remedy for a missing re-render — all three are currently the model's default reflexes and all three either mask the bug for one cycle or corrupt Date values. Note the carve-out so the rule is not over-applied: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` remains the correct LWS proxy-unwrapping idiom for `console.log`, per skills/lwc/lwc-debugging-devtools.

Add a two-branch 'the wire never fired' procedure to the Data axis. Before hypothesising, the agent must ask for the DevTools Network tab filtered to `/aura?...ApexActionController` (Apex wires) or `/ui-api/` (UI API wires): ZERO matching requests means an `undefined` reactive parameter and the adapter genuinely never ran — look upstream at whoever sets the param, typically an `@api recordId` undefined on first render of an App Builder-placed component; a request present with `"<param>":null` in the body means the call DID reach the server with null, so the defect is server-side (NPE, unfiltered result set) and the component is innocent. These two produce identical UI and need opposite fixes, and the agent currently has no step that distinguishes them — Mandatory Read 6 (wire-service-patterns) only teaches the undefined half.

Fix a broken Mandatory Read. Item 20 cites `skills/lwc/virtualized-lists` — the 3,152-byte stub (26 chunks; its llm-anti-patterns.md is 220 bytes, a hard-gate G3 failure) — where the real package is `skills/lwc/lwc-virtualized-lists` (39,935 B / 74 chunks, with the 1,000-row × 5-column ceiling, the IntersectionObserver shadow-DOM gotchas, and the key-stability anti-pattern). Every audit that has hit the '>500-row list' branch has been reading the stub. Repoint the citation, and flag the two colliding slugs for consolidation before `lwc/lwc-list-rendering-and-keys` is scaffolded — three list-shaped LWC packages competing in one 30-chunk window is the domain's worst retrieval collision.

Add a pre-emit self-check block (behavioural gate, distinct from the skill content it enforces) that blocks the bundle if any of these are present in generated output: `@track` on a primitive-initialised field; `key={index}` or a key bound to a `for:index` variable; a boolean `@api` property initialised to `true`; a field or method named `slot` / `part` / `dataset` or matching `data[A-Z]`; `event.target.key` in any handler; a CustomEvent name containing an uppercase letter, a hyphen, or an `on` prefix; `{ bubbles: true, composed: true }` on an event that is not a genuinely global signal. These are all compile-time or silent-failure classes the agent can check mechanically against its own draft before writing files, and the current 36-item Mandatory Reads list has no list-rendering entry at all — add `skills/lwc/lwc-list-rendering-and-keys` under 'Forms, datatables, modals, files, charts' once it exists.

decision_tree_upgrades: No new decision tree is warranted for this domain, and I want to be explicit about the two candidates I rejected. `lwc:if` vs CSS-hide is a single-technology trade-off inside one framework, not a cross-technology route — `standards/decision-trees/README.md` scopes trees to queries that 'straddle more than one technology', so this stays as a Decision Guidance row in lwc/lwc-conditional-rendering (with the wire-cost column added per the absorb above). Likewise wire vs imperative Apex is already resolved inside lwc/wire-service-patterns' own table.

One concrete change: the refresh-primitive choice (`refreshApex` vs `RefreshEvent` vs `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable` vs reactive-param re-provision) IS a genuine four-way routing decision with a canonical table that already exists in lwc/lwc-wire-refresh-patterns' Decision Guidance — but it is invisible from the trees layer. Add a single 'see also' line in `standards/decision-trees/README.md` pointing UI-refresh questions at that table, rather than authoring a fifth tree. Cost is ~150 bytes in a file that is not part of the skill retrieval budget; benefit is that the three run-time LWC agents get one canonical pointer instead of three independent Mandatory Reads each rediscovering it.

Do NOT push any of this domain's practices into `automation-selection.md` or `async-selection.md`. Everything in the research is intra-LWC correctness; adding LWC render/wire vocabulary to those trees would pull them into LWC queries they cannot answer and would compete with the LWC packages themselves in the lexical window.

absorb.practice: NEW anti-pattern: "Classifying HTTP 300 from an External ID upsert as transient or as a redirect." Correct pattern: 300 is a permanent data defect — route it to a dead-letter queue and a duplicate-resolution task, never to a retry queue; never enable follow-redirects on the upsert client. Detection hint: any retry predicate keyed on `>= 400`, or any status handler enumerating 200/201/4xx/5xx that omits 300.

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha: "A dirty file is a throughput problem, not just a data-quality problem." Any error inside a Bulk batch causes Salesforce to fall back to single-row processing for that batch. Quote LDV best practices: "Ensure that data is clean before loading when using the Bulk API 2.0. Consequence: a 2% bad-row rate does not cost 2% of throughput — it collapses the batch from set-based to row-by-row. This is the mechanism behind "fine in sandbox, 14 hours in production."

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha: "A requeued Bulk v1 batch does not retry the rows it already marked failed." Bulk API v1 does not error immediately on a lock — it waits a few seconds, marks the record failed, and "If there are problems acquiring locks for more than 100 records in a batch, the Bulk API places the remainder of the batch back in the queue for later processing. When the Bulk API processes the batch again later, records marked as failed aren't retried... it's placed back in the queue and reprocessed up to 10 times before the batch is permanently marked as failed." So a job can report Completed after nine internal requeues that permanently dropped rows on each pass. Name the levers: `TooManyLockFailure` may be returned mid-batch; `Sforce-Disable-Batch-Retry: TRUE` suppresses retries; default retry count is 10 for bulk uploads and 15 for bulk queries. Contrast v2.0: batch fails after 5 minutes, retried up to 20 times, then the whole ingest job moves to Failed. Do NOT design around the non-GA "Bulk API 2.0 Automatic Record Lock Handling" pilot.

The failure — job Completed, rows silently dropped — defeats any reconciliation that checks job state alone, and no LLM knows the platform already requeues 10 times, so its client-side backoff advice double-counts platform behaviour while missing the actual data loss.

The agent currently reasons in records only — the unit the org does not run out of first.

When lock contention is predicted, the agent must propose sort-by-parent-Id FIRST and may only recommend serial mode when the operation is one of the four Salesforce names (creating users, updating ownership on private-sharing records, updating user roles, updating territory hierarchies) or when reorganising batches is demonstrably impossible. If v1 is selected, the plan must state that a requeued batch does not retry already-failed rows, so reconciliation cannot rely on job state alone.

Constrain the header forms the agent may emit: `ObjectType:RelationshipName.IndexedField` ONLY for polymorphic fields (and never for non-polymorphic ones — both omission and inclusion are errors); `RelationshipName.IndexedField` otherwise; reject any two-level chain (`A__r.B__r.C__c`) at authoring time; and verify the target parent field is indexed (External ID for custom, `idLookup = true` for standard) before proposing it as a resolution key. Branch: default 2.0; choose v1 only when you need serial concurrency mode, ingest-side PK chunking, or `Sforce-Disable-Batch-Retry`. Carry the retry-semantics difference as the consequence (v1 requeues 10x and skips already-failed rows; v2.0 fails the batch after 5 minutes, retries up to 20, then fails the job).

standards/decision-trees/performance-tuning.md — expand the UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW route (line 65, currently 'lock contention is a SOQL/sharing problem' → Q5) into an ordered mitigation ladder for the LOAD case: (1) sort the CSV by parent Id; (2) partition threads so no two threads touch children of the same parent and never run a parent pass concurrently with a child pass; (3) defer sharing calculation; (4) serial mode LAST, justified only by one of the four named operations; (5) Granular Locking via Support for extreme skew. Today the tree routes lock errors to a sharing/SOQL diagnosis, which is the wrong first question for a bulk load.

standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md — add an idempotency cost gate ahead of the write-pattern choice (near line 79, 'Yes (designed idempotent) → Retries safe; use Bulk API 2.0'). Make the cost explicit as the routing criterion: insert < update < upsert in throughput, and splitting upsert into create()+update() is a documented Salesforce optimisation. Route: if the source cannot reliably partition new vs existing rows, keep the single upsert and accept the cost; if it can AND the load window is binding, split. The tree currently asserts idempotency is free.

absorb.practice: NEW Anti-Pattern 7, full quad form — "Listing encryption as the control that restricts which users see the data." What the LLM generates: asked "how do I stop non-privileged users seeing the encrypted SSN field?" it answers "remove the View Encrypted Data permission from their profile"; or it produces a security design whose access-control column reads "Shield Platform Encryption" for PII fields. Why it happens: Setup calls both Classic `Text (Encrypted)` fields and Shield-encrypted fields "encrypted fields", so the model merges the features and inherits Classic's permission model. Correct pattern: encryption at rest defends against an attacker who obtains the storage, not against an authenticated user — FLS plus sharing are the only controls that restrict authenticated users; `View Encrypted Data` applies only to the Classic 175-character `Text (Encrypted)` field type. Detection hint: any remediation naming `View Encrypted Data`, or any control matrix where a Shield-encrypted field's "who can see it" row cites encryption rather than a permission set.
absorb.why_here: The moat entry — the research's deepest LLM failure mode, in the prioritised file. Keep it to ~1,100 bytes because of the G1 ceiling; the SKILL.md de-dup pays for it.

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha — reserved runtime masking notification strings, as an incident-runbook table. Destroyed key: Email / Phone / Text / Text Area / Text Area (Long) / URL render `?????`; Custom Date renders `08/08/1888`; Custom Date/Time renders `08/08/1888 12:00 PM`. Service unavailable: `!!!!!`; Custom Date `01/01/1777`; Custom Date/Time `01/01/1777 12:00 PM`. The silent-failure half: these strings are reserved and cannot be stored — "While you aren't restricted from saving a record with one of these reserved masking notification strings into an encrypted field, the field is saved with a blank value." A Bulk API load carrying `?????` as an anonymisation placeholder writes empty fields with a SUCCESS row and no error line in the result file. Runbook rule: `?????` in an encrypted field means read the key state in Setup > Key Management before touching the data — do NOT start a restore, because a restore overwrites good ciphertext. Cite Salesforce Security Guide "Runtime Masking Notification", p.116.

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha — do not encrypt the standard User.Email field. Encrypting it silently stops Salesforce's own Product & Service Notifications, including org-migration and service-degradation emails to admins, with no error and no setting indicating why. If the org uses Login Discovery, the Login Discovery Handler's email lookup fails and users are blocked at login — a self-inflicted outage discovered only at login time. Two compounding facts: Lightning Sync and Einstein Activity Capture copy User.Email into a second database column stored UNENCRYPTED for any user in a sync configuration, so the compliance control is defeated at the moment it is applied; and Einstein Conversation Insights video calls require User.Email under case-insensitive deterministic encryption specifically, not probabilistic. Cite Security Guide "General Shield Platform Encryption Considerations — User Email", p.205.
absorb.why_here: A named do-not-encrypt field with a stated blast radius is a pre-flight gate for the rollout runbook this skill owns. It cannot go in platform-encryption (3,294 bytes of headroom) and it is not a query-pattern fact.

absorb.practice: NEW worked example — "Sizing encrypted fields in bytes before the rollout." Ship the published cap table as API length / byte length / non-ASCII characters: Last Name (Contact, Lead) 80/240/70; Email (Contact, Lead) 80/240/70; Name (Custom Object) 80/240/70; Name (Opportunity) 120/360/110; Title (Contact, Lead) 128/384/126; First Name, Middle Name, City, Phone, Fax (Account/Contact/Lead) 40/120/22; Assistant Name (Contact) 40/120/22; Site (Account) 80/240/70; Subject (Email Message, probabilistic or case-sensitive deterministic) 2207/3000/1000; Address To/CC/BCC (Email Message) 2959/4000/1333. Then the working artifact Salesforce explicitly recommends: a validation rule enforcing the reduced length, e.g. `LEN(LastName) > 70` on Contact, with the note that the API still reports 80 so nothing else in the org predicts the failure. Add the Email-to-Case caveat that the characters U+FFFE and U+FFFF cannot be encrypted at all. Cite Security Guide "Field Limits with Shield Platform Encryption", p.214.

absorb.practice: NEW gotcha — the error-code substitution. "When you query encrypted data, invalid strings return an INVALID_FIELD error instead of the expected MALFORMED_QUERY." State both consequences: integration error handling keyed on `MALFORMED_QUERY` will not catch it, and an admin reading `INVALID_FIELD` starts checking FLS and field API names on a field that exists and is accessible. Pair with the probabilistic carve-outs from the same page — probabilistically encrypted fields cannot appear in `MAX()`, `MIN()`, `COUNT_DISTINCT()`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` or `ORDER BY`; and probabilistic encryption is not supported at all on Contact.Email (use deterministic there or self-registration produces duplicate Accounts). Cite Security Guide "Tradeoffs and Limitations — SOQL and SOSL", p.206 and "How Deterministic Encryption Supports Filtering", p.136.

absorb.practice: NEW Anti-Pattern 6 — "Misdiagnoses INVALID_FIELD on an encrypted-field query." What the LLM generates: given `INVALID_FIELD` from a query touching an encrypted field, it says check the API name, add the `__c` suffix, or check field-level security — the same misdiagnosis it makes with `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED`. Why it happens: the model maps error codes to causes from generic SOQL training data and has no representation of encryption rewriting the error class. Correct pattern: on any query filtering an encrypted field, treat `INVALID_FIELD` as a malformed-value error first; verify the filter literal against the field's scheme before touching the field definition. Detection hint: the remediation edits a field API name or an FLS grant on a field the query already read successfully elsewhere. ALSO REQUIRED for hard gate G3: all five existing anti-patterns in this file lack the "Detection hint" leg of the quad form — add one to each.

What the LLM generates: a sharing design with one criteria-based rule per region, product line or segment value, arriving at 80+ rules with no comment. absorb.practice: NEW gotcha — the Spring '25 `View All Fields` object permission (API v63.0). It grants read on every field of the object AND auto-grants read on every field created on that object afterwards, with no review step. Two consequences: it is a legitimate replacement for hand-maintaining hundreds of field permissions on an analyst permission set, and it is a standing grant against fields that do not exist yet, so a future field holding regulated data is exposed the moment it is created. Available on all standard and custom objects that support field permissions. The sharp edge is the audit consequence — an FLS audit enumerating `FieldPermissions` rows will not see holders of this permission at all, because there are no per-field rows to enumerate; you must query `ObjectPermissions` for the object-level grant separately.
absorb.why_here: `python3 scripts/search_knowledge.py "View All Fields object permission grants read on every field including fields created later Spring 25"` returns admin/permission-sets-vs-profiles (1.292) as top skill with zero relevant chunks, and `grep -rn 'View All Fields|ViewAllFields' skills/` returns nothing repo-wide. This package owns the FLS-via-permission-set story (its Anti-Pattern 4 is about profile/permset FLS interaction) and has 16,833 bytes of G1 headroom.

absorb.practice: NEW anti-pattern, full quad form — "FLS audit that only enumerates field permissions." What the LLM generates: an FLS audit script or checklist that queries `FieldPermissions` (or walks each field in Setup) and reports which permission sets grant read on a sensitive field. Why it happens: the model's mental model of FLS is per-field rows, which was complete before Spring '25. Correct pattern: also query `ObjectPermissions` for the object-level `View All Fields` grant on the same object — a holder reads every field including ones created after the audit ran, and produces no `FieldPermissions` row for the auditor to find. Detection hint: an FLS audit whose only source table is `FieldPermissions`, or a "nobody can see the Salary field" conclusion drawn without an object-permission query.
absorb.why_here: This is the audit blind spot — the LLM-specific half of the practice and the reason the fact matters operationally. Pairs with the gotcha above in the same package.

(1) No such skill exists: `find skills -maxdepth 2 -type d -name '*restrict*'` returns only apex/soql-object-limits-and-restrictions and security/ip-relaxation-and-restriction, neither related. (2) The library already has a DANGLING POINTER to it — security/record-access-troubleshooting/SKILL.md:168 lists `security/restriction-rules-patterns` under Related Skills and that path does not resolve; the design intent was recorded and never built. (3) The obvious absorption target cannot take it: security/record-access-troubleshooting measures 46,557 total .md bytes against the 50 KB G1 ceiling, so the eligibility matrix, edition caps, operator constraints and applicable-features list would push it over the hard gate.
